A 49-group postscript in the code THE=972. The code was recovered from a State Department clerk’s pencil decodes of Armstrong’s 1806 despatches on NARA microfilm, merged with Tomokiyo’s partial table from a known-plaintext letter, with remaining groups inferred from their alphabetical position. All 49 groups are decoded, the last with one digit emended: Armstrong wants Russel as consul at Paris, not the Irish-born Warden. With about 160 more values the same table then decoded twelve further despatches of 1807–1810, among them the warning of February 1808 that France offers alliance with one hand and menaces war with the other. 1394 · 1116 · 1273 · 250 · 1165 · 1405 972 · 148 · 1459 · 1482 · 1201 · 821 1320 · 384 · 1280 · 1216 · 1481 · 1483 United States · diplomatic code · 1808 Armstrong's coded postscript to Madison, 1808 from John Armstrong → to James Madison Go to the full text ↓ Bourbon-l'Archambault, 30 August 1808 · Library of Congress, James Madison Papers, Series 1, reel 10 · Founders Online, Madison/99-01-02-3466 The “THE = 972” code was recovered from the State Department's own pencil decodes of Armstrong's 1806 despatches and from Tomokiyo's partial table, then applied to the postscript: 48 of the 49 groups give sense, and the last does so with one digit emended. Where Library of Congress, Madison Papers reel 10, frame 0521. Founders Online prints it undeciphered. The cipher A word-and-syllable code of about 1,600 groups used 1804–1810, labelled 972 after its group for “the”. How it was read The table was rebuilt from NARA M34 roll 13, where a State Department clerk pencilled the decode above a long despatch of October 1806. About 580 groups are known, enough for the postscript; thirteen further despatches of 1807–1810 then decoded, all but one at 95% or more. What it says Armstrong recommends Russel as consul at Paris over O’Mealy and Warden, who are Irishmen. Still open The groups of the 1,600-group code not yet recovered. Credit Tomokiyo had read about a third of the groups from one letter with known plaintext. Companion: John Quincy Adams’s St Petersburg despatches, said to be in this code, are in another, and Erving’s 1807 letter is in Pinckney’s: two legation codes .

The letter is a "private" one, written from the spa town of Bourbon-l'Archambault where Armstrong was taking the waters. Its clear text answers Madison's private letter of 20 July: it dismisses the complaints of Fulwar Skipwith (the departing commercial agent at Paris), warns that the embargo is "not felt" in France and "forgotten" in England, and says of David Bailie Warden, secretary of the legation and candidate for the Paris consulate, only that "a letter of the same character from me to the President … will give you my opinion of the fitness of M. Warden for the consular office at Paris: to this therefore I refer." The opinion Armstrong would not put in clear follows in code, as a postscript. Armstrong's despatches from Paris between 1804 and 1810 use a single large code in which 972 = the . Ralph Weber's survey of American diplomatic codes notes some forty letters in it among the Despatches from United States Ministers to France (DUSMF, NARA Record Group 59, microcopy M34, rolls 13–14). It is not the code of Armstrong's letter of 20 February 1808, a distinct system whose key has not been recovered. Its structure, as recovered: Groups run from 1 to about 1600. Each stands for a whole word ( Emperor 32, Spain 326, Minister 61), a syllable ( con 470, tion 352, ness 832), or a single letter ( s 1116, n 821, d 1001). Names are spelt out in syllables: Gu-sta-va-us , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo , Dan-ish , O-mea-ly . The vocabulary is laid out in many short alphabetical runs , not one alphabetical sequence. For instance 1–130 is one run of words ( circumstance, commerce, communicate, character … Minister … these, thousand, toward … week, without, yesterday ), 130–417 a second ( America, between, business, confide, contrary, country … Prince, Queen, reason, report, Russia, second, secret … which, whom, word, would, your ), and above 417 the syllables come in blocks that restart the alphabet every few dozen numbers (1201 a … 1230 c ; 1268 ed … 1298 ex ; 1302 ide … 1348 broa ; 1405 be … 1443 good ; 1500s fa … man … now ). Within a run the order is alphabetical, so the value of an unknown group is bracketed by its known neighbours. Common elements have homophones: re is 555, 561, 562, 869, 871 and 1379; on is 945 and 946; an 1210 and 1216; ing 1478 and 1594. Armstrong writes a point after each group; the clerk who decoded despatches at the Department wrote the plaintext in pencil above each group and a short dash above groups that continue a word already written out ( Et |–|–, for Etruria ).

3.1 The known-plaintext letter of 4 May 1806 Tomokiyo had already used the one letter for which both the coded original and a clear copy survive, Armstrong to Madison of 4 May 1806 (Founders 99-01-02-0393) on the Spanish minister's discovery of the confidential Florida proposals, to assign about 230 groups, with a few marked doubtful. This gave a base of 68 firm values used here, among them the, of, to, is, he, a, and, by, in, s, n , and showed the alphabetical layout. 3.2 The Department's pencil decodes (M34 roll 13) The main source is the microfilm itself. NARA has digitised M34 roll 13 ("Nov 12 1804 – Dec 27 1807", catalogue ID 188671172; 393 frames). Frames 0192–0201 carry a long political despatch of October 1806 (written just after Lord Lauderdale's departure from Paris, with news of "two Russian armies now entering Silesia") whose every code group has the clerk's decode written above it. A scoring pass over the roll for faint mid-grey pixels away from ink located the annotated frames; the pairs were then transcribed by eye, frame by frame, and recorded with a confidence grade and their frame/line reference. M34 roll 13, frame 0200, right-hand page (p. 13 of the despatch). Ink: Armstrong's code groups; pencil above: the State Department's decode: "she wears is nearly transparent — the late meeting of the Hungarian Diet & a pleasure camp in October which is to assemble a great proportion of her army under the command of Prince Charles can deceive no body … Two Russian armies are now entering Silesia and a third is destined for Moldavia …". Image: U.S. National Archives, RG 59, microcopy M34 roll 13, frame 0200, via the National Archives Catalog. About 500 pairs were collected this way, 352 of them legible with confidence. Merged with the 4 May 1806 values the table stands at 580 distinct groups (§7). Ambiguities in the pencil (the roll is a 1940s microfilm of faint graphite) were resolved by requiring each reading to sit in its alphabetical slot and to recur consistently across frames. 3.3 Interpolation Twenty groups needed for the postscript and the February letter were not in either source. Each was inferred from context and then checked against its alphabetical slot; all twenty fit. Examples: 1394 between 1393 purp and 1395 Italy must open a new run, and it gives ru in three independent places ( ru-in , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo ); 250 lies between 249 other and 252 own and reads ought ; 1273 between 1272 eight and 1279 Emp reads el ; 384 between 383 w and 385 was reads ward ; 1320 between 1319 li and 1325 long reads like ; 1483 between 1482 is and 1484 it reads ish . 3.4 A control text: the letter of 22 February 1808 Armstrong's private letter of 22 February 1808 (Founders 99-01-02-2733) contains about 150 code groups embedded in a clear political survey of Europe. It shares no groups of interest with the known-plaintext letter, so it serves as an independent check. With the merged table it decodes, with gaps, as follows: The ruin of Gustavus is at last resolved. Russia is to seize Finland, while France & Denmark take possession of Sweden. Denmark cannot ha[ve] very willingly … independence. And it is certainly amongst the most cruel circumstances of the British attack on her Capital that it … her … of her … and [like]wise … of conduct, and thrown her completely into the arms of France, while the Danish Minister was this morning pouring out his complaints to me upon this subject, and stating the … of his government and the means taken by it to avert the introduction into Denmark of a general army … of Hamburg waited in the antichamber, with the intelligence that the Prince of Ponte Corvo had already entered Holstein … There is no one of even tolerable knowledge and sagacity who does not see this. Yet wonderful to tell Russia not only does not … but actually assists him in accomplishing one half of the object. Can Finland compensate for a state of things which shall put it in the power of France to lock up the Baltic …? The sentences that come out whole ( the ru-in of Gu-sta-va-us is at last resolve-d , the Dan-ish Minister was this morning po-ur-ing out his com-plain-t-s to me upon this sub-ject , a-ve-rt the in-t-ro-duct-ion into Denmark , as-sist-s him in ac-com-pli-sh-ing one half of the object ) confirm the table and fix the values ru , ish , Russia (305, which the pencil on frame 0200 also gives) used in the postscript. One group there is anomalous: 946 is on in the 4 May 1806 letter but must be Gu in Gustavus (914 = gu elsewhere): a homophone, or a slip in the manuscript or the transcription.

Next to him in fit-ness is O-mea-ly , but he is like Ward-en an Ir-ish-[man] . 4.1 The people Warden. David Bailie Warden (1772–1845), born in County Down, a United Irishman exiled in 1799, naturalised American, Armstrong's private secretary and then secretary of legation. He was the front-runner for the vacant Paris consulate and got it; Armstrong removed him in 1810, and when Madison reinstated him in 1811 Armstrong protested in a letter of 3 March 1811 that Warden was "without a single grain of attachment to the U.S." and asked whether "our own country furnish[es] no native citizen willing & able to fill the consulate at Paris". The postscript shows the same animus three years earlier, and its cause: Warden was not American-born. O'Mealy. Michael O'Mealy, a Baltimore merchant resident in France since 1793 and still there in 1810 (identified in the Papers of James Madison , Secretary of State Series 10:497 n. 2). The name, of obvious Irish origin, is spelt O-mea-ly . Russel. Spelt Ru-s-el . The most probable candidate is Jonathan Russell of Providence, Rhode Island (1771–1832), a merchant in the European trade whom Madison did in fact appoint chargé d'affaires at Paris when Armstrong left in 1810; the identification is inferential, since no other document places him in France in 1808.

Collect the ciphertext. Founders Online transcriptions of Armstrong's coded letters (4 May 1806, 22 February 1808, September 1807, 30 August 1808) were gathered, and the LOC manuscript images of the 30 August letter retrieved for collation. Locate the decoded despatches. The NARA catalogue entry for M34 roll 13 was downloaded (393 frames). A simple image score (the proportion of mid-grey pixels not adjacent to dark ink) was used as a triage aid while browsing the roll; the annotated frames 0190 and 0192–0201 were confirmed by eye. Rerun over all 393 frames on 16 September 2026 the score does not locate them on its own: grey blank leaves outscore the annotated pages, and only the first, densest page of the October despatch ranks high (third of 392) once the score is restricted to the interlinear band near ink. See targets/armstrong/NOTES.md. Harvest. Each annotated frame was cropped into thirds, contrast-enhanced, and transcribed group by group; every pair was recorded with frame/line and a confidence grade (H/M). Groups seen on several frames were cross-checked. Merge and rank. A script merges the 4 May 1806 values, the harvested pairs and the inferences, ranking readings H > C > M > inferred, and renders any coded passage with unknowns and doubtful values flagged. Infer and verify. Remaining gaps were filled by context and checked against the alphabetical slot; the 22 February 1808 letter served as the independent control. Collate the manuscript. The LOC image of the postscript was enlarged to check every group against the Founders text.

Two letters of the nuncio to Maximilian II survive entirely in a numerical syllabic cipher in the Ambrosiana register Trotti 22, and Dengel’s edition prints neither. Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from the ciphertext alone and tested it on a held-out part of the first letter (0.761 against at most 0.500 for 200 control keys). The second letter reads at 95.0%: Biglia answers reproaches for a bad start to the negotiation on the connubio and discusses the offer of 4,000 foot or 2,000 horse. The cipher Digits written without spaces, words separated by 00: one digit is a vowel or bare consonant, two digits are a row consonant and a column vowel, with codes (59 qua, 97 che, 19 per) and a small nomenclator (11 S.M., 21 Imperatore, 87 connubio). In late 1565 Pius IV had sent Biglia to the Emperor Maximilian II, who asked that priests in his lands be allowed to marry (the connubio ). Rome refused and offered military help against the Turk. The Ambrosiana register of Biglia’s letters holds two letters entirely in cipher; H. Dengel, who edited the nunciature in 1926, prints neither. The neighbouring letters of the register (to Altemps, 15 November 1565; to the Emperor, 16 January 1566) are in plain text. Letter 2 is published here.

A single digit is a vowel or a bare consonant (2 e/s, 3 u/l, 4 i/t, 5 a/n, 7 o/r); two digits are a row consonant (0 m/g/v, 1 c/p, 2 s, 3 l, 4 t, 5 n, 6 d/f, 7 r, 8 soft c/b, 9 gn) and a column vowel (1, 2, 8 e; 3 u; 4, 6 i; 5 a; 7, 9 o). Values taken from context (bare 1 = c/p, 6 = f, 8 = b) count as probable at best.

Letter 2 has 381 words: 313 certain (the exact output of the frozen key), 42 probable, 7 restored and 19 unresolved. Read by sense that is 362, 95.0%, exactly the bar; strictly certain plus probable it is 93.2%. The date is restored from the year: “di decembre del sesanta” is read, the day is not. The sentences hold with holes, so the text is coherent but raw. A nomenclator value counts as certain only with three independent contexts; S.M. (11) designates the Emperor.

19 unresolved words in 7r ll. 38–41 and 7v ll. 10–23. The recipient, restored as V.S. (code 45), and the day of the date. Letter 1 (fols 6v–7r l. 27): 729 words, 604 certain, 68 probable, 17 restored, 40 unresolved by the contributor’s count; its text is not published, so the target stays partial.

The cipher A simple substitution: one sign per letter, a sign for et , and a code sign for Francesco Piccinino. How the text was obtained Birago’s key sheet is in Milan (DECODE R5316, never connected to a letter). With it the cipher reads as the same letter as the clear f. 32 mounted above it. All 513 signs are on the key, and the decode agrees with f. 32 throughout. What it says Orlando Pallavicino, reconciled with Sforza, asks Birago’s help to get home. Birago encourages him, because the Milanese mean to give Francesco Piccinino “tucto quello gli sa domandare”. Still open Nothing in the text. A leaf-by-leaf check of the 1447–48 cipher letters in the Sforza papers in Paris found a decipherment beside almost every one: a later clear copy, a fifteenth-century clear text, or glosses between the lines ( Barbavara and Pusterla is the first group written up). One leaf had none: italien 1585 f. 33. It is eleven lines from Pavia, wholly in cipher, signed by Andrea da Birago, in an alphabet unlike the others in the volume. Mounted above it is f. 32, a clear letter in the same hand and of the same day. It looked like a separate letter. It is the same letter: once the key was found, the cipher decoded as f. 32 nearly word for word. Birago sent Sforza the letter twice, once in clear and once in cipher, presumably by two routes. f. 32, the clear duplicate: “Sonno stati da mi doy famigli de orlando palauiciano. Et hame dicto per parte sua sotto littera de credenza…” Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1585 f. 32, via Gallica.

DECODE’s metadata knows only the sixteenth-century Lodovico Birago. The Milan archive’s Sforza key sheets are on DECODE as the records of Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1597, catalogued by number alone. Reading the headings of the first forty (R5301–R5340) found no. 16, R5316, dated “1450” on DECODE and otherwise undescribed. It is headed Andreas Biragus . The sheet gives one sign for each letter of the alphabet (none for b ), a sign for et , and one code sign, for “Francisco Piccinino”. The letter uses all 22 of them, and no other sign: s is 6, o Δ, n Λ, l +, e ∞, x ≡. The scribe kept the word gaps. It is the simplest cipher in the Sforza papers of these years. The key sheet itself is the Milan archive’s and is not reproduced; its signs are listed in key_R5316.tsv .

Decoded and split at the scribe’s gaps ( decode.py ), the cipher reads: sono stati da mi dui famigli de rolando palauiciano et hamme dicto per parte sua soto letere de credenza como la excelentia uostra ha concluxo cun lui et chel lo conforta ad andare a caxa ilche lui uole fare et per andargli ma fato domandare per questi famigli gli uogla dare adiuto et faure io glo dicto de darghelo et cosi faro et holo confortato ancora mi a questo maxime che sento li milanexi uoler far a [Francesco Piccinino] tuto quelo li sa domandare et in specialita tutte le terre sue ilche seguendo el dicto rolando meglio stara a caxa sua cha a milano questo per auixo de la excelentia uostra senza carigo de la quale gli daro questo adiuto et fauore Two servants of Orlando Pallavicino have come to Birago under a letter of credence. Sforza has come to terms with Orlando and urges him to go home, and Orlando means to; he asks Birago for help and an escort. Birago will give it, and has urged Orlando on. He hears that the Milanese, the Ambrosian Republic that took over Milan at the Visconti duke’s death, mean to give Francesco Piccinino whatever he asks, “and in particular all the lands”, so Orlando would do better at home than at Milan. Birago writes it for Sforza’s information, and will give the help at no charge to him. The cipher differs from f. 32 only in spelling and small forms, 35 in all ( texts/f33_vs_f32.md ): Lombard spellings: caxa , concluxo , auixo , milanexi ; “rolando” for orlando , both times; ilche for siche . It also settles one word of the clear letter. After Senza , f. 32 has a long-shafted word hard to read; the cipher has carigo there, so it is incharicho , incarico . Francesco Piccinino is the only name in code; everything else, Orlando included, is spelled out.

Two cramped signs: line 6, the g of darghelo (closer in shape to c ); line 9, an i of milano . The sense fixes both. The sign transcription was made by a subagent and checked here on lines 1–2 and line 7 (the Piccinino sign).

Translation f33_en.md # Andrea da Birago to Francesco Sforza, Pavia, 28 February 1448 (BnF italien 1585, f. 33, deciphered; clear copy f. 32) Most illustrious and excellent lord, my most honoured lord. Two servants of Orlando Pallavicino have been to see me. On his behalf, and under a letter of credence, they told me that Your Excellency has come to terms with him and is urging him to go home, which he means to do. To help him get there he has had these servants ask me to give him help and support. I told them I would, and I will. I have also urged him on myself, all the more because I hear that the Milanese want to give Francesco Piccinino whatever he asks of them, and in particular all of [Orlando's] lands. So if this goes ahead, the said Orlando would be better off at home in his own house than in Milan. I tell Your Excellency this for your information; I will give him this help and support at no charge to you. Pavia, 28 February 1448. Your servant, Andreas Biragus. *Notes.* "senza carigo de la quale gli darò": *senza carico* = without burden, i.e. at no cost to Sforza (a reading "without your commission" is possible but less natural). The f. 32 reading is *incharicho* (incarico). "Rolando/Orlando" is Orlando Pallavicino. "li milanexi" are the government of the Ambrosian Republic. Francesco Piccinino was then a condottiere in the Republic's service. Key: key_R5316.tsv

Français 5160 f1r Monsieur Depuis que Heron est party, ne s'estant rien passé de nouveau et ayant satisfait il y a deux temps aux choses que vous demandez, les ordres pour la restitution de Verue vous ayant esté adressez, je pourrois me dispenser de vous escrire, mais vous seriez et avec raison en peine sy l'ordinaire de Rome passoit par Thurin sans vous porter de mes lettres. Ce qui est porté en la vostre du xxviii du passé qui me feut rendue le viiᵉ du courant peut recevoir deux interpretations, et il sera bon de vous esclaircir quel peut estre le sens de leurs altesses, car craindre quelque inconve[?]nient au sujet du cardinal de Rets . C'est estre persuadé que l'auctorité est foible . Et peut estre le dire et le prendre pour un pretexte de s'acomoder avec les Espagnols , lesquels n'oublieront aucune sorte de diligence à faire pour y reduire monsieur et madame de Savoye. C'est une tantati f1v on forte que l'offre du mariage de li infante. Mais si la roy[ne] d'Espagne que on assure estre grosse accouchoit d'un fils, le mariage de l'infante ne seroit plus consideré comme il le peut estre dans le doubte de cogno[istre] la roine mettra au monde, ou n'ayant que des filles. Et vous devez avec adresse en faire apprehender à madame la conclusion, sans rien dire qui marque que nous l'aprehendions. Et de faict elle ne conservera nulle part au [?] si elle a pour belle fille cette princesse, n'ayant pas en sorte satisfaict les f2r grands de son pais qui le ne prennent aisement parti de plaire à li ifante . Et ce n'est pas chose aisée de regner malgré l'envin de tous, ni de conserver un devoir et un respect au prince qui peut donner ses affections à une femme et qui y est porté par ceux qui l'aprochent. C'est son affaire et de n'estre point surpris e par les assurances que les Espagnols luy donneront qu'elle aura l'auctorité entiere dans le pays et sur l'esprit de l'infante . Selon toutes sortes d'apparences nous aurons dans ce jour des f2v nouvelles de nostre armée. Elle a pris Chasteau-Porcien ou le tient encore assiegé et resolue d'y attendre celle de l'ennemy s'il eust songé de la venir attaquer, je serois trompé sy l'[?] l'entreprennent. Mais il n'est pas inconven[ient] qu'elle destache de ses gens et en couvre sa marche, faisant front à la nostre, desquels la garnison de Rethel, estant fortifiée fera perdre l'envie de l'attaquer, favorisez qu'ils sont de la saison qui est bien avancée. Sy le courrier que on attend, qui doibt porter l'advis d'un combat ou que l'ennemy ne l'a osé donner, arrive avant que je signe cette lettre, je vous feray part de ce qu'il nous aura apporté. Je presse que on execute ce qui paroist raisonnable à tous pour tenir monsieur et madame de Savoye en leur premier engagement . Mais la mort de M. de la Vieuville rend les affaires plus difficiles f3r qu'elles ne l'estoient de son vivant, parce que l'auctorité des directeurs n'est pas en sorte establie qu'ils puissent recevoir de l'argent . Et tel qui en a le secret soubz l'esperance que l'offrant à celuy qui sera nommé surintendant il en sera consideré. Jusques à present la Reine n'a point declaré qui succedera à l'autre ou sy la charge demeurera supprimée. Je suis Monsieur, vostre tres humble et tres affectionné serviteur, de Loménie Brienne. À Paris le x janvier 1653. Servien. f9r Monsieur Je croy que vous vous souviendrez bien des divers ordres que vous avez receuz de la conduite que vous auriez à tenir envers monsieur et madame de Savoye . Sy contre l'attente des gens de bien le fils s'oublioit de ce qui pouroit devoir à sa mere, il embrassoit des conseils qui levassent l'autorité ou la parence de l'otorité à la mere, qui estoient de l'assurer que la protection de f9v cette couronne ne luy defaudroit jamais et [e]n toute rencontre on feroit cognoistre au duc qu'il en avoit esté deffendu et en seroit à l'avenir protegé par consideration en laquelle se trouvoit madame royalle, et de mesnager en sorte vos parolles que l'ou en[?] f18r Les sages en jugent autrement, je m'en remettray à leurs sentimens. Pour avoir droit de se plaindre du duc de Mantoue des graces qu'il depart aux Espagnols , il faudroit l'en rechercher de semblables ou de quipolentes , et sy il s'y rendoit difficile on pouroit avec justice luy reprocher sa conduitte. Mais de luy imputer à crime la liberté qu'il donne aux Espagnols de sejourner dans ses estatz et sur ce pretexte les envahir pourroit luy faire prendre la resolution que nous f18v devons craindre qui[l] embrasse et s'oubliant de ses interests et de ceux des autres princes italiens se lie entie[re]ment aux Espagnols avec lesquels il aura peine [de] viure, soit parce que ils voudront exiger de luy des choses desraisonnables, que pour le soubçon qu'il prendra qu'ils ne veulle[n]t se rendre maistres de la ville de Casal . Et comme il est du service public ou qu'il le re f19r mette aux François ou qu'il le garde en sorte que les Espagnols ne puissent reussir de s'en emparer. Il est aussi du mesme de le mesnager . Et sa Majesté auroit peine de prendre une resolution esloignée de celle en laquelle elle est entrée à moins que le duc de Mantoue ne l'y contraignist par son mauvais procedé ou qu'elle ne se trouva si puissamment arme de par de là qu'elle peust reussir f19v à reprendre ce dont on la chassée, sans se souvenir des obligations desquelles on estoit redevable à sa couronne, et de le tante[r] inutilement on demeureroit exposé à tant d'inconveniens que il ne faut point que l'on se surprenne sy nous ne nous y portons pas à l'estourdie et avec la precipitation qui nous pourroit estre suggerée par d'autres . Le Comte Philippes que le f20r duc de Savoye despesche vers l'Empereur reviendra peu satisfait de cette Majesté sy elle ne change de pensée, ayant paru jusques à present sy esloignée d'investir M. de Savoye de la partie du Montferrat qui luy a esté adjugée et confirmée par trois traittez solemnels. Mais nous en tirerons cet advantage qu'il sera tesmoing que nous n'oublions à passer aucun office qui puisse advancer le contentement de son f20v maistre et il demeurera esclai[rci] que nous parlons avec tant de force à Ratisbo[nne] pour les interests du duc qu'il aura subjet d'en re[ndre] tesmoignage à son altesse et elle d'en deme[urer] tres obligée à sa Majesté, qui m'a paru? que [?] Savoye est attaqué en cette partie de ses Esta[ts] qu'elle employera ses forces et les moyens que Dieu luy a mis en main pour l'y conser[ver]. En peu de temps à l'aide de Dieu serons nous en estat d'estre plus considerez que du pas[sé], car la cheutte de la ville de Bordeaux augmentera les conquestes de sa Ma[jesté] et en ses ruynes seront ensevelies la guer[re] civille laquelle en ces dernieres années n[ous] a affligez, et il pourroit arriver que les Espagnols destrompez de miles chim[ères] desquelles ils se sont remplis l'esprit rechercheront la paix de laquelle ils se sont fa[it] f21r voir sy esloignez de conclure entre leurs Couronnes. Savoye sera investy et laissé en la possession de ce qui luy appartient, et Mantoue ne se tiendra pas malheureux de jouir paisiblement des Estats qui luy appartiennent et pour sa seureté recherchera ce qu'il eust peu avoir avec facilité, veu la disposition en laquelle nous estions. Sa Majesté est revenue pleine de santé et de gloire du voyage qu'elle a voulu faire, et elle a fait voir sa fermeté en diverses rencontres, comme d'avancer elle mesme la garde de l'armée, empeschant qu'on ne rompist des ponts sur lesquels celle de l'ennemy auroit peu passer sy elle avoit eu la hardiesse de venir affronter la sienne. Les soldats et leurs officiers en sont entrez en admiration, et c'est ce qui luy a fait meriter la gloire que je dis qu'il y a gaignée. Je suis Monsieur, vostre tres humble et tres affectionné serviteur, de Loménie Brienne. À Paris le 1er aoust 1653. M. Servient. Le Roy venu dix[?]. A week after the duel with Hamilton, Burr wrote to his son-in-law with ten lines in a cipher of figures and stroke signs (Gilder Lehrman GLC01523), catalogued as undecoded. It is a simple substitution, its key recovered here from the cipher alone, and all 132 signs read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter Aaron Burr to his son-in-law Joseph Alston, New York, unsigned and undated, between 18 and 21 July 1804; to be sent under cover to Charles Biddle in Philadelphia. One page in clear with ten lines in cipher. Where Gilder Lehrman Collection, GLC01523. The Institute calls the cipher undecoded and counts two sheets of numbers as the letter’s second and third pages; those are a separate set of letters of 1808 in another cipher, with their own page . The cipher A simple substitution: figures for a to l, hatched groups of strokes for m to u (the Institute’s transcript writes them as Roman numerals II to X), and three odd signs for v, w and y. Words are divided, and clear words stand between. How it was read The key came from pattern words in the cipher itself ( the , than , what , materials , in this state ). Every sign was checked on the image; the Institute’s transcript drops two words the page has. What it says “If the inquest of murder be found, what would you advise – To stand – to go to Europe or what?” Burr counts “the little band”, about 20,000 in the state, as standing firm. Still open Nothing. One word, “pleant”, is one sign off “pliant”.

Hamilton died on 12 July 1804, the day after the duel. On 13 July Burr wrote to Joseph Alston, his daughter Theodosia’s husband, that the “malignant federalists or tories, and the imbittered Clintonians” were stirring up feeling against him; on 18 July that a coroner’s jury would sit that evening “the fourth time”, with the object “to obtain an inquest of murder”, and that Alston should write under cover to Charles Biddle in Philadelphia. Both letters are printed in Matthew L. Davis’s Memoirs of Aaron Burr (1837); this one is not. It is unsigned and undated. The clear part reports that the jury “have adjourned over to Monday Eveg (23d.)”, that “The result will determine my Movements”, and that federalists and “The virulent Clintses.” are in perfect harmony: in their estimation Cheetham “is a gentleman and a soldier”. Then Burr thanks Alston for his letter of 20 June, “I concur fully with your opinions”, and goes into cipher. The foot of the page is directed “Enclose to Chs. Biddle, Phila” and addressed “J. Alston Esqr”. Burr left New York on 21 July; the jury returned “wilful murder” on 2 August. The cipher lines on the clear page. Clear words such as “made of more”, “The advice comes with double force” and “being about 20,000” stand between the cipher words. Image: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, GLC01523, the clear page, via the Hamilton Education Program.

Clear words in italics, as Burr left them; punctuation as on the page. – as you are not made of more pl[e]ant materials than myself. The advice comes with double force – The little band – being about 20,000 in this state [one word struck out] stand firm – If the inquest of murder be found, what would you advise – To stand – To go to Europe or what? – Burr is answering Alston’s letter of 20 June, written before the duel: Alston had evidently urged him to hold firm, and Burr says the advice comes with double force now. “The little band” is his following in New York, which he puts at about 20,000. The question is the one the coroner’s jury would decide eleven days later: if it found murder, should he stay and face trial, or leave for Europe? In the event he did neither. He went to Philadelphia, then to St. Simons Island in Georgia and to South Carolina, and was back presiding over the Senate in November; he was indicted for murder in New York and New Jersey and never tried.

A simple substitution, one sign per letter, with the words kept apart. The key is built in runs: letters signs a b (c) d e f 5 4 (3) 2 1 0, counting down g h i 6 7 8, counting up l 10 (written like “lo”) m n o p q r s t u hatched stroke groups numbered II to X in order v w y a hooked sign, a sign like λ, a barred circle c, j, k, x and z do not occur. The Gilder Lehrman transcript writes the stroke groups as Roman numerals, and that notation is kept here; on the page they are clusters of short strokes crossed by bars, IX and X with a cross. Twenty-one signs occur, 132 times in all.

The cipher lines were transcribed from the Hamilton Education Program image (1200 × 1400 px) in two- and threefold crops, starting from the Gilder Lehrman transcript’s sign labels and checking each sign. In line 19 the image has two words the transcript leaves out (II X VII 2 1 VII · 4 1, “murder be”). Word division and 21 signs point to a simple substitution. Pattern words gave the key: IX 7 1 occurs as a three-letter word before a noun ( the ); IX 7 5 III after a comparative ( than ); 8 III IX 7 8 VIII VIII IX 5 IX 1 after “being about 20,000” ( in this state ); II 5 IX 1 VII 8 5 10 VIII after “made of more …” ( materials ). With those values every word reads, and the key’s structure (the runs above) holds for every sign. A statistical check ( docs/_validate.py , English letter model): the reading scores −1.90 per letter against −7.51 for 200 random keys of the same shape and −4.06 for keys refitted to shuffled text: a pass.

pl[e]ant (V 10 1 5 III IX): the third sign is clearly the e-sign, so the letter gives “pleant”; “pliant” is meant or misspelt. Grade C. One word in line 18 is inked out by Burr and not read. Kline and Ryan’s Political Correspondence and Public Papers of Aaron Burr (1983) lists no letter to Alston in July 1804 in its contents; its annotation for July 1804 was not read and might mention this letter.

Where Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Zbiór Dzieduszyckich 24/11 no. 116 (DECODE R7484, R7485, catalogued “Krakow_UNK_3/4” with no shelfmark) and 26/32 nr 13 pp. 31–34 (R7476). The cipher Three-digit numbers for syllables, in alphabetical bands (a 6–8, b 14–21 … z 320–333), names heading their band (Cesarz 42, Moskwa 160, Turcy 271), mixed with clear Polish. How it was deciphered A second hand glossed the numbers syllable by syllable between the lines, and on R7485 also wrote the passage out in clear. The glosses were transcribed and checked number by number; the faint ones of R7476 were re-read at high contrast. What it says The Seraskier and the Khan, the road to Bender, the hospodar of Wallachia: “Seraskierowi Turcy wierzyc nie chcą i Han[o]wi”. Still open R7476 as a whole: about forty doubtful words under glosses unreadable on the DECODE images, so it is decoded, not read; 83 of its tokens give no word. In R7484, 18 tokens in three short passages; the faint clear body of R7485. DECODE catalogues these records with letters in other keys, which have their own pages (a different cipher in each): Brâncoveanu and Cantacuzino ( sieniawski1708 ), news from Bender in 1709 ( turculet1709 ), an adviser’s letter ( r7475 ) and a Vienna agent to Baron Schenck ( schenck1706 ).

R7485, Chomentowski: the syllabary, glossed “Seraskier o wi Turcy …”. Image: Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Zbiór Dzieduszyckich 24/11 no. 116, p. 115, via DECODE R7485. R7484 and R7485 are one archival unit, Zbiór Dzieduszyckich 24/11 no. 116 (the archive wrapper gives it; DECODE has “Krakow_UNK_3/4”). R7484 is dated Adrianople, 9 May 1713. R7485 is undated; its cipher passage is written out in clear at the head of the page by the hand that glossed it. In the writer’s spelling, as the figures carry it (restored on 23 October 2026 from a modernised version; slips in brackets): “Seraskierowi Turcy wierzyc nie chcą i Han[o]wi, i dla tego mnie prosto wo[ła]ia. Seraskier pisał do hospodara, aby mi perswadował, y namawiał, zebym na Bender iechał.” R7476 (nr 13 pp. 31–34) was bound with the Brâncoveanu letters. Code XVIII is glossed Hospodar Multański , Brâncoveanu, who was held in Yedikule from April 1714, so the letter is of May–August 1714, from Constantinople. Its partial reading, in the writer’s spelling since 23 October 2026, has “on z tod nie ruszy, puki m[u] Porta nie da takiego konwoiu” , “z listu przeietego” and “sołtan gałga uciekł do Czerkies” , but about forty words of pp. 31–32 are doubtful, under glosses that cannot be read at three to three and a half times on the DECODE images: R7476 is decoded, not read (explicit-hole share 0.524, below the bar once the doubtful words count as holes).

Although I lately sent presents to the vizier and his kehaya, the vizier received them gratefully and declared that the dispatch will come, [?that] we will not be kept long; but I know [better]. To [?pay] visits to Their Graces the envoys residing at Galata they cannot [?allow]; they did allow it indeed, but on condition that a memorial be handed in for each visit, which we could not accept for two reasons. First, that they could allow one and not another, and so make a difference without it; second, that we could by no means allow this prejudice. Better that it remain their courtesy than our condescension. [?Our detention], moreover, [comes from this], that they fear [?] - [?lest] it come from this - that they want to [?press] Your Grace's passage of the King of Sweden, and to keep us here as a pledge. But it seems to me that if [?] the Turks had sent to Your Grace about the treaty, it [?cannot be known], [?without] the [?commissioners] not seeing the treaty from the Porte, which is to be in the envoys' hands; secondly, not being secure of the friendship of the Porte, since with these documents I do not see the envoy, and such [...] you give me, Your Grace, [...] [?quicker] for their service, haste, and not [?having] [...] anyone [...] and dared. To be informed more fully [...] [?Istanbul] [...]; I may have [?word] [?information] that the Porte [?is sending] to the King of Sweden, letting [?me] know that it has finished with me; and when [he says] that he wants to move from here, this bad lord [answered] that on p. 32 himself and his realm it would fall to answer, that [...] he will not stir from here until the Porte gives him such a convoy that he may return safely with it through Poland to his own states. I believe that the removal [of ...] helped our [?solicitations] not a little, that the rebellion [comes] from here, since a few days ago an order was given to [...] that he should leave here [?]; for his labour they gave [?him] three hundred [?lion-thalers] for the road, and a [?firman] was given that [...] should also leave [...] the Khan [...]. Whether they will give them anything is impossible to find out; but as soon as I learn, I will let you know. We have news from an intercepted letter that Stanisław will make his way [?to his own people], and [...] to Your Grace a few weeks ago his plenipotentiary [...] solicited me for an amnesty, and I did not refuse to give it [?] with a certain assurance, which he refused. Now, after the business was concluded, when he insisted and [?promised] [?to give] [?an assurance], they have no [...] for that, when the Tatars at Wa[...] [?answered] and promised, there [?is] [?delay] [...], and no carts were given me to Chocim; it has not gone and will not go; besides, what [...] wrote to me [...] from [...] yet three weeks ago a [?thousand] Tatars went there towards Muscovy; and further [...] they crossed [with] the son of Devlet Giray Khan; the kalga sultan fled to the Circassians, and there with the Nogais [?and] the Circassians plundered around the Don, and two [?ships] of captives p. 33 were brought in, but the Muscovites keep a great secret of it before us. The fleet put out these days, somewhat larger than usual, yet not well [...] composed: of eleven great ships, four [?frigates] and about thirty galleys. Of the galleys some are to go to the Black Sea, to Azov, [...] went. A week tomorrow since he made his entry; today he is to have [?an audience] with the vizier [...]. We shall see what comes of it, for the Turks are sharpening their teeth on them, demanding for some goods a hundred and some tens of thalers in Istanbul; and the King of Sweden's creditors keep pressing him for money, for it is incredible what he owes to private persons, and the bill merchants will not pay unless he leaves here, saying that they have such an order from their correspondents; but he pays no heed to that and sits here firmly. I beg Your Grace to report all this at once to His Grace the Lord Crown Chancellor; they wanted [...] us to send someone on purpose, but I answered that I would myself have nothing to come with when I announced it; but, all things considered, I think that even [...] himself [...] will not linger. Mr Spiegel left today; what he did here is hard to write, enough that little of all the King's [?affairs] [?misfortunes] [...]; but we recovered [it] through His Grace the secretary. The Khan's vizier left today, they say for the King of Sweden. We shall see what comes of it. p. 34 The hospodar of Wallachia has been brought here and shut up in Yedikule on old suspicions about Muscovy and other things, such as the failure to deliver provisions to Chocim; but the present one is not to be against our interests. And [?him] they have got out of a hard prison, and there is hope that he will come back; the Sultan's mother is pressing for him most urgently. [?That apostate], I beg, should be in just [custody] and [...] brought [...], for I have just documents against him, and I do not fear his memorial here. I wrote to Your Grace in my last letter by way of Vienna that new changes keep being made here. Today [?they agree] [...] spoils the resolution. The Kapudan Pasha, having become vizier, began to change; some say that he has now been talked round, others that he is still in Istanbul. For having confidence [...] of the ferman, and to me this [...] could be. He [?went] as if to visit the King of Sweden, but since he did not want to be at his quarters, only in a third place, he came back without p. 112 seeing the King. On the next day after, the 24th of April, he held a public divan, at which war was declared sub ignoto nomine [under no named enemy]; whence non vanus [is] our metus [our fear is not groundless]. And so it was to turn towards Chocim, and us to the Yedikule; having halted at Chocim, he meant to force the Swede ad agnoscendum Stanislaum [to recognise Stanisław] or eligendum tertium [to elect a third], not wanting King Augustus for fear of the German power and the Muscovite alliance, which they also put into the ferman. A prayer for war was also made. p. 113 On the 26th this same vizier, while with the Sultan, was deposed and strangled, for which reason things are still in confusion; and although we hope that our affairs will go well, since [112] the Istanbul [...], yet they have no conclusion with us, so that Your Grace must be on guard. Yet [it is needed] that Muscovy not be in Poland, that our army not be near the border, and that the King, His Majesty, not leave Poland. Time itself [?will show] the longed-for [...] personaliter [in person] [...] I remain Your Grace's and benefactor's most humble servant Chomentowski. At Adrianople, 9 May 1713. A League-period letter in a homophonic cipher of two-digit figures (BnF Clairambault 357 f. 167). A complete contemporary decipherment is bound with it: a clear text of the first part on f. 168 and plaintext between the lines of the rest. It was transcribed and checked against Tomokiyo’s partial key, which the check extends; Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne, proposes a reconciliation with Navarre. 74 24 34 28 29 72 · 26 43 28 82 · 18 37 19 35 34 25 28 19 26 · 25 24 # g u i e n e · t r e s · c o n f i d e n t · d u [Roy de Navarre] Angoumois → a League leader · homophonic cipher of two-digit figures · 28 October 1586 An anonymous letter to a League leader, October 1586 Go to the full text ↓ BnF Clairambault 357 ff. 167–168 · a Catholic nobleman writes to a League leader during Catherine de Médicis’s talks with Navarre · listed as “two thirds of the first page unread” A complete 1586 decipherment is bound with the letter: a clear text of the first part on the next leaf and plaintext between the lines of the rest. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (100% of the cipher) The letter An anonymous letter of 28 October 1586 from a Catholic of the Angoumois to a League leader, probably the duke of Guise. Where BnF Clairambault 357, ff. 167r–168r (Gallica btv1b9001053r, canvases 331–333). The letter is not solid cipher; the writer drops into clear for a word or phrase. The cipher A homophonic cipher of two-digit figures. How it was read Not recovered here. Folio 168 is a secretary-hand clear text of f. 167r down to a cross mark; from the cross to the end of the verso the decipherer wrote the plaintext between the lines. Tomokiyo’s partial key agrees with the interlinear words wherever tested. What it says Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne and “tres confident du Roy de Navarre”, has several times proposed a reconciliation between Navarre and the addressee. The letter also covers Catherine de Médicis’s negotiation, what the Queen of England could procure, and Villeroy writing about Mayenne. Still open The transcription has uncertain words, and the verso glosses were transcribed only in part. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo published part of the key and noted that two thirds of the first page was undeciphered.

Clairambault 357 is volume XLVII of the Bossuet-era collection of documents on Henri III’s reign (1583–1587). On Gallica it is btv1b9001053r . Folio 167r is canvas 331, the verso with the date and the sender’s signs is canvas 332, and folio 168r is canvas 333. The letter is not solid cipher. The writer drops into clear for a word or a phrase, and in clear he names Bordeaux and writes “tres fasché du bon terme en quoy sont voz affaires”. F. 167r, the opening. After ✝ C and the dotted groups 45.31.73.65.21 come 67 14 98 43 28 18 18 24 , which is jay receu . Line 2 ends in clear, Bourdeaux , and line 3 begins in clear. F. 168r, the clear text of the same opening: Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps, dont jay faict communication a M r de la Forest et M r de Corbet . The names are underlined where the original has them in cipher. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 357 f. 168r, via Gallica (btv1b9001053r).

Then the writer continues in clear: bien qu’il soit catholique et loyal a . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 357 f. 167r, via Gallica (btv1b9001053r). From f. 168, with uncertain words marked [?] and passages not transcribed …: Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps, dont jay faict communication a M r de la Forest et M r de Corbet. … Indisposé d'une maladye qui ma travaillé pres de deux moys, qui a empesché vous escrire. … comme le voyage et negotiation qu'il entreprenoit [?] estoit contraire a celle de l'an passé, seroit trouvé estrange non seullement de ses amys, catholiques de France, mais des princes estrangers. Sur quoy il apportoit tout ce qu'il pouvoit de raisons. … qui luy promettoit l'asseurance [?] de ne desirer faire la paix qu'a condition qu'il n'y auroit que la Religion catholique en France … que chascun avoit faict son affaire, et l'avoit on laissé seul abandonné. … Je croy que faisant des stances [?] et autres places qui vous ont esté distraictes vous les pourrez avoir ou du moings faire congnoistre que vous n'y quictez rien. From the interlinear decipherment of the rest, transcribed line by line at full resolution on 23 October 2026 with the writer’s clear stretches between the cipher lines, and the few unglossed groups decoded with the key: Je vous diray que j'ay esté pressé, et la seule bonne volonté d'un que vous congnoissez s'y a mis de pratique, au moyen de reputation, qui s'appelle Fumée, vizadmiral de Guyenne, tres confident du Roy de Navarre, bien qu'il soit catholique et loyal a moy, a donné le retour de deça pour quelque negotiation … Il m'a plusieurs foys proposé cette reconciliation, qu'il dict luy estre aussy aysé et facille comme je la luy fais difficille et malaisée … J'ay envoyé a Rendan les lettres pour la Royne de Navarre, et croy qu'elle les aura bien tost. [J'ay] receu hier une lettre de Villeroy, qui me manda que pour contenter Monsieur du Mayne … neantmoings on se servira de ceste occasion a conclure la paix, et si l'on donne quelque advantage aux Huguenotz, l'on se fondera [sur la] rupture de ceste armée, qui nous viendra passer sur le ventre et achever de ruiner ce pauvre pays. “He has several times proposed this reconciliation to me, which he says is as easy and simple for him as I make it hard and awkward for him”: Fumée, on behalf of the King of Navarre, offers to carry the business through, with ships for an embarkation under cover of another voyage; the writer finds it “as thin as it is of little foundation”, like the Queen Mother sending the late Admiral to Florida. On the verso, Villeroy writes that the occasion will be used to conclude the peace, and if the Huguenots gain by it, the breaking up of the army “will come and pass over our bellies and finish ruining this poor country”. The writer is a Catholic nobleman of the Angoumois or Saintonge. He mentions the abbey of La Couronne near Angoulême, M rs de la Forest and de Corbet, and Bordeaux. He writes during the autumn of 1586, while Catherine de Médicis was negotiating with Henri of Navarre (the interviews of Saint-Brice took place that December). The addressee is set against Navarre as head of the other religious party, and Mayenne is named in the third person, so the addressee is most likely Henri, duke of Guise. The identification is inferred; the letter does not name him.

F. 168 is a fast secretary hand, and several phrases are transcribed only tentatively. Examples are the words after Charry , the passage on the abbot of La Couronne, and the last sentence. That sentence seems to pair protecteur with the Catholics, the reverse of what is expected, and needs the matching cipher words decoded. Only sample runs above the cross were decrypted with the key and compared with f. 168. All of them agreed, but the page has not been checked word by word. The interlinear part, transcribed in full on 23 October 2026: a few doubtful words ( son [?edit] , [?des lettres] ), one cut gloss, and a few unglossed figure strings (under “ne pourroit procurer”, in the line “si porte bien”, and the last line before the date) whose strokes run together at full resolution. The interlinear part builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.2%, under the 95% bar; the clear text of f. 168 reads at 95.5%. The sender’s signs at the foot of f. 167v (8 X X 8) are neither glossed nor in Tomokiyo’s table, and Fumée is not identified beyond his office.

Il m'a plusieurs foys proposé cette reconciliation, qu'il dict luy estre aussy aysé et facille comme je la luy fais difficille et malaisée, et en est bien sy avant depuis dix jours qu'il m'a quasy prié de la part du Roy de Navarre la bonne [?proposer], et que si vous y voulliez entendre, il se promectoit mener avec moy se negoce a bonne fin, et par ce seul moyen se faisoit ouverture de la guerre [?sy] en Angleterre, avec promesse et asseurance que la Royne d'Angleterre ne pourroit procurer des Huguenotz de la court, et que luy Fumée, si luy voulliez commettre cette charge soubz couleur d'autre voyage, il vous fourniroit d'autant [de] vaisseaulx qu'il seroit necessaire pour l'embarquement. Je ne me suis de bonne [?heure] [?avancé] de ces choses pour les trouver aussy maigres que peu de fondement, et m'est [advis] quant la Royne mere envoyant le feu admiral a la Floride; mais c'est pour vous […] juger que, vous fondant d'une part, l'on en faict autant d'ailleurs, [?a voz serviteurs]. J'ay envoyé a Rendan les lettres pour la Royne de Navarre, et croy qu'elle les aura bien tost. [J'ay] receu hier une lettre de Villeroy, qui me manda que pour contenter Monsieur du Mayne, a l'instance, prieres et requestes qu'il a faicte, son [?edit] a premier de son [?retour], comme aussy se retirent les reistres et Suisses et la reste. Car [?moy] je croy qu'en deffault qu'il y a de toutes choses, et mesmes d'hommes, il ne pourroit faire au[…]; neantmoings on se servira de ceste occasion a conclure la paix, et si l'on donne quelque advantage aux Huguenotz, l'on se fondera [sur la] rupture de ceste armée, qui nous viendra passer sur le ventre et achever de ruiner ce pauvre pays. [Il] si porte bien, [?je suis vostre serviteur]. Je [vous] envoye [?des lettres] de M^r de la Forest. Du 28^me octobre 1586. ## Notes - The recto ends "et que luy" and the verso opens "Fumée, si luy voulliez": one sentence across the page. - Glosses that correct earlier fragment readings: "Cambaronne" is "l'embarquement" (51 20 19 16 14 43 85 24 28 64 28 19 26); "Coride" is "a la Floride" (20 70 20 35 70 37 88 34 25 28), with "le feu admiral" (Coligny) before it; "Saisonne" is "vaisseaulx"; the sign before "envoyant" is glossed "la Royne mere"; ✝o is glossed "la court" and R "Nerac"; the sign after "pour" in "les lettres pour …" is glossed "la Royne de Navarre"; ⊖ is glossed "Huguenotz" twice. 73 = d is confirmed ("45 31 73 D" glossed "d'Angleterre"). - "ne pourroit procurer" is the gloss; the figures under it read "ne s…roict" (sauroict?) and were not settled. - The figure line at the end (45 31 73 70 28 47 88 28 …) is glossed only in part ("de M^r de la Forest"); the decode gives "lettre … de … rousse", so "[?des lettres]" is bracketed. Names modernised here only. ## Translation I will tell you that I have been pressed, and the sole goodwill of a man you know has set things in motion, by means of his reputation: his name is Fumée, vice-admiral of Guyenne, a close confidant of the King of Navarre, although he is a Catholic and loyal to me. He has made the return journey here for some negotiation, for I know how [things went] on this journey to Nérac and to the court, and he is well informed. He has several times proposed this reconciliation to me, which he says is as easy and simple for him as I make it hard and awkward for him; and he has gone so far these ten days that he has all but begged me, on behalf of the King of Navarre, to [?propose] it in good part, and that if you would agree to it, he promised himself to bring this business to a good end with me; and by this one means an opening would be made for the war [?if] in England, with a promise and assurance that the Queen of England could not obtain [help] from the Huguenots at court; and that he, Fumée, if you would entrust him with this charge under cover of another journey, would supply you with as many ships as would be needed for the embarkation. I have not [?early] [?pressed on] with these matters, finding them as thin as they are of little foundation, and it seems [to me] like when the Queen Mother sent the late Admiral to Florida; but it is for you […] to judge whether, relying on one side, the same is done from elsewhere, [?to your servants]. I have sent to Randan the letters for the Queen of Navarre, and I believe she will have them soon. [I] received yesterday a letter from Villeroy, who wrote to me that, to satisfy Monsieur de Mayenne at his urging, prayers and requests, [the King] has made his [?edict] at the first [?return], as the reiters and Swiss and the rest are also withdrawing. For I [?myself] believe that, for want of everything, and even of men, he could not do […]; nevertheless this occasion will be used to conclude the peace, and if some advantage is given to the Huguenots, they will rely [on the] breaking up of this army, which will come and pass over our bellies and finish ruining this poor country. [He] is well, [?I am your servant]. I send [you] [?letters] from M. de la Forest. 28 October 1586. Key: key.md

A letter of the marquis of Finale to his agents in Milan, its first eleven lines in a homophonic cipher with no decipherment of the time. Brice Dudout broke the key on eight lines and validated it on the other three (0.961 against 0.263): 95.6% of 182 cipher words, on Count Spinola and a man sent to His Majesty as trustworthy. up cOqqmenD 4m deD pO mpxeG qCaO … il beccaria ha fra le altre cose … Regensburg → Milan · homophonic substitution of Italian · 2 September 1576 · key recovered from the ciphertext Alfonso II del Carretto to his agents, 2 September 1576 Go to the full text ↓ The marquis of Finale writes from the imperial Diet to his agents in Milan about a man sent to the King as trustworthy, in a cipher whose key was recovered from the ciphertext alone. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 6 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter Alfonso II del Carretto, marquis of Finale, to his agents Lodovico Allaria and Paolo Fenocchio in Milan, Regensburg, 2 September 1576, signed “il principe marchese del Final”. The first eleven lines are in cipher, the rest in clear. Where Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera D, Del Carretto, Alfonso II, c. 10 (Lodovico Media Library). Not on DECODE. The cipher A substitution of Italian with homophones for the vowels and Latin, Greek-like and digit shapes for the consonants; word division kept, an isolated o as a null, no nomenclator seen. How it was deciphered The key was broken on lines 1–8 alone by annealing with a model of 16th-century Italian, frozen, and checked on lines 9–11 against an independent machine break of those lines: 0.961 of characters against 0.263 for the best of 200 shuffled keys. What it says Beccaria has said that no one could carry out His Majesty’s orders better than Count Spinola; the marquis will make the truth known, though the man was sent to His Majesty as trustworthy, and “neither he nor the one behind him will reach his aim”. Still open Six words of the torn margin note, and 25 probable words that depart from the key by one sign. The persons named are not identified. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed the cipher, recovered and validated the key and read the letter, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The letter came from Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 2164).

In the late summer of 1576 the Diet of the Empire sat at Regensburg, where Maximilian II would die in October. Alfonso II del Carretto, marquis of Finale on the Ligurian coast, was there and wrote to his two agents in Milan. The upper part of c. 10r is eleven cipher lines with a torn note in the left margin and one interlinear insertion; the rest of the letter is in clear. The neighbouring c. 9, a letter of 1574 to the same agents, is in clear and mentions letters “in ziffra”. No decipherment of the time is on the leaf, and no edition was found.

The vowels have several signs each (a = D, m; e = G, O, t, l; o = C, i and two groups written oPo and oP; i = u, n; u = 7 and a dotted rho), and the consonants single shapes (h = 4, d = ezh, f = d, r = e, s = a, t = x, n = k, m = h). The key was found by simulated annealing on lines 1–8 with a four-letter model of 16th-century Italian learnt from other texts; six seeds gave the same key. One value was corrected by sense on those lines (d = f, in fra , far , difficultà ), and the key was frozen. Lines 9–11 (54 words) were fixed as the held-out part before any calculation. They were broken a second time, alone and automatically, and that independent break was frozen before the frozen key was applied to them. The two agree on 0.961 of characters, against 0.263 for the best of 200 shuffled keys; the thresholds set in advance were 0.85 and a margin of 0.30. The reference is a machine break, not a clear text of the time, and the transcription was made in one pass.

182 cipher words, 174 in the block and 8 in the margin: 149 certain, 25 probable, 2 restored and 6 unresolved, all six in the torn margin. That is 95.6% without the restored words. The probable words depart from the key by one sign each; several are probably slips of the single-pass transcription, and harbbian for habbian , twice, looks like a habit of the encipherer. The Italian and an English translation are under Full texts.

Six margin words are lost or cut by the tear of the left edge of c. 10r. Twenty-five words depart from the key by one sign (D/G, ezh/reversed c, e/c, rho-o/u); a blind second reading of those signs on the full-resolution images has not been done. Beccaria, Signor Pietro and the man in question are not identified; Cavagna’s study of the marquis’s library (2012) and the agents’ papers in Genoa or Milan were not checked. Context (to be checked by a historian): Alfonso II del Carretto, marquis of Finale, at the Diet of Regensburg (1576), writes to his agents in Milan, Lodovico Allaria and Paolo Fenocchio, about a man recommended to Philip II and about Count Spinola; Finale was then contested between its marquis, its subjects, Genoa, Spain and the Empire. Number-cipher passages and a slip wholly in cipher, in letters from unnamed writers in Catalonia to the Aragonese chronicler Diego José Dormer during the French war. Brice Dudout recovered the simple substitution from the ciphertext and cribs, then measured it on two held-out sets (0.577 and 0.594, key partial): 91.7% of 290 counted words. 8.13.8.20.3.17.8.20.16. … 3.15.2.3.19.16.15. … ALASEPASO … ENGERONA … Catalonia → Diego José Dormer · simple number substitution · 1693–1696 · key recovered from the ciphertext “Ex Conde” to Diego José Dormer, 1693–1696 Go to the full text ↓ Unnamed informants in the Catalan war send the Aragonese chronicler a cipher slip on the muster at Gerona and short ciphered phrases blaming the generals, read with a key recovered from the ciphertext. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 6 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (92% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (92% of the cipher) The letters Letters signed “Ex Conde”, “El Conde” or with pseudonyms (“Rojo”, “Zabulón”, “El Chismoso”) from Barcelona, Mataró, Hostalric and Zaragoza, 1693–1696, to Diego José Dormer, and a slip wholly in cipher. The writers are not identified. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/8387, Cartas políticas y particulares dirigidas a Diego José Dormer , vol. VI (BDH bdh0000064262), views 132–197. Not on DECODE. The cipher A simple substitution, one number from 1 to 25 for each letter, written with dots between the numbers. The alphabet runs in two pieces: a–h downward from 8, i–z upward from 11. How it was deciphered The key was recovered on the short passages of views 132–168 from frequencies and cribs suggested by the clear text around them, then frozen and measured on two held-out sets: 0.577 and 0.594 against 0.033 and 0.042 for shuffled keys, under the 0.60 threshold, so the key is partial. What it says The muster at Gerona held under a proclamation of death, but leaving out the sick and the new cavalry, “all to reduce the numbers so as not to march out of Gerona”; a night with no generals and no rounds; the viceroy Villena; later, “I am an enemy of Bavaria”. Still open The verso of the slip loses every line end in the binding (79.6% of its visible words). Doubtful signs at 120 ppi, three unseen numbers, and the identity of the writers. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) found the cipher in the volume, recovered the key, transcribed, read and translated the pieces, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The volume came from Daniel Bourdeau’s BNE sweep (catalogue 1272).

Diego José Dormer (c. 1640–1705) was chronicler of Aragon, and his correspondence fills several volumes at the Biblioteca Nacional. In vol. VI, 26 of 269 views carry cipher: one line of geometric signs on view 10, which belongs to another system and stays open in the catalogue, and views 132–197, all in one number cipher. These are letters of the Nine Years’ War in Catalonia, when the French took Gerona and Palamós in 1694 and Barcelona fell in 1697. Two documents are worked: a slip wholly in cipher, fol. 190r–v (974 signs, undated, before June 1694 since Palamós is still in Spanish hands), and the ciphered words and phrases inside letters in clear (1,735 signs). Three web searches found no source naming Dormer’s correspondents in Catalonia in these years, so the writers are left unnamed.

The values are 1 f, 2 g, 3 e, 5 d, 6 c, 7 b, 8 a, 9 h, 11 i, 13 l, 14 m, 15 n, 16 o, 17 p, 18 q, 19 r, 20 s, 21 t, 22 u, 23 x, 24 y, 25 z; 4, 10 and 12 never occur and are given no value. The key was built on the training passages of views 132–168 only: frequencies, a short list of cribs fixed in advance from the clear text around the passages (“amigo” before “Dormer”, “Cataluña”, “guardias”, “caballo”, “Villena”), then annealing on Spanish quadgrams constrained by those cribs. It was frozen before either held-out set was decoded. With no decipherment of the time, the measure is the share of the decoded letters that Spanish words of five letters or more cover. On the slip (974 signs) the frozen key scores 0.577 against 0.033 for the best of 200 shuffled keys; on the passages of views 169–193 (261 signs) it scores 0.594 against 0.042. Both clear the margin by far and both miss the absolute threshold of 0.60. The slip’s verso, cut in the binding, and the very short passages of the second set pull the measure down; nothing was changed for them.

The readings were made after the measurements and counted by script, cipher words only. The slip’s recto reads at 98.5% (133 words), its verso at 79.6% of the visible words (103), and the held-out passages of views 169–193 at 98.1% (54 words). In all, 290 words: 255 certain, 11 probable, 16 restored and 8 unresolved, 91.7% without the restored words. The training passages decode to Spanish as well but are not counted, because the key was learnt on them. The slip tells of the muster at Gerona, held under a proclamation of death and twelve doubloons to informers, which left out the sick and the newly arrived cavalry and did not merge the officerless troops into the old companies, “all to reduce the numbers so as not to march out of Gerona”; 2,562 foot were found inside Gerona and 1,500 could be drawn from Castellfollit and Palamós. The passages speak of a night with no generals and no rounds and the cavalry caught unsaddled (“El Chismoso”, 3 May 1694, before the battle of the Ter), the viceroy Villena, a deposit of money at the Treasury, and later of Montalto put at the head. The Spanish and an English translation are under Full texts.

The slip’s verso: the end of all 24 lines is hidden in the binding; 14 words are restored and 7 unresolved. View 193: one word restored ( [s]e before Villena ). Doubtful signs at 120 ppi (15/19, 17/19, 5/13) are settled by the sense in the readings only. Numbers 4, 10 and 12 never occur. The writers and the pseudonymous addressees (“Zacarías”, “Astulio”) are not identified; the other Dormer volumes (MSS/8382–8386) were not opened. No human has checked the transcription against the images.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Five cipher pieces of the Emperor Ferdinand III to Field Marshal Hatzfeldt in 1641, among them the ciphered copy of a bond of the city of Aachen. Hermann Stützel printed the key in 1963 and no text; Brice Dudout transcribed and read the pieces, 94.1% of 859 cipher words. SEX CAN SAG SEX 10 SUN TAU 8 VIR ABAR W AQU 7 SUN 65 SUN 70 PSC SQ … RDIRANBEFOHLENENIMP … Regensburg → Hatzfeldt’s army · zodiac, aspect and planet signs · August–September 1641 Ferdinand III to Hatzfeldt, August–September 1641 Go to the full text ↓ The Emperor orders troops, money and wagons for his field marshal in the Rhineland in five cipher pieces whose key was printed in 1963 but whose texts had never been published. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (94% of the cipher) · On the map With Brice Dudout (transcription) · Also credited · Hermann Stützel (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (94% of the cipher) The pieces Letters of the Emperor Ferdinand III to Field Marshal Melchior von Hatzfeldt of 21 August, 7 September and 14 September 1641, an undated postscript, and a ciphered copy of the bond of the city of Aachen of 12 September, enclosed with the last letter. Where Hohenlohe-Zentralarchiv Neuenstein (Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg), Ni 10 (Rosenberg-Hatzfeldt) Bd 242, fols. 46–49, 90, 93, 95–105. Not on DECODE. The cipher Homophonic substitution with ten nulls: zodiac signs for a–m, aspect signs and planets for the rest, numerals as homophones of the vowels, no word division. How it was deciphered With the key of Hermann Stützel, “Chiffrierwesen im Dreißigjährigen Krieg” (1963), applied unchanged. Stützel says the letters could all be translated but prints none of their texts. What it says Orders, money, troops and provisions: 20,000 reichsthalers on a two-month credit and 500 cuirassiers (in both the bond and the letter), the Mandelsloh regiment, sixty Austrian ox-wagons, the Franconian Circle and the Bishop of Würzburg. Still open Fols. 97v–98r of the 14 September letter are missing from the copies; 49 words carry a scribe’s slip; the clear passages were transcribed by AI agents only. Credit The key is Hermann Stützel’s and is not claimed. Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) ordered the copies, transcribed and read the pieces, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

The five pieces are cipher blocks inside letters from the imperial court at Regensburg during the Reichstag of 1640–41. P1 (21 August, fols. 46r–49v) is endorsed “in Ziffern geschrieben”; P2 (7 September, fols. 90r–90v) and P3, a postscript in a lighter hand, follow; P4 (12 September, fols. 95r–96r) is the ciphered copy of the bond of the city of Aachen, signed by its delegate Caspar von Schwarzenburg; P5 (14 September, fols. 97r and 98v–105v) is endorsed “Schreiben ganz mit Ziffern”. Only the cipher pieces were reproduced. The copies are private research copies and are not shown here. The pieces confirm each other. P4 and P5 give the same 20,000 reichsthalers, two months and 500 cuirassiers, independently; P1 and P5 share the Mandelsloh regiment, the sixty ox-wagons, the Franconian Circle and the Bishop of Würzburg; P2 and P5 share Leipzig and a half-cannon.

Stützel broke all four systems of the Neuenstein letters to Hatzfeldt and printed their keys; group I (Ferdinand III to Hatzfeldt, 1641, Anlage 1) is the system of Bd 242. It is a homophonic substitution: the twelve zodiac signs stand for a–m in order, the aspects for o–r, the planets and the Moon for s–z, numerals are homophones of the vowels (3, 10, 25 = a; 7, 8, 65 = e; 5, 70, 81 = i; 30 = o; 4 = u), and ten signs are nulls. His table is applied here unchanged. Two features of the 1641 hands are shapes, not changes to the key: u is mostly a single loop with a cross above and b an 8 with a cross above, and y is an 8 with a cross below and x a single loop with a cross below. Thirty-seven and ten signs were reviewed on the images and corrected. A second transcriber, blind to the first, redid one page per hand (1,576 tokens) and matched 91.5% of tokens exactly and 94.4% on the key value.

The count is made by script. Of 859 cipher words, 677 are certain, 131 probable, 49 restored and 2 unresolved: 94.1% read, 98.9% by letters. The letter of 14 September reads at 95.3% and is classed as complete; the 21 August letter (93.0%), 7 September (90.7%), the postscript (50.0%) and the Aachen bond (94.9%, one word short) stay partial. Restored words are mostly one slip of the scribe in an otherwise certain word and count as holes. The German and an English translation are under Full texts.

Fols. 97v–98r, the middle of the letter of 14 September, are not among the copies supplied. Other cipher letters of 1641 may lie in the folios not reproduced and in Bd 243, which has been ordered and not received. Six letters (two words) stay unresolved after a blind review of 18 doubtful signs: one word of the postscript and two letters of a marginal insertion on fol. 103r. Glyph variants outside Stützel’s list (56 letters) were assigned to his signs by shape and context and counted as probable, never certain. Nine signs not reviewed are left as Venus or Mercury. The clear passages, the signatures and the pale abstract on fol. 49v were transcribed by AI agents, not by a palaeographer. One reader made the decipherment into sense while seeing the decryption; the key was frozen before and not changed. The Aachen agreement may be printed in the digital edition of the Reichstag of 1640/41 now in preparation (Deutsche Reichstagsakten), to be checked when it appears.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. High- and well-born, dear and faithful. High- and well-born, dear and faithful. We have duly received your most obedient report from Dorsten dated the eleventh of August, and have graciously learnt from it how, as soon as Dorsten is taken, you most obediently offer to carry out the order sent to you through Our Court War Secretary Vincentz [?] Ottman,* ‹and what way in particular you intend to take in doing so›. *Since We* ‹entirely approve of it, We have at once informed Our beloved brother, the Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria, His Highness, and reminded him to send you urgent orders to follow you in that same enterprise as soon as you have finished with Dorsten›. [?] *you will persevere in the enterprise against the said Dorsten (since you have already got so far with it), and will not need to give it up even if its surrender should be delayed somewhat beyond the end of this month of August.* ‹You shall not lack the supply of more provisions, ammunition and foot when you march up here; We mean then to send to join you the Mandelsloh regiment and whatever else can be spared from Franconia and Swabia. Translation by Claude Opus 5.5 for Brice Dudout; not reviewed by a human translator. ## P1 — Regensburg, 21 August 1641 (fols. 46r–48v) *Ferdinand the Third, by the grace of God elected Roman Emperor, at all times Augmenter of the Empire. High- and well-born, dear and faithful. We have duly received your most obedient report from Dorsten dated the eleventh of August, and have graciously learnt from it how, as soon as Dorsten is taken, you most obediently offer to carry out the order sent to you through Our Court War Secretary Vincentz [?] Ottman,* ‹and what way in particular you intend to take in doing so›. *Since We* ‹entirely approve of it, We have at once informed Our beloved brother, the Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria, His Highness, and reminded him to send you urgent orders to follow you in that same enterprise as soon as you have finished with Dorsten›. [?] *you will persevere in the enterprise against the said Dorsten (since you have already got so far with it), and will not need to give it up even if its surrender should be delayed somewhat beyond the end of this month of August.* ‹You shall not lack the supply of more provisions, ammunition and foot when you march up here; We mean then to send to join you the Mandelsloh regiment and whatever else can be spared from Franconia and Swabia. We are also sending into Franconia, to the same end, sixty ox-wagons that were destined for the Upper Rhine and have already arrived up here from Austria, so that on your coming they are ready at hand and can bring the provisions to you; and We are likewise asking the Franconian Circle Estates, by separate letters, for a contribution in provisions, to be set against their next imperial contribution, and are enclosing these letters with today's ordinary post of His Grace the Bishop of Würzburg.› *Although We have also learnt from your said letter that you have so far sent several of your reports to His Highness the Archduke by the shortest way to the main army and have had answers, We nevertheless think it safer that, besides what you can still send to Our main army by that way — which must always be done in well-kept cipher — you also send the same every time in duplicate to Us here … The two regiments in the land of Jülich, Jung Nassau and Craffts [?], you will leave standing there … until [?] the promised Rhenish guilders come in at the same time, [?] further resolution will be taken on how to deal with them … and We remain graciously well disposed to you. Given in Our and the Holy Empire's city of Regensburg, the twenty-first of August 1641, in the fifth year of Our Roman, the sixteenth of Our Hungarian and the fourteenth of Our Bohemian reign. Ferdinand. — Heinrich Schlick, Count of Passaun. — By His Sacred Imperial Majesty's own command. Jo. [?].* Address (fol. 49v): *To the high- and well-born … Melchior Count of Hatzfeldt, Lord of Wildenberg, Our War Councillor, Field Marshal and Colonel.* Endorsement: *His Imperial Majesty from Regensburg, 21 Aug. 1641 — written in cipher.* ## P2 — Regensburg, 7 September 1641 (fols. 90r–90v) *Ferdinand the Third … High- and well-born, dear and faithful. then We assure you that it shall be repaid to you at once out of the said Aachen money as soon as it comes in, and [placed] in your hands› *[?].* ‹As to the goods of the city of Bremen that have been held up,› *We leave things as they are* ‹until the city itself applies to Us about it›, *when We will decide on it according to the circumstances and to fairness. And We remain graciously well disposed to you. Given … Regensburg, the fourteenth of September 1641 … Ferd[inand]. By command … Jo. Jörg [?] Püchner [?].
