I believe this will have made you change your decision to leave and come home, as your last letter showed you meant to do; for you have judged well enough that at this juncture my affairs over there must not be left without your presence, and I am so sure of your devotion to my service that you would not want to fail me at the moment when your staying there is most necessary and useful. The continual difficulties that attend my affairs have not allowed the said marquis to leave as soon as I would have wished: he set out only ten or twelve days ago, somewhat unwell, which may delay the speed he could and would otherwise have made. Lambert has gone with him, sent by me to return to the Levant. I am sending you everything he carries, so that you may see it and add to it or cut it back as you think fit, to give the sieur de Brèves better instructions for the charge I am giving him; I wanted it to pass through your good judgement, for the experience and knowledge you have of affairs over there. I only hope that the despatch arrives safely, since I expect that by means of it the matters touching my service may begin to recover some shape there and be handled with a little more dignity and respect. Meanwhile I was very glad of the warnings you gave the English ambassador and the said sieur de Brèves, both about the particular approach your last two letters mention, so that they may watch it and prevent anything being done there to my prejudice, and to stir up the advances begun against the house of Austria, which I know the King of Spain resents almost as much, as an obstacle and setback to his designs, as if they were in his own lands. And since it is against me that his ambition overflows, I have reason to wish and seek that every means by which he could harm me be cut off from him. I think you will have heard of the war the sieur de Lesdiguières has opened on the side of Piedmont. That is reason enough to invite our friends to help him, if they wish to see themselves avenged on one who would not spare them if he had as much means to harm them as he has the will. You will do adroitly whatever good offices you can to encourage them in this. For the rest, we shall see what the Pope resolves concerning this kingdom on the despatches sent him from here, after which he will have no more occasion for the dissimulation that, I have been told, he was forced to practise until some way opened for him to show his goodwill towards the preservation of this Crown. f. 373, 7 Nov 1592 (figures of the whole cipher transcribed and aligned with the Brienne 13 fol. 104v-106v clear copy) Henri IV acknowledges Maisse's letter of 4 October and will wait for the outcome of the Gondi and Pisany mission; urges the Venetian friends to help him with money and to work on the Pope, since only his person can preserve the Crown; approves Maisse's handling of the third-party (tiers parti) rumour; the duc de Retz has left without funding the Swiss, the League expects reinforcements while Parma is ill; Lesdiguières must be supported in Piedmont; Brèves has the Levant charge and Maisse is asked to stay at Venice a little longer. A clear postscript announces Joyeuse's defeat and death before Villemur. On 23 Oct 2026 (r2f) three more words were settled on the figures: *Verac* (copy *Vivac*), *charmez* (copy *chauvez*) and *sainement*. **r2l (23 Oct 2026): the whole cipher transcribed group by group** (`f373_figures.txt`, 3,958 groups in 66 lines, f. 373r ll. 3-53 and f. 373v ll. 1-15, from the full-size views 422-423) and aligned letter by letter with the copy (`f373_figures_vs_copy.md`, `research/reading_audit/r2l_align373.py`): 3,972 of the 4,062 copy letters of the cipher passage agree (97.8%), 29 substituted, 48 missing from the figures, 13 in the code group 24. The reading now follows the figures where they differ from the copy in wording (*vous pouvez tascher de* for *pourrez tascher a*, *fort bon* for *tres bon*, *asseurer ce faisant*, *Verac sa partialité* without *et*, *combien qui* for *qu'il*, *par faulte d'estre*, *le moien que j'ay*) or spelling (*atendre, moiens, amys, ruine, reduit, cheute, flaterie, ceste, cogneues, oultre, laquele, cele, ceulx, aider, contraint, commancement, infaliblement ...*): spelling of the cipher passage is the figures', of the clear parts the original's. The postscript is in the original only (the Brienne copy stops at *mondict service*). ## Reading Monsieur de Maisse, le mesme jour que partit la derniere depesche que je vous ay faicte, de laquelle la duplicata va avec la presente, je receuz la lettre du quatriesme du passé et ay veu et bien consideré tous les poinctz y contenuz, esquelz j'ay esté fort aise que vous m'aiez representé si particulierement avecque vostre advis sur iceulx, d'autant que cela me peut beaucoup ayder a me resouldre en mes affaires selon le fondement que je puis faire sur ce qui peut dependre des moiens et resolutions de dela. Combien que j'estime devoir atendre d'en faire le dernier jugement, sçavoir qui succedera du voiage du Cardinal de Gondy et marquis de Pisany, en quoy je pense avoir si avant satisfaict a ce que mes amys et mes serviteurs Catholiques pouvoient desirer de moy autant que la raison et seureté presente de mes affaires me [?peut] permetre. Que si lesdictz amys ont la volonté qu'ilz ont declaree assez souvent de me vouloir ayder, ou si seulement ilz veulent bien sainement considerer leur propre interestz, le chemin leur en est ouvert de ma part et l'estat de mes affaires les y convie. Car ilz ne peuvent doubter de la ruine et necessité ou la longueur de la guerre m'a reduit et les effortz que le Roy d'Espagne faict pour m'acabler, que je n'aye besoin d'estre secouru, dont peu me peult plus aisement faire subsister que beaucoup davantage me relever d'une grande cheute, si par faulte d'estre assisté j'y estois tombé. Et diray de plus, sans flaterie de moi mesme et sur les discours qui se font qu'il leur suffit pourveu que ceste Couronne soit conservee, que cela ne se peult en autre personne que la mienne, dont les raisons sont si cogneues, oultre le droict et le moien que j'ay de l'empescher a tout autre, qu'il n'est besoin m'en expliquer davantage. Mais de vous mesme vous pouvez tascher de les insinuer dextrement es espritz desditz amys et les animer a conforter le naturel du Pape, puis qu'on cognoist en estre besoin, a embrasser un oeuvre si saint et si necessaire que la restauration de cest estat, et asseurer ce faisant le repos de tous les autres de la Chrestienté. Cependant je trouve fort bon ce que vous avez faict pour faire continuer une diversion d'une partie des effortz que les ennemys pourroient faire contre moy, et aussi que vous aiez rejecté sur Verac sa partialité ce qui se publie par dela du tiers party, en quoy vostre opinion n'est mal fondee que qui pense le pouvoir retenir peult estre soupçonné d'y avoir bonne part et intelligence. Mais je loue la façon de laquele vous vous y estes conduict de monstrer tout autre creance que cele la et de recevoir tout ce qu'ilz en disent a office d'amitié. Vous n'avez aussi esté deceu du jugement que vous avez faict des belles promesses du duc de Retz, duquel vous aurez entendu le retour par dela avec son frere le Cardinal, ce qu'il veult que je croye estre pour donner plus d'avancement a mes affaires. Mais le pis est que je me trouve descheu de quelque esperance qu'il m'avoit donnee d'aider a ceulx que j'ay en Suisse, et specialement pour une nouvelle levee qui n'est si necessaire, s'en estant allé sans y avoir donné provision a chose quelconque pour mon service, comme je ne doubte que le sieur de Sillery ne vous en ait adverty. Cela me vient tres mal a propos veu le licenciement que j'ay esté contraint faire des Suisses que j'avois, en retenant seulement une petite partie, et qu'au lieu que je demeure affoibly les ennemis atendent en brief un bon renfort, lequel combien qui ne puisse estre tel qu'ilz le veulent faire a croire a ces peuples de la ligue pour leur tenir tousiours les espritz charmez, et que le duc de Parme ne puisse si tost venir en personne pour estre encores fort mal disposé, si est ce qu'il ne sçauroit estre si petit qu'en l'estat ou je me trouve cela ne me donne de la peine. Vous adviserez d'en donner soubz main tout le sentiment que vous pourrez aux amys afin de les inciter a m'y subvenir de quelque chose de leurs moiens, et taschez aussi de les faire resouldre s'il est possible a ne laisser perdre le fruict du beau commancement que le s.r Desdiguieres a donné du costé de Piemont, ce qu'il seroit contraint d'habandonner comme infaliblement il adviendra s'il n'est assisté. Se seroit eslever de tant l'insolence et audace de cet ennemy que peu de ses voisins se [?pourroient promettre] de demeurer en paix et repos avecq luy, et ne faut doubter qu'il ne remuast en Italie s'il y voyoit tant soit peu de subiect, comme il a commencé de faire ailleurs. Mais avec quelque petit secours qui soit donné audict s.r Desdiguieres, il luy plantera la guerre si avant dans son pais qu'il luy sera malaisé d'aller travailler ses voisins. Touttes ces nouvelles occurrences et la direction qu'il est besoin que vous donniez pour le commancement a mes affaires de levant, en la charge que j'en ay commise au sieur de Breves, vous feront assez juger le prejudice qui seroit a mon service que vous desempariez encores cele ou vous estes, qui me faict vous prier d'y avoir encores un peu de patience, asseuré que je le vous prolongeray le moins qu'il sera possible, cognoissant bien qu'il est raisonnable que vous ayez le loisir et la commodité de venir pourveoir a voz affaires particulieres. Et quoy neantmoins la saison est encores si mal propre par deça que vous moins regretterez quelque peu de temps que vous pourrez encores donner par dela a mondict service. Sur ce je prie Dieu, Monsieur de Maisse, vous avoir en sa saincte garde. Escript le [?vij.e] jour de Novembre 1592. Henry. Revol. Je adjousteray la bonne nouvelle […] de la deffaicte et mort du duc de Joyeuse devant Villemur qu'il tenoit assiegé, […] six mil hommes [?devant], dont est demeuré plus de deux mil mortz sur la place, le reste mis en routte, [et] ont plusieurs [?noyez] dans la riviere du Tarn, et se sont [?gaignez] cinq canons et vingt six drapeaux. Il est vray […] trouver qui y [?estoient] de sorte […] pour […], en attendant que je vous en envoye le discours plus particulier. ## Notes - The copy's heading (fol. 104r-v): *Autre lettre du Roy du sept.e novembre mil cinq cens quatre vingtz douze receue le vingt cinquiesme decembre par led. Same holes: `[?word]` doubtful, `[…]` unread, `[word]` supplied. ## Translation Monsieur de Maisse, on the very day the last despatch I made to you left (its duplicate goes with this one), I received your letter of the fourth of last month, and have seen and well considered all the points in it, on which I was very glad that you set them out for me so particularly together with your advice on them, since that can help me a great deal to make up my mind in my affairs according to the reliance I can place on what may depend on the means and resolutions over there. Although I think I must wait before making a final judgement, to know what comes of the journey of Cardinal de Gondi and the marquis de Pisany, in which I believe I have gone as far to satisfy what my Catholic friends and servants could want of me as reason and the present safety of my affairs allow. If those friends have the will they have so often declared to help me, or if they will only soundly consider their own interest, the road is open to them on my side and the state of my affairs invites them. For they cannot doubt the ruin and need to which the length of the war has brought me, nor the efforts the King of Spain is making to crush me, nor that I need to be relieved: a little can more easily keep me on my feet than a great deal more could raise me from a great fall, if for want of help I had fallen. And I will say further, without flattering myself, and on the talk that is going round that it is enough for them if this Crown is preserved, that this cannot be done in any other person than mine; the reasons are so well known, besides the right and the means I have to prevent it going to anyone else, that I need not explain myself further. But you can of your own accord try to instil this skilfully into the minds of those friends, and encourage them to strengthen the Pope's natural disposition, since it is known to be needed, to embrace a work so holy and so necessary as the restoration of this state, and thereby to secure the peace of all the rest of Christendom. Meanwhile I think it very well that you have worked to keep up a diversion of part of the forces the enemy could bring against me, and also that you have laid on Verac and his partisanship what is being put about over there concerning the third party; in which your opinion is not ill founded, that whoever thinks to hold it back may be suspected of having a good share and understanding in it. But I commend the way you have conducted yourself, showing an entirely different belief from that one, and receiving all they say about it as an office of friendship. Nor were you deceived in the judgement you formed of the fine promises of the duc de Retz, whose return over there with his brother the Cardinal you will have heard of, which he wants me to believe is meant to further my affairs. But the worst of it is that I find myself let down in some hope he had given me of helping those I have in Switzerland, and especially for a new levy, which is not so necessary, since he went away without having made provision for anything at all for my service, as I do not doubt the sieur de Sillery has told you. This comes very badly for me, given the discharge I have had to make of the Swiss I had, keeping only a small part, and given that, while I remain weakened, the enemy expect shortly a good reinforcement; which, although it cannot be as large as they would have these people of the League believe, to keep their minds ever under the spell, and although the Duke of Parma cannot come in person so soon, being still very unwell, still it could not be so small that, in the state I am in, it does not trouble me. You will see to giving the friends, discreetly, every sense of this you can, so as to move them to help me with something of their means; and try also to bring them, if possible, not to let the fruit of the fine beginning the sieur de Lesdiguières has made on the Piedmont side be lost. He would be forced to abandon it, as he infallibly will if he is not supported; it would raise the insolence and boldness of that enemy so high that few of his neighbours could promise themselves to remain in peace and quiet with him, and there is no doubt that he would stir in Italy if he saw the least occasion, as he has begun to do elsewhere. But with some small help given to the said sieur de Lesdiguières, he will carry the war so far into his country that it will be hard for him to go troubling his neighbours. All these new events, and the direction you must give at the outset to my affairs in the Levant, in the charge I have entrusted to the sieur de Brèves, will make you judge well enough the harm it would do my service if you were to leave the post you hold yet; which makes me ask you to have a little more patience, assured that I will prolong it for you as little as possible, knowing well that it is reasonable you should have the leisure and convenience to come and see to your private affairs. And yet the season is still so unsuitable here that you will regret less some little time you can still give over there to my said service. With that I pray God, Monsieur de Maisse, to keep you in his holy care. Written the [?7th] day of November 1592. Henry. Revol. I will add the good news […] of the defeat and death of the duc de Joyeuse before Villemur, which he was besieging, […] six thousand foot [?before it], of whom more than two thousand were left dead on the field, the rest put to rout, [and] many [?drowned] in the river Tarn; and five cannon and twenty-six standards were [?taken]. It is true […] find who were there, so that […] for […], until I send you a more particular account of it. Key: key1.tsv

DECODE R4500, a German report in the Hesse-Kassel cipher files at Marburg, ends in fourteen lines of digits and symbols. The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone and checked against a contemporary decipherment of the first four lines. About 97% of the symbols are deciphered: the writer has laid the matter before the Emperor and the Elector of Bavaria and asks to be held excused. 6 1 2 q 5 0 9 W 6 0 · damit ich … entschuldigt sein · 0 = n · 6 = e · 12 = r · T4 = ch Unknown writer → Hesse-Kassel · substitution in digits and symbols, with a few homophones · Thirty Years’ War (volume 1635–52) A cipher report to Hesse-Kassel, Thirty Years’ War (HStAM 4 d Nr. 1218, no. 49) Go to the full text ↓ Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 d Nr. 1218, no. 49 (DECODE R4500, “partially decrypted”). One page. The letter has lost its date and signature, and DECODE gives only the volume’s span, 1635–1652. The cipher starts in the middle of a sentence (“noch nicht zu vernehmen,”) and runs until a clear closing that points to a “beygefügter Extract”. Words are separated by spaces. The system is a letter substitution with a few homophones, written mostly in digits: sign letter sign letter sign letter 5, A, 8 a (8 also o) 6 e 0 n 1 d 12 (written together) r 2, d-shaped sign s 3 g 4 h 7 i 9 u w-sign t θ c (θ4 = ch) triangle l 4 with cross stroke m crossed t b superscript w w j d

Lines 1–7 are decoded, not read: the decode of lines 2–4 is garbled, and the contemporary gloss over lines 1–4, the only control, is faded and cramped and does not align with the signs at two places (re-read on native crops on 23 October 2026, no value changed). Their partial reading ( texts/R4500_l01-07_reading.md ; […] unread, [?word] partly carried): … noch nicht zu vernehmen, die Landts[…] […]. […] [?w]ir dennoch nur [?b]eit ihr endes halber […] ursach[…] [?be]schwerungen ich ag[…] [di]eses orts halber […] dagegen denselben etwas tentiert we[r]en solte, zumahl nicht unbewandt, w[?a]s und ob en gebührender manutenirung der [?Keiserm.] Mait. und [?des] Reich[s], wie auch [K. Chur…] bei di[…]n boni […] ungelegen. Lines 8–14, the closing sentence, give German throughout ( texts/R4500_l08-14_reading.md ): … dahero ich nicht unterlassen sollen, die notturft dieser Vestung so wol allerhöchst ihrer Kays. Maiestet als auch ihrer Churf. Durchl. in Bayern ohnlängst nochmals allerunderthenigst und underthenigst anzudeuten, damit ich aus allen fall entschuldigt sein und dessen, meinem gebührenden bericht an gehörigen ort, nicht ermangeln möchte. In English (lines 1–7 only in part): something should be attempted against them, especially since … the maintenance of His Imperial Majesty and the Empire …; I therefore could not fail, lately and once more, to set out the needs of this fortress most humbly to His Imperial Majesty and humbly to His Electoral Highness of Bavaria, so that I may be excused in any event, and not fall short of my duty to report to the proper place.

Simulated annealing without word spaces gave only frequency noise. After a second transcription that kept the word gaps and treated the joined “12” as one symbol, a homophonic solver scored with the de-1500s model produced recognisable words, and those words fixed the key. The gloss over lines 1–4 then settled the superscript symbol (w) and 8 (o). The gloss does not follow the cipher line by line; its phrases occur in cipher lines 3–5, in order. All 126 records of the volume (R4452–R4577) were downloaded to look for the key or a clear copy; none was found.

The last nine symbols of cipher line 1, cramped under the faded gloss: not deciphered. Lines 1–7 as a whole are decoded, not read: lines 2–3 do not build, and the faded gloss cannot settle them; only a better image could. Single symbols in line 7 (“[bey diesen]”): conjectural, graded M. No longer uncertain (corrected 30 September 2026). Line 9: the symbols at its start had been taken as blotted and the phrase supplied as “dieser [sachen]”. They are clear on the scan and give “ser ue st ung” with the key unchanged, so the phrase is “die notturft dieser Vestung”, the needs of this fortress (9 is u, which also stands for v). Line 11: the symbols before “underthenigst” give “s a l er”, and the triangle carries a doubling bar (ll), so the text is “nochmals allerunderthenigst und underthenigst”, the usual pair for the Emperor and an Elector; no word is supplied. Writer, recipient and date are unknown. The deferential tone toward the Emperor and Bavaria makes him an officer or agent reporting to Kassel from the imperial side; “dieser Vestung” places him in a fortress.

Ten cipher lines in a letter from the imperial court at Ratisbon on the war against the Lutherans. A contemporary clear translation on the next leaf covers the whole passage, so WAINUT rebuilt the key from it and read all 62 words. Qua … n j c H d o 8 Lo & l 8 + u Z f s j c H … (ten lines of homophonic substitution, with clear words mixed in) Ratisbon → Milan · homophonic substitution · 12 June 1546 · read from existing decipherment Marignano to Ferrante Gonzaga, 12 June 1546 Go to the full text ↓ A general at the imperial court reports to the governor of Milan that the war against the Lutherans is decided; the cipher passage is deciphered from the translation made at the time. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription, verification) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Gian Giacomo Medici, marquis of Marignano, writes from Ratisbon on 12 June 1546 to Ferrante Gonzaga, governor of Milan. The letter is mostly in clear; ten lines on c. 13r are in cipher. Where Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera M, Medici, cc. 13–16. The record notes that c. 14 “contiene traduzione della porzione cifrata”. Not in the catalogue. The cipher A letter substitution with homophones, in signs that look like Latin letters and others. A small sigma-shaped sign is a null, and eti is a code for V. Ecc.a . Double letters are written once. Words are divided by commas and slashes. How it was deciphered This is a transcription job, not a break. The contemporary clear translation at the top of c. 14r covers the whole cipher passage, and the key was rebuilt from it. What it says The war against the Lutherans is decided. Provisions are being made, and the writer sends to Milan and Genoa for men for the artillery. Still open Three signs are doubtful, the f or sigma in two words is unsettled, and four groups of dotted vowels (nulls or stops) are not proved either way. No human palaeographer checked it, and the images were not seen here. Credit WAINUT (an AI company) transcribed the signs, rebuilt the key and read the passage with AI agents viewing the images.

From the imperial court at Ratisbon, Marignano tells Ferrante Gonzaga that the war against the Lutherans is decided. After the clear opening come ten lines of cipher (306 signs and groups); the letter then goes on in clear, mentioning the despatch to Milan and Genoa for men for the artillery. c. 13v carries the date and signature, and the address and the docket “Il M.se di Marignano” are on c. 14v. Below the translation on c. 14r is a clear postscript about Sebastiano de Perego, which is not part of this reading.

Vowels have two or more signs (for example a is j or 8 ). Several sign names carry two values; most are probably two similar shapes merged under one name in the transcription, and they are flagged in key.tsv . The key was rebuilt step by step from the clear translation and frozen before the final counts. The check script aligns each reading with its decryption letter by letter and fails on any departure from the signs that is not marked.

All 62 cipher words read as sense. 55 come verbatim from the signs and 7 carry a marked repair: four double letters restored, two doubtful signs and one sign read against its value. 59 of 62 (95.2%) have no departure from the signs other than the scribe’s single-written double letters. An independent check gives 60 of 62 (96.8%). Seven clear words in the passage are not counted. The Italian and an English translation are under Full texts.

Three doubtful signs ( di [?l]a , aviso [?a] , and pu{b}lica , where the word is confirmed by c. 14r). Whether the doubtful f or sigma in actende and auctore is one or the other makes no difference to the letter value. The four dotted-vowel groups {onu} , {nao} , {nou} and {anu} . The transcription and key were produced by AI. No person checked them against the images, which were not seen here.

Where Archives nationales d'outre-mer, COL C8 A 79 f. 70, C8 A 79 f. 19 and C8 A 81 ff. 114–116, catalogue item 1203. No decipherment is filed with any of them. The cipher A numeric nomenclator, values 1–845 so far: single letters, syllables and whole words (428 = la Guadeloupe, 268 = garnison), written as dotted numbers inside clear French. How it was read Five letters of 1779 in the same series carry the clerks' decipherment above the groups. Pairing each number with its gloss gave a key of 507 values, which then decoded the three letters as French sentences and passed a statistical check. What they say In 1780 Bouillé sends 400–500 men to Grenada and notes that his regiment is 359 men short; in November the stores of Martinique are “infiniment précaire”; in 1782 he has put every island in a state of defence and sees his own presence becoming useless. Still open Scattered holes in each letter; 538 behaves as two values; a letter of 1779 from Grasse is another code (no key material); the minister's own minutes need a visit to the archive. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) read two 1778 letters of the same series first, with a key from the same glosses; see his write-up . The clerks of 1779 wrote the glosses the key comes from.

Bouillé wrote to the Navy minister every month during the war of 1778–1783, and part of each despatch went into a number code. The ministry's copies are the series C8 A of the Archives nationales d'outre-mer. The three letters here have no decipherment filed with them, and the ANOM calendar lists them as ciphers. The cipher is a numeric nomenclator whose numbers stand for letters, syllables and whole words; it is not the 1761 Windward Islands code or the 1765 d'Ennery form (both tested and ruled out). The letters of 1778 (C8 A 77 ff. 88 and 101) in the same code were deciphered first by Brice Dudout on 28 October 2026; they are described on that page and are not read again here. The key below was recovered independently, before his page was found, and agrees with his on the same words (667 = im, 138 = Dominica, “effectifs”).

The ministry's clerks sometimes wrote the decipherment above the numbers. C8 A 78 f. 123 (11 October 1779) carries it above every group, syllable by syllable, and so do parts of f. 3, f. 5, f. 31 and f. 144 of the same volume. Reading each number together with the word over it gives the key directly, with no search at all. C8 A 78 f. 123: the number 587 carries “la”, 361 “de”, 428 “la Guadeloupe”; “reçu”, “fortifi-ca-tions” and “nouvelles” are spelled syllable by syllable. Image: Archives nationales d'outre-mer, COL C8 A 78 f. 123 (image FRANOM23_C8A_078_0197), via recherche-anom.culture.gouv.fr. The pairing was done from the images over several passes: f. 123 first (77 distinct groups), then f. 3 and f. 31, then f. 5 and the whole of f. 144 (thirteen further pages, read by two helper agents). The key stands at 507 groups, with its provenance for every value in key_bouille.tsv . A value read in two letters is stronger than one read in a single one; where letters disagree, the commoner value is kept and the conflict listed. Several early conflicts were settled on the images or by the new letters (46 = avec, not aux; 279 = non, not pri; 25 = même).

Letter no. 415 is a re-sent copy (“renvoi du 25 octobre 1780”), fourteen lines of cipher after the clear “J'ai l'honneur de vous envoyer”. 182 of its 190 groups have a value. The opening of f. 70 (no. 415): the clear words run into the dotted numbers; 250 287 … is “l'état …”, the groups 267 and 138 are the islands of Martinique and Dominica. Image: Archives nationales d'outre-mer, COL C8 A 79 f. 70 (image FRANOM23_C8A_079_0107), via recherche-anom.culture.gouv.fr. [J'ai l'honneur de vous envoyer] l'état de la situation des troupes de la Martinique, [de] la garnison de la Dominique et [de] la Grenade au 1 er de ce mois, et celui de la garnison de Saint-Vincent au 1 er avril dernier, n'ayant pas encore reçu de M. du Montet son état au 1 er mai. Je compte envoyer [incessamment] à la Grenade quatre à cinq cents hommes de plus … Il manque au régiment de la Martinique trois cent cinquante-neuf hommes pour le mettre au complet, et il est bien intéressant de lui faire passer des recrues. The last two lines of f. 70. A later hand pencilled “int-er-objet-sa-nt de lui faire passer des recrues” over the final groups; it was not used for the reading, and it agrees with it. Image: Archives nationales d'outre-mer, COL C8 A 79 f. 70 (image FRANOM23_C8A_079_0107), via recherche-anom.culture.gouv.fr.

Letter no. 23, a return of provisions, has twelve lines of cipher on image 0029; 147 of 157 groups have a value. The margin carries the cipher heading “Martinique, mois de novembre”. [J'ai l'honneur de vous envoyer] l'état des subsistances existantes dans les magasins du roi et dans [ceux] du commerce au 1 er de ce mois de novembre … Les magasins du commerce sont un peu pourvus par le retour de deux bâtiments du convoi et l'arrivée d'un neutre, mais la consommation est si considérable que notre situation à cet [égard] est toujours infiniment précaire.

Letter no. 12 runs over ff. 114–116 with cipher blocks on five images (three more are covered by modern translation slips): 1,244 of 1,297 groups have a value. The key reads straight through it. Je suis préparé à tous les événements : j'ai eu le temps de mettre toutes les colonies du roi en état de défense … Vous jugerez par l'état des garnisons que je vous envoie qu'à l'exception de la Martinique, où il ne reste plus que deux mille hommes de troupes réglées … Si je ne suis point employé dans les opérations qui doivent avoir lieu … ma présence devient inutile ici. He describes ships sent to cruise off Barbados to cover a convoy from New England and the arriving squadron, the frigate Amphion kept at Martinique, despatches for Spanish Trinidad, and the garrisons of Saint Christopher and Saint Eustatius, taken in the previous year. Complete decryptions and English translations of all three letters are in the full texts below.

The 1,748 read groups of these letters and of f. 88 were scored with a French letter model against random keys of the same shape and against keys fitted to shuffled text: the reading scores −1.99 per letter, random keys −3.13, a key fitted to shuffled text −2.25, and the verdict is a pass. This tests that the key keeps reading new text, not that each single value is right; 538 is the one value that does not hold still (“sept” in the number words of the f. 101 enclosure, “fe” in “effectifs” on f. 88, where f. 123 has 658).

Each letter still has holes: 8 of 190 groups on f. 70, 10 of 157 on f. 19, 53 of 1,297 on f. 114, filled by context where the sentence allows and bracketed where it does not. The three letters read as sentences with scattered holes, so the target stays “read in part”. 538 is polyphonic or a copyist's slip; 307 reads “ba” in “la Barbade” and “ou” in one gloss of f. 3. C8 A 78 f. 1 (Grasse, 4 April 1779, headed “Chiffre de 1777”) is a different code: about 60% of its groups get a value from this key but the result is not French. No key material. The minister's ciphered minutes (C8 A 77 ff. 31, 43) and the Navy's colonial keys MAR/G/178 need a visit to the archive. All of these readings were made by Claude, with no historian's check against the manuscript (grade B in the full texts).

The project's first run of “weight-space programming” used this target: an LLM edits the key under a fixed budget of 25 language-model scores. On the 1778 letter the editors recovered only 2–4 of 45 blanked groups, and about 40% of their fills held against the new glosses, so an editor's fills are leads, not readings. The scripts and results are in research/keyedit/ .

Vous jugerez par l'état des garnisons que je vous envoie qu'à l'exception de la Martinique, où il ne reste plus que deux mille hommes de troupes réglées, mais sur laquelle je n'ai [pas] de crainte, elles ont toutes des garnisons suffisantes et proportionnées. La Grenade seule aurait exigé deux ou trois cents hommes de plus, et pour y suppléer j'ai envoyé le vaisseau l'Expériment, qui n'est d'aucun service ici et dont les troupes et l'équipage pourront se réunir à la garnison en cas de siège. La Guadeloupe, attaquée par dix mille hommes, doit [tenir] deux au moins [...] trois mois. [Deux vaisseaux, deux frégates et une cor]vette doivent être partis aujourd'hui de Saint-Pierre pour aller croiser au vent à la latitude de la Barbade jusqu'au [...]. Quand même je ne réussirais pas à y porter un secours de mille à douze cents hommes, ce qui me paraît aisé et ce qui doit la garantir d'être prise. La Dominique doit tenir autant que la Grenade, à l'exception qu'il me serait aisé de jeter un secours dans la première et presque [impossible] d'en faire parvenir un dans la seconde. Saint-Christophe ne peut être prise que par famine et [a] pour six mois de vivres dans la forteresse. Les petites îles de Saint-Vincent et [...] exigent un siège, qui est une opération longue et meurtrière dans ces pays-ci ; mais je ne peux [at]tendre de les sauver si elles sont attaquées, sans courir le risque de compromettre infiniment les secours que je voudrais y porter, et qui ne seraient pas d'un grand [...]. [Pour répondre à votre dépêche du 10 octobre et vous instruire des] dispositions que j'ai faites relatives [à la défense] : deux vaisseaux, deux frégates et une corvette doivent être partis aujourd'hui de Saint-Pierre pour aller croiser au vent à la latitude de la Barbade jusqu'au vingt de ce [mois], afin d'intercepter les bâtiments ennemis qui pourraient être séparés du convoi d'[...] et [...] attendus de la Nouvelle-Angleterre, chargés de troupes et de munitions de guerre. À cette époque deux frégates iront croiser au vent de [...], sur la pointe Saint-Gilles ; elles communiqueront, au moyen d'un ou deux petits bâtiments intermédiaires, avec cette île, où je ferai parvenir à M. le vicomte d'Arnot, qui y commande, les nouvelles que je recevrai et qui pourront intéresser l'escadre et le convoi. Quant aux deux vaisseaux, ils continueront leur croisière jusqu'au vingt ou vingt[-cinq] janvier ou jusqu'à la rencontre de l'escadre, à laquelle ils se réuniront d'après l'ordre de l'officier français qui la commande. Je garde ici l'Amphion et quelques frégates pour être employées aux circonstances ; j'enverrai une frégate commandée par un [...] officier intelligent à la Trinité espagnole, et j'écrirai au gouverneur, homme de beaucoup de mérite et dans lequel on peut avoir toute confiance, ainsi que toutes les [mesures] pour la sûreté de l'atterrage du convoi et tous les moyens propres à instruire l'officier français qui commande l'escorte. Je n'ai pu trouver sur [...] le port [...] les escadres [...]. [...] doivent se réunir de [...] que je prends le parti d'envoyer à la Trinité espagnole les bâtiments que je destine à porter les dépêches de M. de Vaudreuil et les avis pour M. de Solano, en priant le gouverneur de cette île de lui procurer un [pilote] et les moyens de remplir sa destination. Vous jugerez par l'état de situation des troupes des [îles] que le corps destiné à les défendre est de quinze hommes plus faible qu'il n'était l'année dernière à cette époque, depuis laquelle deux îles ont été mises sous la domination du roi, Saint-Christophe et Saint-Eustache, qui exigent une garnison de seize hommes entre elles deux [...] ; le roi peut être [...] sur ses colonies [...] et il peut être assuré [que je] ferai tout ce qu'il est possible à des hommes de faire. Si je ne suis point employé dans les opérations qui doivent avoir lieu au [...] et si, après l'arrivée et le passage des forces de mer et de terre dans ces mers, je me trouve dans la situation de n'avoir [rien] à attaquer ou à défendre, ce qui est très vraisemblable, ma présence devient inutile ici. Translation f114_en.md I was to sail [...] with the Amphion and some frigates and troops to capture a convoy that the English were assembling at Tortola [...]. I am prepared for every eventuality: I have had time to put all the king's colonies in a state of defence; they are perfectly supplied with munitions of war and provisions, having no less than six months' food; I have sent reinforcements of troops and munitions of every kind to all of them. You will judge from the state of the garrisons that I send you that, apart from Martinique, where only two thousand regular troops remain, but for which I have [no] fear, they all have sufficient and proportionate garrisons. Grenada alone would have needed two or three hundred more men, and to make up for them I have sent the ship the Experiment, which is of no use here and whose troops and crew can join the garrison in case of siege. Guadeloupe, attacked by ten thousand men, must [hold out] at least two [...] three months. [Two ships, two frigates and a cor]vette are to have left Saint-Pierre today to cruise to windward at the latitude of Barbados until [...]. Even if I do not manage to carry a relief of a thousand to twelve hundred men there, which seems easy to me and which should save it from being taken. Dominica should hold as long as Grenada, except that it would be easy for me to throw relief into the first and almost [impossible] to get any into the second. Saint Christopher can only be taken by famine and [has] six months' provisions in the fortress. The small islands of Saint Vincent and [...] require a siege, a long and murderous operation in these countries; but I cannot [expect] to save them if they are attacked, without running the risk of greatly compromising the relief that I wish to carry there, which would not be of great [...]. [In answer to your despatch of 10 October and to inform you of] the dispositions I have made [for the defence]: two ships, two frigates and a corvette are to have left Saint-Pierre today to cruise to windward at the latitude of Barbados until the twentieth of this [month], in order to intercept enemy vessels that may be separated from the convoy of [...] and [...] expected from New England, laden with troops and munitions of war. At that time two frigates will cruise to windward of [...], off Saint Giles point; they will communicate, by means of one or two small intermediate vessels, with that island, where I shall send word to the vicomte d'Arnot, who commands there, of the news I shall receive that may concern the squadron and the convoy. As for the two ships, they will continue their cruise until the twentieth or twenty-fifth of January or until they meet the squadron, which they will join on the order of the French officer commanding it. I keep the Amphion and some frigates here for use as circumstances require; I shall send a frigate commanded by an intelligent officer to Spanish Trinidad, and I shall write to the governor, a man of great merit in whom one can have every confidence, as well as all the [measures] for the safety of the convoy's landfall and every means suitable to inform the French officer commanding the escort. I could not find [...] the port [...] the squadrons [...]. [...] must assemble [...] so that I decide to send to Spanish Trinidad the vessels I intend to carry M. de Vaudreuil's despatches and the advice for M. de Solano, asking the governor of that island to find them a [pilot] and the means of fulfilling their mission. You will judge from the state of the troops of the [islands] that the force intended to defend them is fifteen men weaker than it was at this time last year, since when two islands have been brought under the king's rule, Saint Christopher and Saint Eustatius, which require a garrison of sixteen men between the two [...]; the king may be [...] on his colonies [...] and may be assured [that I] shall do all that men can do. If I am not employed in the operations that are to take place at [...] and if, after the arrival and passage of the sea and land forces in these seas, I find myself in the position of having [nothing] to attack or to defend, which is very likely, my presence here becomes useless. Two Union telegrams to General Robert Milroy in Stager Cipher No. 7, a word route transposition in six fixed columns whose indicator word gives the number of lines. Richard Bean solved them with Claude Opus 5 in 2026; two routes of Milroy’s own copy were checked here against his grid and nothing was added. China quest whether transportation in reach what is if bully imboden by to forward … If your information as to Imboden is confirmed, let me know by what route you shall try to reach him … Union telegrams to General Milroy · Stager Cipher No. 7, word route transposition · 1861–62 · known key applied The Milroy telegrams, 1861–62 Go to the transcriptions ↓ Two Civil War telegrams enciphered by writing words into six columns in a set route, solved by Richard Bean in 2026; two of their routes checked here on Milroy’s own copy. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 31 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Credits · Richard Bean (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The telegrams Cox to Milroy, 3 December 1862, and a telegram of Bascom, 4 December 1861, both among the papers of General Robert H. Milroy. Where The text used here is Milroy’s own copy of the Cox telegram, as transcribed in a Jasper County Library lesson plan. The transcription is unreliable in places. The cipher Stager Cipher No. 7: the words are entered into a grid of six fixed columns, up or down each column in a set sequence, and the plaintext is read along the rows. An indicator word gives the number of lines: “China” is 8, “Turkey” 12, “Austria” 9. How it was read Richard Bean, working with Claude Opus 5, published the solution in 2026 (listed as solved on Tomokiyo’s cryptiana). Here, one run and one reversed run of Milroy’s copy were found to fit Bean’s grid. What it says Cox asks Milroy, if his information about Imboden is confirmed, by what route he will try to reach him and how far forward on the Moorefield road. Bascom reports that General Kelley has been told by General Halleck to hold himself in readiness to move. Still open Our own route search did not converge, so no part of the decipherment is independent; the full Bascom text is on the cryptiana page only. Credit Richard Bean found the system and the plaintexts. This page records a check and adds nothing to them.

The Cox telegram, as Milroy’s copy gives it, is a run of ordinary English words in the wrong order, with an indicator word in front (“China”) and a few words that are nulls or code words: China quest whether transportation in reach what is if bully imboden by to forward Jrsisert also are Cumberland hole that the will the him route confirmed your health information let you also morsefield supply roads with stine at connection's for co your far try know w to fight as me shall hour road your and Kelley x Guusmat road country you of communications avoid you drink to your direction extest Mountain Moonfield morning star answer from can - Winchester by being

The words of the message are not changed; their order is. They are written into a grid of six columns, going up or down each column in a fixed sequence, and the message is read off the rows. “China” as the first word means eight lines. The result is a telegram that looks like a list of words but that a telegraph clerk could undo with the route.

Bean’s decipherment of the Cox telegram begins “If your information as to Imboden is confirmed, let me know by what route you shall try to reach him, also how far forward in the Moorefield Road…” The Bascom telegram begins “General Kelley having received directions from General Halleck to hold himself in readiness to move under orders from army head quarters…” The check here ( route.py in the repository folder) used Milroy’s copy. The run “imboden by to forward” is column 6, rows 1 to 4, read downward, and the run “what is if” is column 1, rows 3 to 1, read upward. Both agree with Bean’s grid. A blind bigram search over all six-column routes did not converge, because the transcription is unreliable and the grid holds nulls and code words, so it was not pursued.

The transcription of Milroy’s copy has misread words (“Jrsisert”, “Guusmat”, “extest”), so the full decipherment cannot be reproduced from it unaided. Only two routes were checked. The rest of the grid, and the Bascom telegram, rest on Bean’s published solution.

Six DECODE records catalogued with no sender and dated 1566 are, by the archive’s description of the volume, Cardinal Alessandrino’s ciphered letters of 1567 to the nuncio at Madrid. George Lasry’s reconstructed polyphonic key, attached to the records, was applied unchanged; each digit stands for two letters, and a language model chose between them to decrypt all six. Subjects: Philip II’s journey to Flanders, Borromeo against the Milan senate, the unconfirmed archbishop of Cologne, and advice to imprison the Constable Montmorency. 1 0 1 0 · 7 6 5 2 7 6 7 4 · 0 1 0 2 · 0 8 6 7 1 2 3 2 8 4 1 5 … [Nostro Signore] desidera … certificato … 1 = u|t · 2 = i|m · 4 = a|l · 5 = o|s · 6 = e|n · 7 = d|r · 0 = null · 1010 = Nostro Signore · 2090 = che Rome → Madrid · polyphonic cipher, two letters to a digit · 1567 Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 from Cardinal Alessandrino → to G. George Lasry’s key (2020) is attached to the records, with no plaintext posted. Applied with a language model it gave only fragments; a contemporary decipherment of one letter and three copies of another, found among the record’s images, supplied the missing code values, and all six are now deciphered word by word. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter Six ciphered enclosures of Cardinal Alessandrino (the cardinal nephew) to the nuncio in Spain, Giovan Battista Castagna, in 1567, 7,817 digits in all. Where Vatican, ASV i. 1025, Segretario di Stato, Spanish nunciature papers; DECODE R85–R90 (catalogue item 261), listed with no sender, no recipient and the volume’s opening date, 1 January 1566. The cipher A polyphonic cipher where each digit stands for two letters, with a nomenclator of four-digit groups, dotted pairs and 0 as a null. How it was read George Lasry’s 2020 key, attached to the records with no plaintext posted, is the same key byte for byte that decrypted Alessandrino’s 1568 letters. The same decoder, run unchanged, resolves all six. What it says The Pope wants Philip II to make his journey to Flanders; the archbishop of Cologne is to be deprived; the King of France should imprison the Constable Montmorency and his son until Condé and Coligny lay down their arms. Still open One recurring word, some dotted groups outside Lasry’s list and single-letter choices. The printed correspondence (Serrano 1914) could not be reached.

DECODE lists the six as “ASV i. 1025, Segretario di Stato, doss. I”, records ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_I-1 to I-6, with the archive’s list of the volume’s units in the comments. Their folios are 165r (R85), 236r (R86), 249r–250r (R87), 301r–v (R88), 314r–v (R89) and 324r (R90): 7,817 digits in all, transcribed for DECODE by RebAn in 2016. Each cipher is the enciphered part of a letter that opens in clear: f. 163r, before R85, is about hurrying the archbishop of Toledo, Bartolomé Carranza, to Rome; f. 299r, before R88, is about “il negotio di Milano”. No decipherment is written on those pages. Lasry’s key “ASV – S6” (24 October 2020), on every record: 1 u|t · 2 i|m · 3 f|g · 4 a|l · 5 o|s · 6 e|n · 7 d|r · 8 b|c · 9 p|z · 0 null, with a nomenclator of four-digit groups X0Y0 (1010 Nostro Signore, 2090 che, 3010 Re, 4030 S. M.tà, 8010 Re di Francia …) and dotted pairs. The full table is on the 1568 page . The decipherment of R87 and the copies corrected and extended it (22 October 2026): 8010 is [la] Regina [di Francia] , the Queen Mother, not the King; 4010 is S.M. (Philip II in R87, Charles IX in R85, R88 and R89), not Sua Santità; 1020 essere, 1040 lettera, 8030 religione, 8070 ugonotta, 8080 heretici, 8090 havere; 3 0̇ 9 is qua , and 209 is chi as a syllable.

R88 and R89 are two copies of one cipher, and R90 continues R89; the damaged figures of R88 (rows 10–17 of each page) are supplied from R89. From the reading of R89 (f. 314r–v, texts/R89_reading.md ): … ma [la] Regina è tanto timida et crede tanto al cancelliere, a Morviglier, a Limoges et a l’Abaspina, suoi consiglieri, che non si sa risolvere a far cosa buona, et va sempre medicando il male col peggio. … Et per dirvi, [la] Regina a iuditio mio non è ugonotta, credo bene che sia una mala cristiana … In tanto vi dirò questo solo, che se S.M. facesse mettere in una prigione sicura il Conestabile et Memoransi suo figliolo, protestandoli che se in termine di tre giorni non facessero deponere le armi al Amiraglio et al principe di Condé li faria tagliare il capo, vedereste che si metteria fine a tanti tumulti assai presto … [la] marks a word the code carries without the article; … marks a stretch left out here. “The Queen is so timid, and trusts so much in the Chancellor, Morvilliers, Limoges and l’Aubespine, her counsellors, that she cannot bring herself to do any good, but always doctors the evil with worse … in my judgement she is no Huguenot; I truly believe she is a bad Christian … Meanwhile I will tell you only this: if His Majesty had the Constable Montmorency and his son put in a secure prison, warning them that unless within three days they made the Admiral and the Prince lay down their arms he would have their heads cut off, you would see an end to these troubles, and soon, for it is believed the whole plot was laid with the knowledge of the Constable and his son … and the Queen will find herself deceived one day, and repent too late of not having believed the good.” The passage is a chapter of a letter from France to a gentleman at the Roman court, passed on so that the nuncio can use it with Philip II. Earlier decodes had made the subject the King of France: code 8010, which the decipherment of R87 shows to be the Queen Mother. The Prince is Condé and the Admiral Coligny, in arms after the Surprise of Meaux (28 September 1567); the Constable died of his wounds at Saint-Denis on 12 November. The letter therefore belongs to October or early November 1567. R90 (f. 324r) carries the close: the King should be “instrutta delli humori di quella corte et della natura di [la] Regina principalmente”, and should let the Queen know that “poco fideli li saranno quelli che sono infideli a Dio”. Its second sentence is also written in clear on f. 302r of the R88 copy. f. 301r (R88), the first four lines, with the reverse bleeding through: the opening on the troubles of France, which the reading of the copy R89 gives as Quanto alli tumulti di Francia, se la Regina vol far da vero finiranno presto … Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 1 f. 301r, via DECODE R88.

R85, f. 165r. The Pope wants to be sure whether the King’s journey will take place, because if so he would meet him “in quello loco che li fusse più comodo”. The Queen of France and her son wish to be asked to a parley with Philip; the Pope does not know how far to trust “parole di donne”, but urges the King not to doubt that such a colloquio could bring “gran frutto alla religione catolica”. Two code groups (3050, 3020) are open. R86, f. 236r. Milan: the Pope means to proceed against the authors of the attack on the archbishop’s jurisdiction, above all the senate, “con le sue armi spirituali”; the dignity of the Holy See requires proceeding at least against the Capitano di giustizia and the fiscal, “il quale ha fatto il peggio di tutti”, and some of the senate; the King should deprive his two ministers of their office. One code group (2020) is open. R87, ff. 249r–250r. Read with its contemporary decipherment (f. 251r). The Pope wants the King’s journey to Flanders, for religion there, in France and in Germany, and would have him invite the Queen of France to a colloquio . Then: “N.S. vuole ancora che V.S. facia intendere a Re che l’arcivescovo di Colonia eletto già sono molti anni non à mai ottenuto la confirmatione da questa santa sede”, nor made the profession of faith “in quella forma che ordina il Concilio di Trento”; he is treating with the Duke of Cleves; the Pope means to proceed to his deprivation, and since “il capitolo di Colonia non è in tutto catolico”, the King should see that it does not choose a suspect person. Friedrich von Wied resigned in 1567. R88, f. 301r–v; R89, f. 314r–v. France, above; one group of R88 (7 3 8) is unread. R90, f. 324r. The close of the France letter: the Queen Mother does not have the good counsellors she thinks she can trust.

The decoder is targets/alessandrino1568/decrypt.py , copied without change: a search that tries, at each digit, both of its letters, the null, and any nomenclator group starting there, and keeps the best-scoring partial texts under the repository’s shared Italian five-gram language model (it-cinquecento, no spaces). The six pages decode at −1.7 to −1.9 nats a letter, the level of the 1568 letters, and end in a few letters of clerk’s padding. The two copies R88 and R89, decoded independently, give the same text wherever their transcriptions are clean, which is a check on both the key and the letter choices. The re-reading of 22 October 2026. The character decode above gives fragments, not sentences. R87’s contemporary decipherment on f. 251r (its top lines lost; it stops at “resistere”) was transcribed and aligned with the figures, and R88, R89 and R90 were compared with each other and against the clear sentence on f. 302r. These fixed the code values above, and every letter was then deciphered word by word on the figures, every word aligned with its figures ( research/reading_audit/b09_align.py ), with twelve transcription labels corrected on the images. Of the words, 169 of 190 (R85), 155 of 164 (R86), 437 of 448 (R87), 326 of 361 (R88), 336 of 349 (R89) and 45 of 48 (R90) are carried by their figures; the rest are bracketed. The readings, texts/R85_reading.md to R90_reading.md , have English beside them.

Three code groups are not resolved: 3050 and 3020 (in this use) in R85, and 2020 in R86. A few words are only partly carried and marked [?word] (R86 [?quel] fatto , [?havere] , [?via] ); in R85 one group is blotted and one run ticked through; in R88 one group (7 3 8) is unread. The group earlier decoded as “colospo” is colloquio (col-lo + 509 qui + o), resolved by the R87 decipherment. The last four rows of R87 rest on the figures alone, since the decipherment stops at “resistere”; where the decipherer and the figures differ ( dal qual , ma perché , esso pretenso arcivescovo , o dependente ), the figures are followed. Not compared with Serrano’s edition of the Pius V correspondence (1914), which prints Alessandrino–Castagna letters and may give some of these in clear; it could not be reached (HathiTrust 403, not on the Internet Archive).

Et benché N.S. fin qui non veda di havere ottenuto cosa alcuna che sia in servitio de Dio da S.M., ne anco di riforma, ma che differisca il tutto a tempo più comodo, ### f. 249v pur N.S. giudica che saria bene che Re invitasse [la] Regina di Francia a colloquio per satisfattione del mondo et per maggior servitio ancora delle attioni sue, perché quando non si venga a riparare alle ruine di Francia con questa andata pare a N.S. che poca altra speranza se ne possa più havere. Però che N.S. ### f. 250r è per procedere contra di lui alla privatione; ma perché, si come suol fare il demonio, verrà a concitar molti suoi membri ad opporsi a questo suo disegno, desidera che Re quanto più presto vada in Fiandra et veda con suoi confidenti et vassalli de impedire tale opera, perché oltra che saria molto dannosa a Germania saria ancora non meno nociva alli stati bassi di Re. S'intende ancora che esso pretenso arcivescovo tratta di volere resignar la chiesa; et perché il capitolo di Colonia non è in tutto catolico, si dubita che non si facino prattiche di disegnarla a persona suspetta o dependente da heretici o debole, sì che non possa resistere a chi vorrà oppugnare lo stato ecclesiastico di quello arcivescovado. Translation R87_en.md # R87 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio Castagna, cipher of [about 2 August 1567]) Translated from `R87_reading.md`; holes as there. ### f. 249r His Holiness wishes the King to go to Flanders as soon as possible, trusting in God that this journey of his must set the world to rights and be a reform of all Christendom; and therefore he thinks that it will serve to restore religion not only in that province but also in France and in Germany. His Holiness is given to understand that the Queen [Mother] of France has a very great desire to be invited by the King to a meeting, from which it is believed great good and profit could be drawn for Christendom, and that the King, who as far as is known seeks nothing but the service of God and the public good, will obtain whatever he knows how to ask. And although His Holiness does not see that he has so far obtained anything from His Majesty that is in the service of God, nor even of reform, but that he puts everything off to a more convenient time, ### f. 249v His Holiness nevertheless judges that it would be well for the King to invite the Queen of France to a meeting, to satisfy the world and for the greater service of his own affairs too, because if the ruin of France is not repaired by this journey, His Holiness thinks little other hope can be had of it. His Holiness further wishes Your Lordship to let the King know that the archbishop-elect of Cologne, elected many years ago now, has never obtained confirmation from this Holy See, because His Holiness does not mean to confirm him unless he first makes the profession of faith in the form the Council of Trent prescribes; and that it is understood that the said elect is making certain treaties or alliances with the Duke of Cleves, who is held [by] His Holiness to be little of a Catholic, and that together they are concerting to make of the archbishopric a mere temporal dominion. Therefore His Holiness ### f. 250r means to proceed against him to deprivation; but because, as the devil is wont to do, he will come to stir up many of his members to oppose this design, he wishes the King to go to Flanders as soon as possible and see, with his confidants and vassals, to prevent such a work, because besides being very harmful to Germany it would be no less harmful to the King's Low Countries. It is also understood that this so-called archbishop is negotiating to resign the church; and because the chapter of Cologne is not wholly Catholic, it is feared that schemes may be made to designate it to a suspect person, or one dependent on heretics, or weak, so that he cannot resist whoever will attack the ecclesiastical state of that archbishopric. So it is wished that the King will perform the office that is hoped of him, and that His Holiness be [?then] informed of everything. R88, Spagna 1 item 4, f. 301r-v [autumn 1567] Rome, 4 Nov 1567, a chapter of a letter from France passed on to the nuncio: the Queen Mother is timid, trusts the Chancellor, Morvillier, Limoges and l'Aubespine, and keeps the kingdom divided to rule; not a Huguenot but a bad Christian; if the King imprisoned the Constable and his son until Condé and the Admiral laid down arms, the troubles would end. Translation R88_en.md # R88 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio Castagna, cipher of Rome, 4 November 1567) Translated from `R88_reading.md`; holes as there. Same text as R89 + R90 (another copy); differences are of spelling and a few words ("keeping the kingdom" for "maintaining the kingdom divided"). ### f. 301r As to the troubles of France, if the Queen [Mother] will act in earnest they will soon end, for one may reckon this a fire of straw; but the Queen is so timid, and trusts so much in the Chancellor, in Morvillier, in Limoges and in l'Aubespine, her counsellors, that she cannot resolve to do anything good, and keeps treating the evil with something worse. And believe me, she does not sin from ignorance, for everything that has happened to her was foretold to her many times; but there is so much ambition to rule in her that there is not as much in the whole world. And to tell you, the Queen in my judgement is not a Huguenot, but I do believe she is a bad Christian, and that neither love nor charity nor even justice reigns in her, letting herself be persuaded that keeping the kingdom divided is the true way to rule; and how much she deceives herself anyone can easily see. If I had the chance to speak with you I would disclose a great many things that I will not commit to the pen. Meanwhile I will tell you only this: that if His Majesty had the Constable and Montmorency his son put into a safe prison, declaring ### f. 301v to them that unless within three days they made the Admiral and the Prince of Condé lay down their arms he would have their heads cut off, you would see an end put to so many troubles very soon; because it is believed that this plot was laid entirely with the knowledge of the Constable and his son, and so it is feared they may make some shameful patch-up; and it cannot be otherwise, the Constable being with His Majesty, who will lead him to do whatever he wants. And the Queen, who believes she will rule by some means, will find herself deceived one day, and will repent too late of not having been willing to believe the good. […] I have wished to share with you this chapter of a letter that came from outside to a gentleman at this court, so that you may confer it with the King, so that, should he think fit to do some office with that Majesty, he may do it on firmer ground, assuring her that the said letter is written by a person very well informed of the humours of that court and above all of the nature of the Queen. Marks: [?word] partly carried, [word] supplied, […] unread. ## Reading ### f. 314r Quanto alli tumulti di Francia, se la Regina vol far da vero finiranno presto, potendo far conto che questa sia un foco di paglia; ma [la] Regina è tanto timida et crede tanto al cancelliere, a Morviglier, a Limoges et a l'Abaspina, suoi consiglieri, che non si sa risolvere a far cosa buona, et va sempre medicando il male col peggio. Et pensate pur che ella non pecca per ignoranza, perché tutto quello che li è successo li è stato pronosticato più volte; ma in lei è tanta ambitione di dominare che non ce ne è altrettanta in tutto il mondo. Et per dirvi, [la] Regina a iuditio mio non è ugonotta, credo bene che sia una mala cristiana, et che in lei non regni né amore né carità né manco iusticia, lasciandosi persuadere che il mantenere il regno diviso sia la vera via di dominare; et quanto ella s'inganni ogniuno lo può facilmente conoscere. Se io havessi commodità di parlarvi vi scoprirei delle cose assai che non voglio commettere alla ### f. 314v penna. In tanto vi dirò questo solo, che se S.M. facesse mettere in una prigione sicura il Conestabile et Memoransi suo figliolo, protestandoli che se in termine di tre giorni non facessero deponere le armi al Amiraglio et al principe di Condé li faria tagliare il capo, vedereste che si metteria fine a tanti tumulti assai presto; perché si crede che questa trata sia fatta tutta consaputa del Conestabile et del figliolo, et però si dubita che non facino qualche impiastro vergognoso; et non può essere altramente, trovandosi il Conestabile con S.M., che lo condurrà a fare tutto quello che vorrà. Et la Regina, che crede per qualche via di dominare, si troverà un giorno ingannata, et si pentirà tardi di non havere voluto credere ai buoni. Ho voluto farvi parte di questo capitulo di lettera venuta di fora a un gentilhuomo in questa corte, acciò che possiate conferirlo con Re, perché, parendoli di far qualche offitio con quella Maestà, lo possa fare tanto più fondatamente, assicurandola che detta lettera viene scritta da persona molto bene ## Notes on the figures - Codes: 8010 = [la] Regina [di Francia] (the Queen Mother, Catherine de' Medici; "ingannata", feminine; R87's decipherment reads 8010 "la Reg.na di Francia"); 4010 = S.M. Translation R89_en.md # R89 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio Castagna, cipher of [4 November 1567]) Translated from `R89_reading.md`; holes as there. The passage is the "chapter of a letter from outside" that the cardinal passes on (see the last sentence). ### f. 314r As to the troubles of France, if the Queen [Mother] will act in earnest they will soon end, for one may reckon this a fire of straw; but the Queen is so timid, and trusts so much in the Chancellor, in Morvillier, in Limoges and in l'Aubespine, her counsellors, that she cannot resolve to do anything good, and keeps treating the evil with something worse. And believe me, she does not sin from ignorance, for everything that has happened to her was foretold to her many times; but there is so much ambition to rule in her that there is not as much in the whole world. And to tell you, the Queen in my judgement is not a Huguenot, but I do believe she is a bad Christian, and that neither love nor charity nor even justice reigns in her, letting herself be persuaded that keeping the kingdom divided is the true way to rule; and how much she deceives herself anyone can easily see. If I had the chance to speak with you I would disclose a great many things that I will not commit to the ### f. 314v pen. Meanwhile I will tell you only this: that if His Majesty had the Constable and Montmorency his son put into a safe prison, declaring to them that unless within three days they made the Admiral and the Prince of Condé lay down their arms he would have their heads cut off, you would see an end put to so many troubles very soon; because it is believed that this plot was laid entirely with the knowledge of the Constable and his son, and so it is feared they may make some shameful patch-up; and it cannot be otherwise, the Constable being with His Majesty, who will lead him to do whatever he wants. And the Queen, who believes she will rule by some means, will find herself deceived one day, and will repent too late of not having been willing to believe the good. I have wished to share with you this chapter of a letter that came from outside to a gentleman at this court, so that you may confer it with the King, so that, should he think fit to do some office with that Majesty, he may do it on firmer ground, assuring her that the said letter is written by a person very well R90, Spagna 1 item 6, f. 324r [autumn 1567] End of the same text: the writer is well informed of the French court and the Queen Mother; the King should let the Queen know that her counsellors, unfaithful to God, will be little faithful to her. A German letter of the Emperor’s resident in London with fourteen passages in a homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator, a few groups glossed at the time. The key filed beside it belongs to Windischgrätz and contradicts the glosses. A ciphertext-only solver failed on 162 letter tokens, and a matched control shows the text is too short; not deciphered. 53. 474. selbst ist sich 38. 33. 799. 48. 40. 49. 23. 20. 210. 48. 35. 36. seiner … glossed at the time: 33 = e · 23 = n · 10 = d · 15 = t · 40 = ſ · 230 = der London → Starhemberg / Visconti · homophonic cipher with nomenclator · March 1727 Palm to Starhemberg and Visconti, 1727 to Gundaker Starhemberg British Library, Add MS 32270 ff. 16–18 and 41 (DECODE R7927–R7930). The two records behind the catalogue entry hold one German letter with ciphered passages and one decipherer’s worksheet for another letter that is not imaged. Where British Library, Add MS 32270, ff. 16–17; DECODE R7927. Related records R7928, R7929 and R7930 do not supply a usable key. The cipher Numbers 2–79 for letters, about two per letter, and three-figure groups for words and syllables. How it was tried The R7928 key contradicts the glosses. Annealing with a German 5-gram model on 162 letter tokens did not converge, with or without the gloss values fixed. Why it resists A synthetic control of the same shape recovered only 44–50% of tokens, so a text this short cannot be deciphered without the key. Still open All 14 passages. Needed: Palm’s key, the Deciphering Branch’s clear copy, or images of R7929. f. 16v (DECODE R7927, image 2): the clear text “So sehen sie doch den ihrer Meinung nach bevorstehenden Krieg …”, then the first ciphered passage with the decipherer’s glosses. Image: British Library, Add MS 32270 f. 16v, via DECODE R7927 (image 2).

Record Folios What it is R7927 ff. 16–17 Docket “Palm & Staremberg / German”. A letter fragment in German with 14 ciphered passages. Images 1 and 4 show only the other side of the leaf through the paper. R7928 f. 18 “Count Windischgrätz & C t Staremberg”: a letter key 1–50 with about 30 values filled in (2 b, 5 n, 8 u, 9 c, 10 i, 20 o, 40 r …). R7929 ff. 19–40 The Emperor to Starhemberg, 42 pp., marked “Decrypted”. No images on DECODE. R7930 f. 41 Cover “Palm to Visconti 1727 … Visconti to Palm”. On the verso is a decipherer’s tally grid, 1–500 (Addresse 21, Hollande 109, Italie 120, Traité 215, syllables in the 300s and 400s, several nulls). This is a different system, and no ciphertext is imaged.

162 letter tokens across 47 values (2–79) and 23 code tokens across 10 values: 124, 138, 170 (five times), 210 (three), 230 = der (six), 380, 423, 432, 474 and 799. The glosses, in German Kurrent script, give 33 = e, 23 = n, 10 = d, 15 = t, 40 = ſ, and probably 9 = u and 4 = z. The clear text concerns how England saw the war then coming over Gibraltar and the Hanover alliance, and the rumours that a rupture would bring (“dass im Fall es zu einer Ruptur kommen solte, man …”). One passage ends in … d ſ ? e t z e n zu bringen .

The R7928 key applied to the passages: it gives 40 = r and 23 = u where the glosses have ſ and n. Ruled out. Simulated annealing on the letter values (the project’s de-modern 5-gram model), with the codes drawn from a list of German words and syllables and the clear context kept for scoring. With and without the gloss values fixed, the output was not German. A control on synthetic German of the same shape (162 letter tokens over 47 values), with the true values of the six commonest symbols fixed, recovered only 44–50% of the tokens. At that rate the text cannot be made out, so a text of this length cannot be deciphered without the key. A web search for a printed decipherment of Palm’s 1727 intercepts found nothing.

None of the fourteen passages was deciphered. With about two homophones per letter and only 162 letter tokens, a ciphertext-only attack has too little to work on. What is needed: Palm’s Imperial cipher (Vienna, HHStA, England, Berichte 1727), the Deciphering Branch’s clear copy (other Willes volumes, SP 107), or images of R7929.
British Library, Add MS 32270 ff. 16–18, 41: DECODE R7927 , R7928 , R7929 , R7930 (login required). Transcription, glosses and solver scripts: targets/palm1727/ .

Where Nationaal Archief, 2.01.08, inv. 318; DECODE R1942. The matching codebook is R1035 (Legatie Rusland, inv. 228). The cipher Mostly one- to three-digit groups marked with bars, ticks, dots and waves. The numeric transcription has 286 groups and 218 distinct values. How it was tried Not attacked. The subject was identified from Sillem’s 1890 biography, whose footnote cites “dispatch of the same day, no. 12, ciphered”. What it says Dissatisfied with Chancellor Vorontsov, Hogendorp sought another route to the Emperor through General Van Suchtelen. This is a paraphrase of Sillem, not decoded text. Dirk van Hogendorp, the Batavian Republic’s envoy in Russia, sent the dispatch from St Petersburg to Maarten van der Goes, the Batavian agent for foreign relations. The clear address names both men and the first leaf carries the dispatch number. The rest is in numerical code groups, mostly of one to three digits, distinguished by bars, ticks, dots and wave-like marks above the figures. Dispatch no. 12, 5 July 1803: the clear address to Maarten van der Goes followed by the marked numerical groups. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 inv. 318, dispatch no. 12, via DECODE R1942. The numeric-only transcription has 286 groups and 218 distinct bare values. That count ignores the marks, although 73 with a bar and 73 with a wave are different codebook entries. A transcription with the marks exists in draft; the pale marks still need a second check against the scans.

J. A. Sillem narrates Hogendorp’s first approaches in St Petersburg on pp. 151–153 of his biography. Dispatch no. 10 of 5 July supplied the argument for a Russo-Batavian commercial treaty: Russia should have an immediate interest in the Batavian Republic’s continued existence as an independent state, and concluding the treaty would demonstrate that interest. Vorontsov was not persuaded. Sillem continues: Hogendorp vond zijne houding althans “zo wonderlijk” dat hij naar andere kanalen zocht om den Keizer onze belangen voor te dragen. Hij meende een gelukkigen greep gedaan te hebben door de tusschenkomst in te roepen van den Generaal van Suchtelen, Nederlander van geboorte, die in russischen dienst tot Opperbevelhebber der genie was opgeklommen, en het volste vertrouwen genoot van Czaar Alexander, met wien hij dagelijks omging. The footnote attached to that passage reads: “Rijksarchief. Dep. van denzelfden dag No. 12 gecijferd.” In English: “National Archives. Dispatch of the same day, no. 12, ciphered.” The manuscript supplies No. 12 ; Sillem supplies the content; and his preceding note fixes “the same day” as 5 July 1803.

What is established is the subject and the argument. Vorontsov’s attitude and answer struck Hogendorp as so strange that he sought another route to the emperor. He chose Van Suchtelen because the general’s Dutch origin, senior position and daily access to Alexander made him a plausible intermediary. The object was to place the Batavian Republic’s interests (in context, its independent survival and the desired commercial treaty) before the emperor by a channel outside the chancellor. A concise English reconstruction is: Chancellor Vorontsov’s attitude and answer appeared so strange to me that I sought another way to bring our interests to the emperor’s attention. I believe I have found it in General Van Suchtelen, Dutch by birth, commander of the engineers in Russian service, who enjoys Emperor Alexander’s full confidence and sees him daily. This is an editorial paraphrase of Sillem’s account. It is not a quotation from a decoded text. Connectives, spelling, the exact request made of Van Suchtelen and any material Sillem omitted remain unknown.

DECODE R1035 is catalogued as Legatie Rusland, inv. nr. 228, codebook, 1803 . Its twenty images show the same system used in R1942: numerical entries extended by superposed marks, with values for letters, syllables, word parts, whole words, names and phrases. DECODE’s downloadable partial transcription contains 1,849 distinct entries. It places the letter in the documented 1803 Russian-legation system and is the route to an exact decoding. It does not by itself decode the dispatch: the CSV is partial, and the letter’s marks must be transcribed accurately before the corresponding rows can be selected.

Number. The leaf itself says No. 12 . Date. The docket and DECODE record give 5 July 1803. Source citation. Sillem assigns the Van Suchtelen paragraph to the ciphered no. 12 of that same day. Separation from no. 10. His preceding footnote names no. 10 as the source for the commercial-treaty exchange with Vorontsov. The two dispatches cannot be conflated. System. The 1803 Russian-legation codebook R1035 matches the manuscript’s marked numerical format. The identification needs no cryptanalysis. It rests on a contemporary archive number, visible on the cipher sheet, that a printed account repeats while stating what the dispatch reported.

Exact marks. Every bar, tick, dot and wave over the 286 groups needs independent visual verification. The current transcription of the marks is preliminary. Exact plaintext. R1035 must be applied group by group, with its images consulted wherever the downloadable CSV has no entry. Until then, no wording of the original is claimed or graded (H, C, M or I). Sillem’s omissions. His paragraph may compress, modernise or omit part of the dispatch. Only a complete alignment can show how much. Related traffic. Dispatch no. 10 of the same day and no. 21 of 19 August frame the approach: proposal, attempted alternative channel, then Vorontsov’s definitive refusal. Comparing their code groups may settle doubtful marks.
