Sillem, Dirk van Hogendorp (1761–1822) (Amsterdam, 1890), pp. 151–153: Internet Archive scan ; p. 153 on Google Books . Nationaal Archief, inventory 1.02.13, Legatie Rusland . The scans, numeric and marked transcriptions, partial R1035 table, evidence note and machine-readable profile are in the repository folder targets/R1942/ . The modern reconstruction is editorial and must not be cited as Hogendorp’s verbatim plaintext.

The ministerial rescript sent to Michell the same day as the King’s own letter, intercepted and copied at The Hague (DECODE R1955), not in print. It is in the code of Michell’s own reports, not the cabinet code. WAINUT built a table from the contemporary Dutch decipherments of two of those reports (R1050, R1051) and decoded 95 of the 360 groups (26.4%): fragments about Dutch affairs and a negotiation with Vienna. 3222 450 340 = cet avis et 1401 450 1242 = depuis avis est · 1000 357 = ce projet Berlin → London, intercepted at The Hague · numerical code (Michell’s envoy code) · 28 December 1751 · decoded, not read: 95 of 360 groups, fragments only Frederick the Great’s ministerial letter to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 from Frederick II Go to the transcriptions ↓ The second letter sent to Michell that day, in the code of his own reports: a table from two contemporary Dutch decipherments gives about a quarter of its groups, enough for fragments but not for the sense. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Frederick II to his resident in London, Louis Michell, Berlin, 28 December 1751: the ministerial rescript, issued in the King’s name through the foreign department. It opens in clear, Toutes vos dépêches m’ont été bien rendues . Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, archive of Prince William V, inv. 198, the Dutch interceptors’ copy. DECODE R1955, listed as not decrypted. The cipher A large numerical code: groups from 2 to 5346, half-groups such as 150½, and homophones even for de and que . It is not the King’s cabinet code. How it was tried WAINUT built a table of 271 code values from the Dutch decipherments written over two of Michell’s own reports (DECODE R1050, R1051) and found that it fits this letter. What it says Fragments only: an avis , a negotiation with Vienna, the Prince Stadholder, the States, ce projet . Still open The letter as a text: 265 of the 360 groups have no value, so it is decoded, not read. More decipherments of Michell’s reports are not online. On 23 October 2026 the Hague decipherment registers on the Nationaal Archief IIIF were checked heading by heading: Fagel 5208 holds the Dutch clear decipherments of the ministerial rescripts to Michell in this code, nos. 1–8 (2 November to 7 December 1751), and Fagel 5177 the cabinet-code letters, but the rescript of 28 December is in neither, and the copies carry no figures, so they add no values. Credit The match and the partial decoding are WAINUT’s (pull request #29, 11 October 2026); checked here. This letter was written up together with the King’s own letter of the same day until 14 October 2026. That letter, DECODE R1957, is in Frederick’s cabinet code and has its own page, Frederick II to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 : a different cipher, with its own page.

The King wrote to his London resident through two channels: rescripts from the foreign department under Podewils, and his own immediate letters. On 28 December 1751 Michell was sent one of each. Both went by post through the Dutch Republic, where the Stadtholder’s cabinet opened and copied them; the copies are in the papers of William V, inv. 198. The immediate letter tells Michell to report to the King alone, with no copies to the department, which is why the second letter exists. The copy is headed Lettre du Roi de Prusse au Secrétaire Michell du 28 Decemb. 1751 and signed Féderic . The opening is in clear: Toutes vos dépêches m’ont été bien rendues et la dernière est du 14 e de ce mois . Then come the code groups, separated by points, and the date line. The Politische Correspondenz prints only one letter to Michell of that date, the immediate one, so this text is not in print. The heading, the clear opening and the first lines of the code, from 1561 4200 2537 onward. A few groups are underlined. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 198, first page (image P2), via DECODE R1955.

The two transcriptions agree on 352 of 360 groups. This project’s of 19 September counts 362, because it splits a run of nine digits written without separators; WAINUT’s of 11 October keeps it as one group. 296 of the 362 groups are distinct and the commonest occurs only five times. That is a large code with several numbers for each common word, and a single letter of it gives nothing to a ciphertext-only attack. It is not the code of the King’s immediate letters. The cabinet key that WAINUT rebuilt for R1957 gives values to 2.8–5.6% of these groups, against 69.5% of R1957’s. DECODE R1953, von der Hellen’s letter of 4 January 1752 from the same archive, is in a different, smaller code.

DECODE R1050 (London, 5 September 1752) and R1051 (London, 12 November 1751) are Hague copies of Michell’s own reports to the King, with the contemporary Dutch decipherment written over the numbers. WAINUT paired DECODE’s transcriptions of them token by token and got 512 code-word pairs for 271 codes. The code held over the ten months between the two reports: of 40 codes found in both, 32 have the same commonest value. That table gives a value to 95 of R1955’s 360 groups (26.4%). On R1957 it gives only 5.5%, so R1955 is in Michell’s code. The decoded words also sit together sensibly more often than chance: 19 of 30 adjacent pairs are word pairs found in 18th-century diplomatic French, against 11.1 when the same values are shuffled (p = 0.001). The fragments include avis … sur … negociation avec … de Vienne … les difficulte(s) … article … du Prince Stadhouder … maison … cet avis et … états … depuis avis est … ce projet … nouvelle … doit etre … des esperance(s) de (spelled as the table gives them). The letter is about Dutch affairs and a negotiation involving Vienna. More than that cannot be said from a quarter of the groups. WAINUT also tested whether the rescript repeats the wording of a royal letter of the same days printed in the Politische Correspondenz , which would supply its text. The rule was fixed in advance. No letter of 22 December 1751 to 10 January 1752 scores above the controls (best z = 2.69, highest control 4.85), while a 17% sample of a real letter is found at z above 27.

265 of the 360 groups have no value. The table comes from two letters ten months apart, and a changed or homophone value could mislead. The table depends on DECODE’s transcriptions of the R1050/R1051 decipherments, which were not checked against the images line by line. Further decipherments of Michell’s reports are probably in the Koninklijk Huisarchief (A31-1181), not online. Four code telegrams of the Queen’s chief steward: to Paris in 1903, to Naples in 1904, and from London in May 1910, after Edward VII’s funeral. Pencil decodes made at the time, filed among the clear cards of the same unit, give three of them, one with the decoder’s own gaps, and 52 values of a one-part alphabetical code used from 1903 to 1910. The 1910 telegrams concern a British marriage for Manuel II; the 1903 telegram has no decode and stays undeciphered. 7034 · 8747 · 12296 · 19482 · 0320 · 8175 So- · -ver- · -al · diz · ir · tratar one-part code · 11501–23400 = a–h · 0139–9019 = i–v Lisbon and London → Queen Amélie · one-part code, four and five figures · 1903, 1904, 1910 · decodes of the time for three of four The Count of Sabugosa to Queen Amélie: four code telegrams, 1903–1910 from António Maria Vasco de Melo, 9th Count of Sabugosa → to Amélie of Orléans Go to the full text ↓ The Queen’s chief steward wired her from Lisbon and, in May 1910, from London about a British marriage for Manuel II; three telegrams carry decodes of the time, the 1903 one none. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method · m0010 and m0016 (decodes of the time on m0008 and m0009): read from existing decipherment (complete) · m0012-13 (decode of the time on m0005 and m0004): read from existing decipherment (partial) · Sabugosa's alphabetical code, 52 values: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext (partial) · m0014, Lisbon -> Paris, 13 May 1903: not solved (none) · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription, identification) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment, in part · 58 of 106 groups The telegrams The Count of Sabugosa to Queen Amélie: Lisbon to Paris, 13 May 1903; Lisbon to Naples, 24 April 1904; London to Lisbon (Necessidades), 21 and 24 May 1910. Where Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Documentos de D. Carlos, D. Amélia e D. Manuel II , maço 14, PT/TT/CAM/M14, 17 images on DigitArq. Catalogue entry 410. The cipher A one-part (alphabetical) Portuguese code: five-figure groups carry words from a to h, four-figure groups words from i to v. Names are spelled in pieces: Soveral is So / ver / al. How it was deciphered Pencil decodes made at the time are among the clear cards of the same unit (m0009, m0008, m0005 + m0004). Matched to their telegrams by clear words, dates and signatures, they give 52 code values, and the values fall in alphabetical order. What it says Queen Alexandra received Sabugosa after Edward VII’s funeral; the King ended by saying “tratarei de o casar”, “I will see to getting him married”; Soveral will take up the negotiation. Still open The 1903 telegram (43 groups, no decode). In the telegram of 24 May 1910, two groups the decoder left blank and four words he marked doubtful. Credit Transcription, the matching of decodes to telegrams, dating and the code values by WAINUT (27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents; transcriptions made with a vision-capable model and checked against the DigitArq images by a second agent. The decodes are those made for the Queen in 1904 and 1910.

Maço 14 holds four code telegrams (m0010, m0012–13, m0014, m0016; m0017 is a telegram envelope) and clear cards and sheets (m0001–m0009), most of which are pencil decodes of the telegrams. The sender signs SABUGOSO (1903), SABUGOZA (1904) and Sabugosa (1910): the Count of Sabugosa, António Maria de Melo, the Queen’s chief steward (mordomo-mor). Telegram from London received at Necessidades on 24 May 1910, first sheet: 5411 12394 5578 2013 / 23024 2915 19497 2013 / 3578 2606 12190 1738 / 5819 7785 19497 0539. The receiver struck through the groups as he looked them up and circled 1738, which he could not find. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M14, image m0012, via DigitArq. telegram route and date groups decode of the time state m0014 Lisbon → Paris, 13 May 1903 (stamp probable), “AMPLIATION” 43 none found not deciphered m0016 Lisbon (Alcântara) → Naples, 24 Apr 1904 10, among clear words m0009, dated 24-4-04 complete m0010 London (Buckingham Palace) → Lisbon, 21 May 1910 16 m0008, dated 21-5-10 complete m0012–13 London → Lisbon, received 24 May 1910 37 m0005 + m0004, with question marks 32 of 37 For the three handwritten and Naples forms, the word count on the form equals groups + clear words + address words, which checks the number of groups. The first pass had m0014 and m0016 running the other way and m0014 in 1910 with 51 groups; by the forms’ own rule (origin before serial number) they run from Lisbon, and m0014 is of May 1903 with 43 groups.

Each decode was matched to its telegram. m0009 begins with the clear words of m0016 (“Agradeço com vivo reconhecimento telegramma de V. M. que”) and gives ten words for its ten groups. m0008 has the date and signature of m0010 and 15 words for its 16 groups. m0005 + m0004 are signed Sabugosa; their question marks fall where the receiver circled groups in m0012–13, and their first word, Rainha, is the group 5411 that m0008 also reads Rainha. The decode of the telegram of 24 May 1910, first card: “Rainha Alexandra recebeu-me / hontem á noite dizendo-me palavras / muito agradaveis ? S. M. ElRei / terminou dizendo va ? / conde ? socegado ? tratar ei de / o casar não tive occasião ver”. It goes on on m0004. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M14, image m0005, via DigitArq. On m0004 the decoder first wrote a word in So- and struck it, then wrote “ver al”: the name Soveral is three groups, 7034 / 8747 / 12296, and the same three groups stand for Soveral in the telegram of 21 May. He wrote “tratar ei” as two words, tratar + the future ending -ei (group 19719), i.e. tratarei ; an earlier pass had “Tratar é de”.

The three decodes give 52 groups a value, with no conflict between them ( code.py , code_values.tsv ). The code is one-part: five-digit groups (11501–23400) carry words from a to h (agradaveis 12190 … hontem 23024), four-digit groups (0139–9019) words from i to v (informação 0139, ir 0320 … veio 8975), and within each series the numbers follow the alphabet. Among the values taken one group to one word from a decode, 3 of 406 pairs are out of order in the four-digit series and 0 of 136 in the five-digit series; 2000 random shuffles of the same words over the same numbers give at least 117 and 32. The three are tive/terminou and ver/veio. One code served from 1903 to 1910. The 1904 and 1910 values fall into one alphabetical order, and the 1903 telegram shares 19482 (diz), 18063 (de, twice) and 19656 (e, three times). King Carlos used a different code in the same weeks of 1903, and Venceslau de Lima’s of 1909 is a third. The order also weighs the decoder’s doubts. socegado 7114 sits next to socegar 7115 (1904), which supports it. His “va” (0539) stands among i–m words, so it is probably wrong. 13657, which the decode of 21 May renders “assumpto” (the matter), stands just after casar 13616: by its place a word in cas- (casamento, marriage?), with “assumpto” perhaps the decoder’s paraphrase. That is not adopted in the text.

24 April 1904 , Lisbon to Naples (m0016; only “veio … mesmo” is coded): Agradeço com vivo reconhecimento telegramma de Vossa Magestade, que veio socegar meu coração. Ser e serei sempre o mesmo. Estimo muito boas noticias e demonstrações. Escrevo. Beijo mão Vossa Magestade. Sabugoza. “I thank Your Majesty with lively gratitude for the telegram, which has set my heart at rest. I am and always will be the same.” The code has the infinitive “ser” where the sense wants “sou”. 21 May 1910 , London to Lisbon (m0010), the day after Edward VII’s funeral: Hoje ElRei tenciona falar Rainha para Soveral tratar com ella assumpto. Espero amanhã dar informação. Sabugosa. “Today the King [George V] intends to speak to the Queen so that Soveral may take up the matter with her. I hope to give news tomorrow.” Soveral is the Marquis of Soveral, Portuguese minister in London. 24 May 1910 , London to Lisbon (m0012–13), with the decoder’s gaps kept: Rainha Alexandra recebeu-me hontem á noite, dizendo-me palavras muito agradaveis [?]. S. M. ElRei terminou dizendo [?va] [?] [?conde] [?socegado], tratarei de o casar. Não tive occasião ver Princeza. Soveral diz ir tratar [?subsequente] negociação. Sabugosa. “Queen Alexandra received me last night and said very kind words to me. His Majesty the King ended by saying […]: ‘I will see to getting him married.’ I had no opportunity to see the Princess. Soveral says he will go to handle the [further] negotiation.” “Him” is presumably Manuel II; the Princess is not named. These are the 1910 attempts to arrange a British marriage for the young King. Two more cards of the same week are in clear: a decode of 22 May whose coded telegram is not in M14 (Queen Alexandra invites “the Princess” and her family to dinner), and the Queen’s reply of 21 May.

The telegram of 13 May 1903 (m0014, 43 groups) has no decode. Six groups take a value from the other decodes (diz, de twice, e three times); the other 37 have only alphabetical bounds, which do not fix a word. The codebook was not found. 24 May 1910: 1738 and 3667 were left blank by the decoder (1738 lies between ir and me, 3667 just after para). 24 May 1910: the decoder’s doubtful “va” (0539, out of alphabetical place, probably wrong), “conde” (17004), “socegado” (7114, supported by its neighbour socegar) and “subsequente” (7328). Single occurrences. 13657, the decoder’s “assumpto” on 21 May: its place suggests a word in cas-; one occurrence. Sabugosa’s identity as the Queen’s chief steward and Soveral’s as the minister in London are from general knowledge, not checked in the documents. Other CAM units were not searched; they may hold the coded telegram of 22 May, more of Sabugosa’s decoded telegrams or the codebook, any of which would bear on the 1903 telegram.

A cipher letter of Fr. P. de Santa Cruz to Francesc Climent, Benedict XIII’s agent, 22 October 1399, among Climent’s Schism papers in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona. Canon Puig y Puig deciphered and printed it in 1920 (appendix XXIX): the French ambassadors leave Avignon angry, and the besieged household is left in danger of death. No image of the cipher exists, so its key is not known; it was split from Benedict XIII’s own letters because nothing shows it used his key. P. de Santa Cruz, of Benedict XIII’s circle, writing from Avignon, to Francesc Climent, Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and agent, 22 Oct 1399. Where Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona, the Schism papers Climent left to the chapter (doc. 922), today the paper part of the series Cisma d’Occident. Not digitised. How it was deciphered By Sebastián Puig y Puig, canon of Barcelona, who printed it in 1920 in Pedro de Luna , appendix XXIX, pp. 469–470, with the deciphered passages in italics. What it says The French ambassadors leave Avignon angry, and the besieged papal household is left in periculo mortis . Still open The ciphertext: no image of the letter exists, so the cipher and its key are unknown. The original is in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona, not digitised. Puig’s printed text is not in this repository either (Google Books now blocks it to scripts), so its words are not reproduced here (reading audit, 22 October 2026). Credit The decipherment is Puig’s (1920).

Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and treasurer and later bishop of Barcelona; he left his papers to the cathedral chapter. Among them Sebastián Puig y Puig found fourteen letters partly or wholly in cipher, deciphered them, and printed them in the appendix of Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (1920). This is one of them: Fr. P. de Santa Cruz to Climent, 22 Oct 1399 (appendix XXIX, pp. 469–470; doc. 922). Puig prints about 100 deciphered words. The French ambassadors leave Avignon angry, and the besieged papal household is left in periculo mortis . The originals are not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of the Schism papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. Puig’s print may be the only witness.

Puig never printed a key, and the only image of any of these ciphers is his facsimile of one page of Benedict XIII’s own letter of 22 June 1400. From that page the key of Benedict’s letters was rebuilt here: a plain substitution, one sign per letter. Puig writes of “la clave o claves”, the key or keys, he recovered, and nothing shows whether this letter, from another writer, used the same one. So it has its own entry. Benedict XIII’s letters are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different or unverified cipher, with its own page); the other letters of his circle each have their own page for the same reason: Jafet to Climent, 1400 , Exea to Climent, 1408 , Comuel to Climent, December 1415 , Comuel to Climent, June 1416 .
The ciphertext. No image of the letter exists, so its cipher, its key and Puig’s reading cannot be checked. Blocker: needs the original in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona.

Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A32 Wilhelmina, inv. A32-603 (212 scans), with the sibling files A32-599, 601, 602 and 604. Not on DECODE. The cipher Running French in a private symbol alphabet, one sign per letter, a dot above to double it, and names and titles as numbers from a one-part alphabetical code with homophones (Berlin 106, Hertzberg 446–450, Prince 724–733, Roi 809–818, Sa Majesté 857–861). How it was read The alphabet was aligned on Van der Hoop’s ten clear copies (142 of 143 signs agree on a second pair); the code was built from his glosses, his “Déchiffrement” of 14 December 1783 in A32-599 and De Larrey’s key list, then applied to the eleven letters he never copied. Statistical test: pass. What it says “914 [Thulemeier] est un infâme. 446 [Hertzberg] sera envoyé. 818 [le Roi] hait et méprise de bon cœur 724 [le Prince], mais en revanche il aime tendrement 734 [la Princesse].” Later, a plan for a defensive and offensive alliance of the Republic with France, Spain and Prussia. Still open 38 scattered code numbers, 62 scattered signs under blots or a later hand, and a fixed signature formula and an address panel too short to read. No. 3, Potsdam 8 August 1783, the whole letter in cipher: the underlined numbers are names (914 Thulemeier, 446 Hertzberg, 818 the King, 724 the Prince, 734 the Princess). A32-603 holds 43 letters of Schöning, 28 July 1783 to 10 July 1784: 34 to Van der Hoop in French and 9 to the Princess in German, with notes of Frederick II and De Larrey’s memoranda. Twenty-four contain cipher. Van der Hoop made clear copies of ten of them, writing out the symbol text but leaving most code numbers as numbers; the other eleven he never copied. Schöning wrote on 26 January 1784 that Van der Hoop could not read his last letter for numbers missing from his alphabet.

The running text is a private alphabet of hooks, strokes and loops, one sign per letter, with a dot above a sign to double it and a short tick to separate words written together. The three earliest letters use a variant in which one sign serves both o and d. Names, titles and a few words are numbers of two or three digits from a one-part code in alphabetical order, with several numbers per frequent name. The code table rests on Van der Hoop’s glosses, his “Déchiffrement de Lettres de S., communiqué à LL.AA.S.&R. le 14 Dec 1783” (A32-599), glossed copies in A32-602, and a seventeen-entry key list in De Larrey’s dossier (A32-604) marked “Byland”. 188 of the 226 numbers that occur now have a value.

Code values in brackets; Schöning spells by sound (“aumeur” for humeur, “hasar” for hasard), normalised here. Full text and translation in reading.md and reading_en.md . No. 3, Potsdam, 8 August 1783. “… parler [au Roi]. [Thulemeier] est un infâme. [Hertzberg] sera envoyé. [Le Roi] hait et méprise de bon cœur [le Prince], mais en revanche il aime tendrement [la Princesse]. Dans peu un courrier exprès, et alors plus amplement. Le temps me manque, adieu.” — “… [Thulemeier] is a scoundrel. [Hertzberg] will be sent away. [The King] heartily hates and despises [the Prince], but he tenderly loves [the Princess].” No. 1, 28 July 1783. The town is full of Dutchmen “entre lesquels il y en a des faux patriotes”; he told his contact to praise the reigning burgomasters of Amsterdam, and found him furious against Thulemeier. 24 December 1783. The privy council should take care that [the Stadholder] does not thwart Bérenger’s money negotiation, nor the intrigues he will play “pour faire un parti contre l’Empereur par ordre de [Sa Majesté]”. January 1784, the alliance. “Il me paraît qu’une alliance pour quelques années avec [la France], l’Espagne et la Prusse serait non seulement utile mais même nécessaire à [la République]. Cette alliance faudrait être défensive et offensive, pour empêcher [l’Angleterre] et [l’Empereur] qu’ils ne profitent de la faiblesse de [la République].” The Orangists should assure the future French ambassador, de Vérac, that they are “rien moins qu’anglomanes”. 26–27 January 1784. The King is better, “ce n’est qu’une crampe aux bras”; the secret channel “n’est point découvert et ne le sera jamais”; and “rien ne me peut retenir que l’amour pour ma très chère princesse, car mon poste secret je l’abhorre depuis longtemps”. 10 July 1784. The revolt the Gazette placed at Petersburg was at Constantinople, stirred up by “notre” Gaffron, whom [the King] has recalled for Spandau.

Alphabet. Subagents labelled the signs in ASCII (G01–G24) and aligned the 6 January 1784 original with its copy; the table was checked on the 25 November 1783 pair, 142 of 143 signs agreeing ( letter_table.tsv , verify.md ). Code. Glosses, context and alphabetical bracketing ( code_table.tsv ), then a survey of the sibling files A32-599, 601 and 602 and the No. 4 glosses, which added about 128 values ( code_values_new.tsv , applied by apply_values.py ). Reading. The eleven uncopied letters transcribed sign by sign ( dec_*.tsv ); every line checked with a French model ( sense.py ), and the weak lines of No. 1, Nos. 2–3 and the January letters re-read at five to six times magnification. Measure. 4,088 tokens, 3,988 given a value (97.6%); 95.9% of letter signs on lines that read as French; 188 of 226 code numbers known. _validate.py : the reading scores −2.15 per letter against random keys at −5.89 (z 5.7) and a key fitted to shuffled text at −3.26: pass.

38 code numbers with no gloss anywhere in the five files (among them 475, 499, 500, 661, 950, 1066); 500 opens three letters, probably “J’ai” or a formula. 62 scattered signs under blots or under figures a later hand wrote over No. 1. Schöning’s signature formula (30–31 signs in a digit script) and the address panel of s029 (about 33 signs in a third script): one fixed short string each, no clear form in the file. Readings rest on the sign tables and a model check; the decipherer’s copies confirm the tables, not the uncopied letters themselves.

Translation reading_en.md # Schoning's cipher passages, 1783-84: English translation Translation of `reading.md`. Code words in [brackets]; "..." marks clear text not repeated or signs unread. **No. 1, 28 July 1783.** I have the honour to inform you that I arrived yesterday on Prussian territory without the slightest unfortunate accident, except that I am a little unwell ... This town is full of Dutchmen, among whom there are some false patriots ... [I] told him to give well-deserved praise to the reigning burgomasters of Amsterdam. I arrived in time to stop him doing the contrary, for the duke's party had [tried to undo] the good they have just done. He is furiously worked up, that is, the ill humour he speaks of against Monsieur Thulemeier; he gives him no pardon; but I told him to keep calm on this subject and to be very cautious for some time, for fear that he might lack well-intentioned agents ... He suspected Monsieur your brother the general of belonging to the party of the [...]; [...] to undeceive him ... before one is quite sure of success ... [Her Royal Highness] ... Serene, and the unhappy [Republic]. This idea ... with zeal ... the treasury of [...]. **No. 2, 3 Aug 1783.** (I hope to be able) to present myself in person to the King; for the correspondence everything is arranged. (On the 7th I shall be early) at Potsdam, and I believe [the Prince of Prussia] will have made the arrangements needed to be told the moment I arrive and to have his orders sent to me. **No. 3, Potsdam 8 Aug 1783.** [...] speak [to the King]. [Thulemeier] is a scoundrel. [Hertzberg] will be sent away. [The King] hates and heartily despises [the Prince], but on the other hand he loves [the Princess] tenderly. Shortly an express courier, and then more fully. Time is short, adieu. Potsdam, the eighth of August 1783. **24 Dec 1783.** [My] mission ... [to ask the whole] privy council to be well on their guard, so that [His Serene Highness] does not thwart Berenger over the money negotiation for ..., nor the intrigues he will play to form a party against the Emperor on the orders of [His Majesty]. **Jan 1784, the plan for an alliance.** I believe [His Serene Highness] would do very well to try to persuade his friends that they should [show] de Verac, the future French ambassador at [The Hague], by their advice in the [States], that they are anything but Anglomaniacs; that on the contrary they are perfectly convinced that the friendship of [His] Most Christian [Majesty] is dear to them and absolutely necessary for ... the harmony and tranquillity of the [Republic]. They should show themselves on every occasion opposed to an alliance with England, Austria and Russia. On the contrary it seems to me that an alliance for some years with [France], Spain and Prussia would be not only useful but even necessary to [the Republic]. This alliance should be defensive and offensive, to prevent [England] and the [Emperor] from profiting by the weakness of [the Republic]. In that way it would have time, once minds are calmed, ... to improve and fortify the ports and frontiers, to redress the true abuses in the constitution, and to reform ... the ministers. Without such an alliance the Republic runs the risk that [England] and the [Emperor], arms in hand, ... dictate to it what they please: [England] will first seize the Dutch possessions ... and renew the treaty, as harmful as it is dishonourable ...; [...] will open ... navigation ..., and seize all the possessions of [the Republic] ... [France] alone ... because of the disorder of their finances ... Spain has almost no interest ... But if these three powers unite in a defensive and offensive alliance for some years with [the Republic], then the circumstances of the time make all four powers find their interest in it, and, allied together, they will prudently give themselves the forces needed to stop the ambitious views, harmful to all Europe, of the [Emperor] and of [Russia]. Write to me on this subject. **Jan 1784 (s173-s174).** ... what the politicians of your country think of it; and if I am left to act, I shall turn the whole to the good of [the Republic] and of the House of Orange. The change of ministry in [England] will not change the plan formed between the [Emperor] and the King of [England] ... for the needs of my mission ... the purse of [His Serene Highness] in a secret correspondence ... known to [His Serene Highness] ... that [His Majesty] be interested in my mission, and that his interest and the fate of the House of Orange, which alone are dear to me, with regard to [Her Royal Highness], absolutely required it, I would never have revealed myself ... out of love for [Her Royal Highness] ... to watch over the mind of [His Majesty] and make him conceive and accept all that tends to the good of [the Republic] and of the House of Orange ... But if by chance it succeeded, these are the points on which I could make my reckoning: ... to remove Monsieur Larrey's prejudice that I am only a simple carrier of letters ... that is, my true secret, the necessity of my mission, the influence I have over the mind of [His Majesty] ... in political affairs ... with all the King's men of business ... in matters of negotiation ... **26-27 Jan and Feb 1784.** P.S. [The King] is much better today, and at bottom his illness is not dangerous; it is only a cramp in the arms. If the news that reached Holland was not written directly by Madame la Marquise de Chatelet or by Count G. von Goertz, it still comes from that source ... will have told it to Monsieur [...] and Schula will have written it to [Heiden]. As regards the correspondence, the channel is not discovered and never will be ... of [the Prince]; here there must also be a regular exchange of letters ... there is no one of [the Cabal] who knows me ... the confidence of [His Serene Highness] ... informed of much of what passes at foreign courts ... for the interests of the House of Orange and of the Republic ... nothing can hold me but love for my very dear Princess, for I have long loathed my secret post ... underlined letters of [His Serene Highness], [Her Royal Highness], [Van der Hoop], [His Majesty] and [Schoning] ... that he be at [Berlin] ... to the new [...] of [France] ... **10 July 1784.** The revolt the Gazette placed at Petersburg was really at Constantinople, stirred up by "our" Gaffron; [His Majesty] recalled him, and he will be put in Spandau ([the Cabal], [Prussia], [the Stadholder], [the King]). A despatch from the Sienese embassy at Milan to the Officials of the Balìa with eleven lines of cipher and a faint interlinear gloss (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 7, DECODE R4796). The embassy’s filed key of 1454 and five other keys fail the gloss, and annealing with its nine values fixed does not converge. A Sienese orator at Milan → the Officials of the Balìa, Siena · homophonic substitution, key unknown · 1450s · attempted, not solved Siena no. 7: the orator at Milan An eleven-line cipher block in a despatch from the Sienese embassy at Milan; the embassy’s own filed key of 1454 does not fit it, and a reader’s faint gloss gives only nine values. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter A long Italian despatch to the “Officiales Balie” of Siena from an orator at Milan, who names messer Lionardo Benvoglienti and the Duke of Milan; 1450s. The signature and date line are torn. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2 “Lettere in cifra”, no. 7; DECODE R4796 ( Concistoro_2308_50 , 2 pp.), catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher Eleven lines of digits, letters and signs near the foot of page 1, with clear words between the runs. The faint glosses show a homophonic cipher: o has at least two signs. How it was tried The 1454 key of the Milan ambassadors (R4750) and five other filed keys were tested sign by sign against the gloss, and all fail it. Homophonic annealing, with the gloss values fixed or free, does not converge. Why it resists 363 signs over at least 45 sign types are too few for a ciphertext-only break, and no key in the busta fits. Credit George Lasry’s report of 17 October 2026 lists no. 7 as not yet deciphered: “c. 330 symbols, a few words with interlinear plaintext”. The other pieces of the Sienese cipher file are listed by key on the Concistoro 2308 index . No. 8 , of about 1440–41, is a different cipher with its own page; its key does not fit no. 7.

The despatch fills about 45 lines of page 1 and a postscript on page 2. It is addressed to the “Magnifici et excelsi domini Officiales Balie”, names “messer Lionardo Benvoglienti” in the third person, speaks of the Duke of Milan, and in the postscript of the “conte Iacomo” (Jacopo Piccinino?), Genoa and Bologna. Benvoglienti was Siena’s ambassador at Milan in 1454, and fascicle 1 of the busta holds the key made for that embassy (R4750, “a messer Leonardo e messer Antonio, ambasciatori a Milano, 1454”), so the letter is placed in the 1450s. The writer signs “Servitor vester Orator” and a name that cannot be read with confidence. The cipher block, lines 2–12 of the foot of page 1, with clear words between the runs. The faint glosses are over line 4 and line 8. Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 7, p. 1, via DECODE R4796. A reader has written single letters over some signs: over line 8, l a n o t e r o i o above ten signs. The alignment gives 7 = l , q = a , 6 = n , + = o , a barred 3 = t , 2 = e , x = r , a ringed 8 = i , c = o (sign names from the transcription in targets/siena7/transcripts/ ).

The embassy’s key, R4750 (24 September 2026), tested sign by sign on the image: the gloss contradicts it (R4750 makes 7 = o , 6 = i , + = s , 2 = f where the gloss has l , n , o , e ), a fifth of the letter’s signs are not in it, and its only sign for e would be 2.5% of the text. A “milano” reported early on came from free signs in a solver run and was withdrawn. Five more filed keys , R4753, R4754, R4756, R4757 and R4762, transcribed and tested against the gloss: none fits. The others of fascicle 1 were compared by eye. Homophonic annealing (the solver that gave the keys of nos. 14 , 18 and 25 ), first free, then on 18 October 2026 with the nine gloss values fixed (twelve restarts, Italian n-grams of the period): the restarts disagree and none reads, at about −2.04 per sign. The key of no. 8 , rebuilt on 18 October 2026 from its contemporary decipherment: a different key (7 = d , + = c , 2 = a there).

The whole cipher block, 363 signs by this transcription (George Lasry counts c. 330; the difference is in how joined and look-alike signs are split). Without a key, it is too short for the number of signs. A fresh transcription in CTTS, as George Lasry made for the fascicle’s solved pieces, may change the sign count enough for a new solver run with the gloss values fixed.

The telegrams of Sun’s circle copied for the Japanese Foreign Ministry, which could not decode them. Condenser keys of the Swatow telegram’s family were recovered from the telegrams themselves and decode fifty-six telegrams of 1916 and Sun’s exchange with Dai Jitao of 1917, in whole or in part. The two later 1916 systems were decoded by Brice Dudout in October 2026; the June 1917 telegrams are open. Thirtyseventh setilecupi kidepevesu qitonerise qinufugeji zisasotafo cuhelaxeri vodeyucipa … biqucageni Shanghai ↔ Tokyo · telegraph code + code condensers · March 1916 – March 1917 Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 to Sun Yat-sen The copies the Ministry of Communications made for the Japanese Foreign Ministry of every telegram to or from Sun’s people · JACAR, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, 特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, vols 2–4 · no decodes in the files The keys were recovered from the telegrams themselves; there is no decode in the files. Fifty-six condenser telegrams of March–May 1916 decode in whole or in part under five further keys of the Swatow telegram’s family and two tentative ones; so do a Hankow digit telegram and Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917, in another key of the family. The telegrams of July–November 1916 are in two systems outside the family; Brice Dudout decoded them in October 2026 ( section 07 ). The June 1917 telegrams are not decoded. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial The documents Copies of telegrams and letters to and from Sun Yat-sen’s circle, 1916–17, sent by the Communications Bureau of the Japanese Ministry of Communications to the Foreign Ministry. The Swatow telegram of 3 April 1916 ( decoded here earlier ) was one sheet of them. Where Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, volumes 2 to 4, on JACAR (B03050088300 and five further files). The files hold no decodes; the Foreign Ministry could not decode the ciphered telegrams. The cipher Ten-letter condenser words: a hundred syllables numbered 01–00, two syllables to a four-figure Chinese telegraph code group, no additive. One key for each pair of correspondents, all of one systematic family. How it was read A key was accepted only when it stood at z ≥ 6 on one long telegram and then decoded others that played no part in finding it. Rhyme-day date codes in the signatures agree with the dates on the forms. What it says The telegrams follow Sun’s party through the end of Yuan Shikai’s monarchy, ending on 19 May 1916 with the news that Chen Qimei (Yingshi) was shot dead by assassins the day before. Credit Brice Dudout decoded the two systems of July–November 1916 (checked here on three telegrams) and found that most of the one-letter changes first blamed on copying clerks were misreadings of the forms. Still open Most long telegrams keep a few undecoded groups, marked [?]. The June 1917 telegrams are not decoded.

The series is 各国内政関係雑纂／支那ノ部／革命党関係（亡命者ヲ含ム）／特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, volumes 2 to 4, on JACAR as B03050088300, B03050088400, B03050089100, B03050090000, B03050090100 and B03050090200. Each batch comes under a covering note headed 特定人發着郵便物等取調ノ件 (“inquiry into mail etc. sent and received by specified persons”), from the Director of the Communications Bureau (逓信省通信局長 田中) to the Director of the Foreign Ministry’s Political Affairs Bureau (政務局長 小池, Koike Chōzō). A typical note, 秘第八?之一號 of 25 May 1916, received the next day, reads 別紙寫電報及左記郵便物有之候: “attached are copied telegrams and the postal item noted below”. The telegrams are copied onto the Imperial Telegraphs’ own forms. Outgoing messages from Tokyo are on “Forwarded” forms, signed 中山 (Nakayama, Sun’s Japanese alias) or, in May, with the handler’s name 林蔚陸 (“Linwailuk”). Incoming messages are on “Received” forms addressed to “Rosamonde Tokio” (Soong Ching-ling), to “Linwailuk Tokio”, or to Nakayama at 109 Harajuku, Aoyama. The correspondents are Yamada Junzaburō in Shanghai (“Junzaburo Shanghai”), “Konglipo” in Manila, Kayano Nagatomo and Ju Zheng’s men at Qingdao (Seitō), “Youngchina” at San Francisco, Honolulu, Hankow, and the Shanghai leadership: Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi and the rest. Some of the traffic is in clear English (“2000 through Shokinginko”), and some is in plain telegraph code. Most of it is in ten-letter condenser words. The files hold no decodes. The Foreign Ministry did try. In B03050089100, frames 0076–0078 are a notebook copy of a long romanised kana stream (126 ten-letter groups, ending owari ), and frames 0079–0081 are the analysts’ worksheets on it. They copy the stream into katakana, divide it with slashes into groups of two or three, and pencil kanji guesses beside the groups, often with a question mark: 事, 先生, 國, 電, 軍, 謀. No continuous sense comes out of them. The stream is not a condenser telegram: it is two telegrams of 20 May 1916 to Huang Xing in the three-kana code, which Satoshi Tomokiyo’s formula (September 2026) decodes. Harumi-Matsuba read both in October 2026, with many spelling corrections; they are written up with Huang Xing’s reply on their own page .

The system is the one described on the Swatow page . Twenty consonants (no w ) and five vowels give a hundred syllables numbered 01…99, 00, and two syllables make one four-figure group of the standard Chinese telegraph code. The syllables run on across ten-letter words without regard to the word breaks, and there is no additive. Every table in the family is a rule: the alphabet rotated or reversed, the vowels in some order, the numbers filled vowel by vowel. What changes between correspondents is the rotation and the vowel order: key row for 01 vowel order used on swatow1916 l e a i o u “Tanaka”, Swatow → Rosamonde, 3 April 1916 ( the Swatow telegram ) shanghai1916 z (alphabet reversed) i o a e u Sun ↔ Yamada Junzaburō, Shanghai; Shanghai (Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi …) → Rosamonde, March–April 1916 manila1916 g o e u a i Sun ↔ Konglipo, Manila; one Shanghai telegram signed by Xu Chongzhi seito1916 m u i e o a Qingdao (Ju Zheng; Kayano Nagatomo) ↔ Tokyo, March–April 1916 sanfran1916 x o e u a i Tokyo → “Youngchina”, San Francisco yamada1916 q e u i o a Tokyo (Xie Chi, “Linwailuk”) ↔ Junzaburo, Shanghai, May 1916 shanghai1917 k a e u o i Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917 ( below ) “Row for 01” is the consonant that takes 01 with the first vowel; the next consonant in the alphabet takes 02, and so on. The key names are those in famtest.py . Two more keys are tentative, each resting on one short telegram: Honolulu (alphabet reversed, filled consonant by consonant, vowels e a o u i ; z 4.9) and Manila in May (row for 01 d , vowels e u a o i ; z 4.4). Finding and accepting a key. The whole family, 57,600 tables counting the fill orders, origins and the ±111 additive, was run on each telegram, and each table was scored with a Chinese character model. The z figures on this page are that score measured against the whole family. A short telegram can put a wrong key on top by chance, so a key was accepted only when it reached z ≥ 6 on at least one long telegram and then decoded other telegrams it had not been fitted to. For example, shanghai1916 was found on a long Shanghai → Rosamonde telegram and then decoded Sun’s own outgoing telegrams to Yamada at z 7–10. The May key yamada1916 decodes every telegram that carries the clear prefix word “Thirtyseventh”. Some short telegrams decode under their pair’s key although another table scores slightly higher on them alone. They are counted as decoded because the text makes sense and the key is fixed elsewhere; their own score does not decide it. The dates check themselves. Chinese telegrams give the day of the month by a rhyme-category character (韻目代日). Where a signature carries one, it agrees with the date on the Japanese form: 支 4, 元 13, 篠 17, 皓 19, 號 20, 箇 21, 漾 23, 有 25, 宥 26, 豔 29. The one exception is a Shanghai telegram handed in on 22 May that ends 馬, the 21st. The date characters come out of the decryption and the key search never looked at them, so the agreement is an independent check. The copies, and our transcription of them. These are copies made by Japanese telegraph clerks of letter strings that meant nothing to them. Some groups decode only after a one-letter change: g ↔ q most often, then x against d or s , h ↔ k ↔ n , e ↔ c , a ↔ o . This page first blamed the clerks for these changes. Most of them were our own misreadings. In October 2026 Brice Dudout checked our transcriptions of the March–May 1916 telegrams against the JACAR scans. This copyist’s q has its loop on the right and his g has it on the left. Of the 47 transcribed g that Dudout checked, 30 are q on the form, and no q is a g . Of the 21 emendations in our transcriptions, 19 are already written correctly on the form. Only two are errors in the 1916 copies: 請 on 4 April and 傷 on 19 May. In all he reports 28 wrong letters. He also found that our transcription of the 3 April Shanghai → Rosamonde telegram had left out a whole word on its second sheet (fr. 0489, sixth line). That is jobusosuji , and putting it back realigns the end of the message: 已澈查局非誣騙 (“we have looked into it thoroughly; it is not a swindle”), where our version had 已[?]非誣騙[?]. Every case checked here since then agrees with him: this one, and the two 1916 forms in section 07 . The March 1917 forms in section 06 show our transcription making the same kind of misreading, and two whole words left out. His full list of 28 has not yet been gone through here, letter by letter. A character in brackets on this page is therefore a change to our transcription. It is not necessarily a slip by the clerk. A dropped pair of letters makes a telegram decode as noise until the pair is restored. The 25 May telegram from Tokyo scores z 4.1 as transcribed and 6.8 once a ge is put back in its first word.

Conventions: [?] = group decoded as written but doubtful; a character in brackets = the decoding after a one-letter change to our transcription (most of these are our misreadings, not the clerk’s; see above); □ = not decoded. Frame numbers are JACAR frames of B03050088300 unless stated. Yuan Shikai announced the end of his monarchy on 22 March 1916. At that point Sun Yat-sen was in Tokyo and his party was planning a rising in Shanghai. 25 March, Shanghai → Rosamonde (fr. 0468; z 6.7) 帝制取消，馮、朱等當漸觀望。滬異派力弱，於我略可從容佈置。海軍[?]發策較萬全，然猶急備未懈… “The monarchy is cancelled. Feng [Guozhang], Zhu [Rui] and the others will now wait and see. The opposing faction in Shanghai is weak, so we can make our dispositions at some leisure. A plan launched by the Navy … is safer, but we are still preparing urgently without slackening …” There is no signature. 26 March, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0465; z 7.4) 京信□□□策：袁暫退，使黎代；俟歐戰終，乃借英力[復]出。故滬事當發於袁退之前乃可。文 “The Peking letter … plan: Yuan to step down for now, with Li [Yuanhong] acting; when the European war ends, he comes back with British support. So the Shanghai action must be launched before Yuan withdraws. — Wen.” The same evening a 38-word telegram from Shanghai signed 美 (Chen Qimei; z 9.2) asked for arms to be shipped and a handover procedure, and closed: 穆日當局允暗濟械，已有接洽否？ (“The authorities have agreed to supply arms secretly: has contact been made?”). 穆 occurs twice with the same letters and is probably a cover word. 27 March, Sun → Konglipo, Manila (fr. 0462; manila1916) 滬電乃崇智所發，勿疑。文 “The Shanghai telegram was sent by [Xu] Chongzhi. Do not doubt it.” Earlier that day Manila had asked who was using the code to send telegrams from Shanghai, calling it 萬可疑, “most suspicious”. Xu Chongzhi’s own telegram of the 26th, signed in clear Shuichunchee , is in the Manila key, not the Shanghai one. 30 March – 4 April: money Much of the traffic is fund-raising. Tokyo asks the Fujian merchants in Manila to 盡力向閩幫籌[款?] (“do their utmost to raise funds from the Fujian guild”); Qingdao asks for fifty thousand, 惟需五萬元，懇速電匯 (“only we need 50,000 yuan; wire it urgently”); Manila reports what seems to be four thousand sent through the Hongkong Bank (a four-word telegram, weakly scored), and Tokyo acknowledges [四?]千圓. From Shanghai on 31 March (z 8.2): 田在滬交五千，到漢匯八千。近[又?]索三萬，無力應之 (“田 [a person] handed over 5,000 in Shanghai, 8,000 to be remitted on reaching Hankow. Lately another 30,000 is demanded; we have no means to meet it”). On the same day Sun warns Yamada (fr. 0485; z 7.9): 北方來電，帝制取消，軍心益振。而[滬?]反[?]觀望。恐前聯絡之人皆多不實，故托此爲辭，[?]得款耳。望兄詳察，勿受其欺。孫文 “Telegrams from the north: the monarchy is cancelled and the army’s spirit rises. But [Shanghai?] is … waiting to see. I fear the people we contacted earlier are mostly not genuine and use this as an excuse to get money. Look into it carefully and do not be taken in. — Sun Wen.” 4 April, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0494; z 9.8, no emendation) 由臺灣電六百金，請交寶昌路寶康里一八三號張宗海，往甘費。聞西林赴南寧組政府，定設法破之。文 “600 gold wired by way of Taiwan: please give it to Zhang Zonghai, 183 Baokang-li, Baochang Road, for the journey to Gansu. I hear Xilin [Cen Chunxuan] is going to Nanning to form a government: I will find a way to break it. — Wen.” This is the cleanest telegram in the files: forty characters and not one letter to change. Two more went out that afternoon. One ends 山東消息甚佳，月內當動。孫文。支 (“news from Shandong is very good; it will move within the month. — Sun Wen, the 4th”). The other, to Kayano at Qingdao (fr. 0492; seito1916, z 7.4), reports fifty thousand sent through the Yokohama Specie Bank, and arms to be shipped under the name of the Qingdao military administration (以寄青島軍政官名義). 13 April, Hankow → Sun (B03050088400 fr. 0517) This telegram is in digits, not condenser letters. It uses the +111 code that Consul Segawa described to the Foreign Ministry that May: each four-figure code group has 111 added, here without the digit reversal. A search over every additive and both digit orders puts −111 175 log-points clear of the next candidate, and the telegram then decodes with no emendation: 武漢發動事，日人謂非念五萬不辦。迭電陸參兩部，桐以軍械運輸困難且爲時久。刻人心已熟，海陸均有七分以上把握，三萬可行。機不可[失]，望速決電示。元 “On the Wuhan rising: the Japanese say it cannot be done for under 250,000. [We] have wired the Army Ministry and the General Staff again and again; 桐 says the arms and their transport are difficult and would take a long time. Opinion here is ripe; army and navy are both more than seventy per cent sure; 30,000 would do it. The moment must not be missed. Decide quickly and wire. — the 13th.”

By May, Sun was in Shanghai, where he arrived at the start of the month, and the Tokyo end was run by Xie Chi (謝持), who signs 持 and dates with rhyme characters. Every Tokyo–Shanghai condenser telegram of that month that decodes at all decodes under one key, yamada1916 (frames of B03050089100). 19 May, Shanghai → Linwailuk, Tokyo (fr. 0066; z 6.0) 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃，捕兇[一?]人，關係者數人。 “Yingshi was shot dead by assassins yesterday afternoon in the Yamada house; one assassin and several accomplices arrested.” Chen Qimei (陳其美, courtesy name Yingshi) was murdered in Shanghai on 18 May 1916 in the house of Yamada Junzaburō, the addressee of most of the Tokyo traffic. Tokyo replied the same day in two telegrams (both signed 持皓, the 19th): 英士被刺，傷[勢?]如何？盼覆 (“Yingshi stabbed: how are the wounds? Please reply”), and then 電悉。英士捐軀，極堪慟悼。主使爲誰？盼覆。先生[?]在滬[?]，務處處戒備。持皓 “Telegram received. Yingshi has given his life; we mourn him deeply. Who was behind it? Please reply. The Master … in Shanghai … must take every precaution. — Chi, the 19th.” Others asked the same question in other ways. From Kobe, 英士君遭難確否乞覆 came in plain code. From Manila, received on 23 May, 聞陳英士死確否？請覆 came to Tōyama Mitsuru in a key of its own. The Shanghai answer of 22 May (z 8.2) gives the instigator as 遣之暗殺主謀爲[政?]府, “the government”, and says that the pistols have been entrusted to Miyazaki to bring back. 23–25 May: arms and the students Tokyo on 23 May (z 8.2): Wu Feiji, back in Shanghai at 26 Rue Joffre, has ordered 300 Type-30 rifles and 100 Browning pistols through the Ōkura company at Dalian, with 2,000 taels already paid as deposit. Tokyo and Shanghai also wire back and forth about 席、趙兩處學生事, the business of Xi Zhengming’s and Zhao’s students at Tianjin, which had been demanding money for a rising. On 22 May Shanghai orders it stopped; on 24 May it says 學生事暫擱 (“shelve the students affair”); on 25 May Tokyo asks which of the two it means. 26 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0092–93; z 9.6) 克強言外務省意先生宜緩赴青島。又軍械事能得青木一電參謀本部較更有力云云… 宥 “Keqiang [Huang Xing] says the Foreign Ministry’s view is that the Master should put off going to Qingdao. Also, on the arms, a telegram from Aoki [probably Lt-Gen. Aoki Nobuzumi] to the General Staff would carry more weight … — the 26th.” Here Sun’s Tokyo office passes the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s own advice to Sun, and the Foreign Ministry was being sent a copy of the telegram. It had no means of decoding it. Earlier that morning Tokyo had asked 報載先生昨[潛?]離滬，確否？ (“the papers report that the Master secretly left Shanghai yesterday; is it true?”). 29 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0113–14; z 6.6) 據譚根云，岑有軍[火]船四艘由神戸回粤，今遣彼來東運機[?]二臺，交該船載[?]…謝持 豔 “According to Tan Gen, Cen [Chunxuan] has four military steamers going from Kobe back to Guangdong, and has sent him to Japan to ship two machine[-guns?] on them … — Xie Chi, the 29th.” Cen Chunxuan is the “Xilin” whose government at Nanning Sun had promised on 4 April to break.

From July the ciphered traffic changes to two systems that are not in the family ( below ), but some telegrams in the later volumes are in plain telegraph code. Two of them belong to the same story. 10 July, Luzhou → “Ilchang Tokio” (B03050090000 fr. 0417) 宥電敬悉。承念甚感。久罹喉病，軍中失調，醫治漸痊，幸釋綺注。鍔叩。蒸 “Your telegram of the 26th received with respect. I am most grateful for your concern. I have long suffered from a throat illness, made worse by life with the army; treatment is gradually curing it; please set your mind at rest. — E, the 10th.” This is Cai E (蔡鍔), who led the Yunnan rising against the monarchy. The throat illness killed him in Fukuoka on 8 November 1916. 13 September, Tokyo (中田) → Huang Xing, Shanghai (B03050090100 fr. 0471) 閱報憂悚。接[?]電，母[恙?]稍安。請靜養。現如何？ “Alarmed to read the papers. […] telegram received; your mother is a little better. Please rest. How are you now?” Huang Xing was already ill, and he died on 31 October 1916, eight days before Cai E. The Japanese clerk’s own kanji glosses on this form differ from the codebook at two groups (4443 and 3225).

B03050090200 (vol. 4, item 5, frames 0503–0513) holds three condenser telegrams of late March 1917. Two are from Sun in Shanghai, signed Sunwen in clear, to “Toi c/o Kikuchi Rioichi” in Tokyo. The third is the reply to “Sun yatsen Shanghai”, signed Tenkiutai (天仇, Dai Jitao). “Toi” is therefore Dai Jitao (戴季陶), staying with Kikuchi Ryōichi (菊池良一). The key is a seventh member of the family: row for 01 k , vowels a e u o i , no additive. It was found by running the family on the 23 March telegram alone, where it scores −321.6 against a population mean of −556.4 and s.d. 25.8, about nine standard deviations up; the next unrelated key is 124 points behind. The Swatow key gives nonsense. The 25 and 26 March telegrams played no part in finding the key, and both decoded under it at once. Dai Jitao to Sun, 26 March 1917 (JACAR B03050090200, frame 0506). The last word, zimucuzahu , ends in zahu = 1359 宥, the rhyme code for the 26th, which is the date on the form. We first transcribed it as zimucuzaku and put the difference down to a clerk’s slip, but the form has h . Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, via JACAR B03050090200, frame 0506. 23 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0504) 前電云三日後商妥□□□□□□□□□接後音。此間必俟前約取消，始可致電北京照辦。各約已取消否？速覆。公司抄件瑞士尚未辦妥。文 “My previous telegram said that after three days [the matter] would be settled by agreement … received further word. Here we must wait until the former contract is cancelled before we can wire Peking to act accordingly. Have the contracts all been cancelled? Reply at once. The company copy … [瑞士?] not yet settled. — Wen.” Words 4 to 7 on the form are pixaqaqe macorarala veyurojiji eianakerele . Our first transcription left out the two middle words, and this page then blamed the gap on the clerk. With them restored, all 22 code words on the form are accounted for. Two faults are on the form itself: pixaqaqe has eight letters, and eianakerele has eleven and begins with ei , which is not a syllable. pi completes 妥, and lebe 接 decodes as written, so “…接後音” is likely. About nine codes between them are still not decoded. If one syllable is put into pixaqaqe , the restored words give ordinary characters (再, 告, 候, 至) instead of noise, which suggests that a syllable is missing there. They do not give a text that can be adopted. 瑞士 needs an x / m change and is the least certain emendation. The telegram’s last word, qixapfete , has nine letters; read qixa pi ne te it gives 辦妥 and 文, Sun’s signature character, which also closes the 25 March telegram. 25 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0507) 函悉。約取消後，當□□□能否。取消卽覆。文 “Letter received. After the contract is cancelled, [whether] … is possible. Reply as soon as it is cancelled. — Wen.” 能 is xubo . We first read its first letter as z , but it has the shape of this clerk’s x elsewhere on the form. Three codes do not decode, and no one-letter variant makes sense of them. 26 March, Dai → Sun (fr. 0506) 本定今日赴熱海。□□來云：彼等須先□定，約三日回。□公司事如何？電示。宥 “I was to have gone to Atami today. … came and said that they must first settle …; [I shall be] back in about three days. How stands the company matter? Wire me. — the 26th.” 公司 has the same qabo for 司 that decodes cleanly on 23 March. The two characters before 來云 do not decode. 小池 (Koike Chōzō, who had left the Foreign Ministry’s Political Bureau in 1916) is two letters away and is no more than a guess. The first word begins with the clerk’s capital Q , so 本 ( qeta ) is as written on the form. The other one-letter changes on the three March 1917 forms have not yet been checked again on the images. Together the three telegrams show Sun, in the last week of March 1917, waiting for “the former contract” to be cancelled before he can wire Peking, pressing Dai for news, and Dai asking after “the company matter”. They do not say what the contract or the company was. That needs the Chinese record for March 1917, which has not been consulted.

The ciphered telegrams of July to November 1916 in B03050089900–B03050090100 were decoded in October 2026 by Brice Dudout, who has published his readings, transcriptions and solver at bdudout.github.io/wenmi ( github.com/bdudout/wenmi , CC BY 4.0). They are in two systems. This page had earlier taken them for a single “文密 code”. Both systems number the syllables consonant by consonant, with the vowel order reversed on every second consonant. Each pair of syllables then gives one standard telegraph code, with no additive. Tokyo → the 軍務院 (Zhaoqing, later Canton), June–September 1916. After the 軍務院 was dissolved, this channel went on to Cen Chunxuan’s headquarters (岑都司令, 13 September, fr. 0455b; 都司令部, 30 September, fr. 0462, with 李印泉, Li Genyuan, named in clear). One telegram, fr. 0406, went to the 中華新報 in Shanghai. Five vowels, and twenty consonants that include w and y and leave out j , in the order h g f d c b z y x w v t s r q p n m l k. The syllables run ha = 00 … hu = 04, gu = 05 … ga = 09, and so on to 99. Most forms on this channel carry the clear prefix 文密 (2429 1378); in Dudout’s set only fr. 0386 and 0462 lack it. Tokyo → Yunnan (Tang Jiyao, the provincial assembly, the finance office) and Shanghai (中華新報), July–November 1916. Six vowels, with y as a vowel, and seventeen consonants in alphabetical order, b d f g h k l m n p r s t v w x z. A syllable’s value is 6 × consonant rank + vowel rank, with the vowels in the order y u o i e a, reversed on odd ranks. The last two cells, ze and za , would be 100 and 101, and are never used. Dudout fixed the grid from a clear-code telegram sent the same day (fr. 0489b). He then tested it on telegrams that played no part in finding it, among them the report of Cai E’s death at Fukuoka on 8 November (fr. 0496). Most forms on this channel begin with Cg in clear, which is counted in the word count; none of the five-vowel forms has it. What it stands for is not known. Both grids were checked here on our own copies of the forms. The transcriptions used were made here, not taken from Dudout’s files. Where they differed from his, the forms agree with him. 5 November 1916, Tokyo → 唐督軍, Yunnanfu (B03050090100 fr. 0489a), six-vowel grid 擬十號南歸。謹聞。伸 歌 “I plan to return south on the 10th. Respectfully reported. — Shen, the 5th.” All nine codes come out as written on the form. The first word is gyrobatapo , as Dudout reads it; our transcription had gyrotatapo and so needed a change for 十. The clear-code telegram on the same sheet, to the provincial assembly (省議會), reads 十號起程月末抵滇 伸 歌 (“leaving on the 10th, reaching Yunnan at the end of the month”). The sender’s address on both forms is written 青山南町四ノ二一 関方 趙伸: Zhao Shen, care of Seki, Aoyama Minami-machi. 伸 is therefore 趙伸 (Zhao Shen), the 軍務院’s commissioner in Japan. Dudout identified him from fr. 0498. 19 July 1916, Tokyo → 軍務院, Canton (B03050090000 fr. 0416b), five-vowel grid 文密 報傳取消，日人態度遽變，確否？速示，俾便行止。伸 [皓] “Reported cancelled, and the Japanese attitude has suddenly changed: is it so? Advise at once, so that I can decide whether to go ahead or stop. — Shen, the 19th.” One one-letter change, i → e , gives 皓, the rhyme-day code for the 19th, which is the date on the form. Dudout makes the same change. This page first had two more changes, and a different ending, 俾便行檄 (“so that the circular can go out”). Both came from our misreadings. The form has xodugoluro , whose first letter has the same shape as both x in the next word, xoxotuhica ; we had read it as r . It has qiheyuxifa , which we had read with a g . The q gives 止 (2972) where g gave 檄 (2907). Dudout pointed out that the companion telegram sent the same day on the other channel ends with the same phrase. Transcribed here and decoded in his six-vowel grid with no change, it reads: 19 July 1916, Tokyo → 中華新報 Shanghai, for Tang Jiyao (B03050090000 fr. 0416a), six-vowel grid 轉文羣轉滇督 Cg 滇索槍萬枝可辦到。因報傳軍院取消，方針遽變，確否？速示，俾便行止。伸 皓 The first six groups are in clear code: “forward to 文羣, to be forwarded to the Yunnan governor”. The rest reads: “The ten thousand rifles Yunnan asks for can be arranged. But on the report that the 軍務院 is to be dissolved, the line has suddenly changed. Is it so? Advise at once, so that I can decide whether to go ahead or stop. — Shen, the 19th.” The decoding is Dudout’s grid applied to our own transcription of the form. A correction. This page earlier treated the July 1916 traffic as a single code and gave the six-vowel system the name 文密. On fr. 0416 the prefix 文密 stands on the five-vowel telegram to the 軍務院. The six-vowel telegram on the same frame, to 中華新報, opens instead with 轉文羣轉滇督 in clear code. The six-vowel search run here (about 200,000 tables) could not have found either grid. It was run only on the June 1917 telegrams, with rotated consonant orders and no reversal of the vowels.

Brice Dudout has since carried the work back into the 1913–1915 volumes of the same series (JACAR B03050087300–B03050087700) and forward into the numeric telegrams of June–July 1916. By 19 October 2026 his site gave readings of 194 telegrams in eight systems, with the scans, his reviewed transcriptions, the raw decodes and working translations ( telegrams , method ). His count, in telegraph codes decoded: System Telegrams Codes Read Doubtful Illegible 文密, grid G0 (five vowels) 7 351 333 12 0 Grid Y0 (six vowels, Yunnan channel) 10 456 412 24 2 Code condensers, 1913–1916, all tables 139 5,179 4,482 612 10 “Hong Kong” digit substitution, 1914 2 44 43 1 0 共密, 容密, 辰密 numeric codes, June–July 1916 (pages: 共密 , 容密 , 辰密 ) 27 2,100 1,940 154 6 Chinese telegraph code in clear 9 410 380 30 0 Total 194 8,540 7,590 833 18 The condenser row includes the March–May 1916 telegrams on this page, which Dudout re-read against the scans, and the tables first recovered here. Not counted: the 22 Rosamonde telegrams in enciphered English ( page ). The condenser tables he added are all of the same family as the keys in section 02 . Each is given here as consonant order / vowel order / filled by vowel (V, value = 20 × vowel rank + consonant rank) or by consonant (C, value = 5 × consonant rank + vowel rank) / first number: “Laisaosang” , Tokyo ↔ Shanghai, June 1914 – February 1915: c…b / o a e u i / V / 01. “New York” , New York → Sun, July 1914 – February 1915: b…z (p and q merged) / a e i o u / C / 00, the simplest table of the family. “Hsuweilin” , San Francisco → “Hsuweilin”, July 1914: b…z without k / a e i o u / C / 01. “Thirtieth” , Shanghai ↔ Tokyo, February–May 1915, named in clear on the forms: v…t / u i e o a / V / 01. “Thirteenth” , Tokyo → Shanghai, February–March 1916, also named in clear: n…m / o a e i u / V / 01. “Sixteenth” and “Seventeenth” , Shanghai ↔ Tokyo, April 1916: t…s / e u o i a and p…n / i u a e o , both V / 01. “Thirtyeight” , Tokyo → Shanghai, early May 1916, the yamada1916 construction with other parameters: k…j / e a i u o / V / 01. It decodes the telegram of 12 May about the iron trunk left with Inuzuka (箱已交犬塚，十五日附法船來) and that of 11 May asking whether Zhang Ji is back in Japan. Huang Xing’s table , Tokyo ↔ Shanghai (“Ylchang”, Huang Xing’s Tokyo address), late May – June 1916: consonants d c b t h j f q g k n m p s r l x w z v / u i o e a / C / 01. The Tokyo telegrams end 覆。興 (“reply. — Xing”), and the Shanghai ones are signed 文 or 孫文. On 3 June Huang reports that he has seen Tanaka and that 槍二千、砲六門不日可運 (“2,000 rifles and 6 guns can be shipped shortly”). The “Hong Kong” telegrams of March 1914 are not condensers. Each letter stands for one digit ( y k u l o c a p i t = 0–9), and four digits make one standard code: kcpk = 1571 = 已. Two keys this page had marked tentative now stand on more than one telegram. The Manila table reads a Tokyo → “Konglipo” telegram of 6 January 1915 with no change (無其事。文覆, “there is nothing of the sort. — Wen, replying”), sixteen months before the telegram it was found on. The Honolulu table reads the “Aloha” telegrams of April–May 1916 if w stands for v . Dudout’s site also names the sender and recipient of every telegram it publishes, with the evidence for each attribution (signature, address, header or series) and a grade of certain or probable. None of these readings has been checked here on the forms, apart from the three in section 07 .

On 27 October 2026 Brice Dudout sent the full texts behind section 08 as pull requests (#144–#163): for each telegram the transcription of the form, the decode group by group, the Chinese text with punctuation and a working English translation. One key is one folder, so each table below has its own folder in the repository. They are his readings, published on his site; they were read through as sentences when merged, but the forms were not re-read here. These tables have no page of their own: this list is their entry on the site. The same folder holds his 28 corrections to our transcriptions ( corrections.tsv ) and his re-reading notes. The numeric codes of June–July 1916 are on three pages, one per key ( 共密 , 容密 , 辰密 ), with his N01 and N09 乾密 texts added the same day, and the Rosamonde telegrams on theirs .

The June 1917 telegrams between Sun and Dai (B03050090200 fr. 0509, 0511) are in neither 1916 grid. They also contain clusters that are not consonant–vowel pairs ( myzoasdoke , liriopen ). The second word of fr. 0509 is written vemucäyri . In Morse, ä (·−·−) is e + k run together, so Dudout reads vemucekyri . Dudout’s search on these telegrams, every table scored with the same language model on the standard telegraph code, has found nothing: alphabetical grids of 17–20 consonants × 6 vowels, in every rotation, both directions, all 720 vowel orders, serpentine or not: about 194,000 tables on a machine transcription, 241,000 on his own and 840,000 with y as a consonant; free consonant and vowel orders, by simulated annealing, for 17 × 6 and 18 × 6 tables filled consonant by consonant (with and without the 1916 alternating vowel order), vowel by vowel (as in the March 1917 key), and vertically serpentine, from 0 or 1. As a positive control, Chinese text of the same length (about 90 codes) enciphered with a random table of each layout came back whole, 88 of 88 codes in every layout. On the June 1917 text the best tables score about +0.9 per code, against about +0.6 for the null, and no two runs agree; a true table should give +3 to +5; the same tables with the Hankow-style transformations (±111, reversal, digit-wise −111); a 20 × 6 coordinate model with anchors (文 or 孫文 at the end of 0509, 戴 at the end of 0511, dates), and 42 probable words (田中, 秋山, 復辟, 張勳, 國會, 政府, 孫文 …) in all 2,101 compatible placements; the known keys: shanghai1917, the Yamada table, seven 1916 condenser keys and both 1916 grids. What is left is a renumbered code book, another table structure, or too little text. Dudout also notes a structural lead. If the second sheet of 0511 is shifted by one syllable, four four-letter groups repeat: cafe twice there and once in 0509, and kige , fojy and mafy twice each. A shift of that kind could come from a dropped letter at the join of the two sheets. Transcribed, not decoded. Late May 1916. No key here decoded the five Tokyo → Junzaburo telegrams without the “Thirtyseventh” prefix, or the Shanghai → “Ylchang Tokio” telegrams that use w as a consonant. Dudout found that Tokyo telegrams without a prefix and the Shanghai → “Ylchang” ones are Huang Xing’s traffic, and decodes nine with a table of their own ( section 08 ). Whether all five of the telegrams listed here are among them has not been checked. Two Shanghai → “Ylchang” telegrams, of 29 May and 8 June, from another sender, still do not decode in it. The kana stream of B03050089100 fr. 0076–0078, which the Foreign Ministry’s analysts worked on, is a different system, the three-kana code: two telegrams of 20 May 1916 to Huang Xing, decoded with Tomokiyo’s formula by Harumi-Matsuba (October 2026) and checked here; see Huang Xing’s three-kana telegrams . The Swatow original. Every Latin-letter form in B03050088300 and B03050088400 was examined, and none is from Swatow. The copy in B03050738800 is still the only one found, and its three garbled tail groups stay lost. Undecoded groups. Most long telegrams keep a few groups marked [?]: names that are not in the model, codes one letter from several readings, and supplementary-code characters. The two keys first marked tentative (Honolulu; Manila) are now supported by further telegrams ( section 08 ). About nine codes of the 23 March 1917 telegram, and the identity of the contract and the company, are open. Dudout’s 28 corrections to our March–May 1916 transcriptions are reported above. He checked each one on the scans, and every check is in his re-reading table ( solver/data/relecture-1916.csv ). They have not been checked here one by one, and the per-telegram transcripts in this repository still have the old letters except where this page says otherwise. Numeric codes 和密 and 乾密. A few short numeric telegrams of June 1916 carry these prefixes, or none. They are too short to attack on their own.

BnF fr. 3022 no. 6, catalogued as an anonymous report to the Emperor, is the Marquis del Vasto’s own letter of early December 1527, partly in his Cipher 2: letters shifted one place, with homophones and three-letter code groups. Français 3022 is a sixteenth-century recueil of originals and copies, mostly imperial correspondence of 1527–28 that came into French hands. There are about twenty letters of Juan Pérez, the imperial secretary in Rome, several of them in clear. There are three letters of the Marquis del Vasto (Alfonso d’Ávalos), who commanded the imperial infantry after the Sack of Rome. There are Spanish “avertimientos” of 1528 from Fuenterrabía and Bayonne, and a small bundle of Italian espionage papers. The notice’s folio numbers run about three higher than the ink foliation. Below, folios are the ink numbers and “views” are Gallica’s (ark btv1b90601558). The catalogue says “no decipherment noted”. No contemporary decipherment of no. 6 was found on the leaves or in the eighteenth-century Clairambault copies of this volume’s pieces. The decipherments are modern. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana pages record that George Lasry sent him a solution of no. 10 in 2023. In 2026 Tomokiyo edited it into a Spanish text and published it as “Gasto–Charles V Cipher 1”. That text is not complete: of its 1,146 words, 47 carry a query, 19 of them a bare “?” for a group not decoded, and a few stretches are garbled; Tomokiyo still asks for someone to finish it. He also published Lasry’s preliminary letter-level decryption of a second cipher, used in no. 6 and in no. 19, asking for someone who knows Spanish to finish that too. No. 10 is in that first cipher, a different system from no. 6’s with its own key: Cipher 1, whose key Lasry recovered from no. 10 itself, is a separate cipher from Cipher 2, whose key reads no. 6 and no. 19. No. 10 is mentioned here as context and was not reworked; this page presents Cipher 2 only. BnF fr. 3022 f. 26r, no. 10: del Vasto from Ischia, 27 September 1527. The cipher letters are disguised Latin letters with word divisions kept, which is why Lasry’s solver could recover the key. The piece catalogued as an anonymous report opens in clear: “A seis de noviembre escrivi a V. M. muy largo y tanbien a xxvij de setiembre, cuyos duplicados van con esta”. The clear first page reports the agreement with the Pope for “la libertad suya y de los cardenales” (the capitulation of 26 November) and says that del Vasto is still in Rome only because the Prince of Orange, “el qual se espera que verna de aqui a tres dias”, has not yet arrived to take the command. That puts it in the first days of December 1527. f. 16v: “y por otros se sabe como han buelto sobre Mylan”, then cipher. The first cipher words, dʃfp nnbt qʃftxp , decrypt to creo mas presto . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 16v, via Gallica (btv1b90601558, view 32). The cipher is a Caesar shift of one place over a 21-letter alphabet, with homophones, plus a nomenclator of three-letter groups beginning with b , c or d . Lasry’s decryption has the letter layer right; it checks against the f. 16v ciphertext word for word. It leaves the groups as [doz] , [deh] and so on. His key also pairs a row of syllable signs two to a label (al, con, de, el, es, la, lo, no, para, por, qve, sin), and checked against the glyphs these pairings merge different signs: boz is esto , not “fin” (“y por esto pienso”, “en estos tiempos”); bab is mas ; bar is tan (“tan adelante”, “tan cerca”); bop is como ; bopt , Lasry’s “con s”, is ellos (“porque ellos no tienen gente”); bie is el , not “al”; bis is de ; and bep is es in some places and en in others. Two of his cipher words are not text at all: at stands at every boundary between clear and cipher, going in and coming out, and quia stands before the cipher on f. 17r and f. 41r. They are switch markers. The barred sign ≡ is a stop. The code groups were identified by taking every occurrence of each across nos. 6 and 19 and reading the Spanish around it. All are grade I (inferred from context); none is confirmed by a key or a clear copy. Del Vasto wants the army out of Rome and moving north before Lautrec settles the matter in Lombardy. His plan: secure Siena, “la qual es muy devota de V. M.”; threaten Florence so that the League must come to its aid; take Perugia, “una tierra del Patrimonio muy rica y muy gruesa”, and the state of Urbino, “en el qual se hallará poca resistencia”; and pass into the Marche, “donde no pueden faltar vituallas”. It ends with a warning that runs through all his letters of that winter: “que el exército por lo de advenir no se puede sostener desta manera”, and that with so many shortages “es imposible que el servicio de V. M. se haga como sus fieles vasallos deseamos”.

Every code value above is grade I, inferred from context. The 34 signs not yet deciphered are these. Ten code groups, eleven signs. Each has one or two contexts, and none fits a single value. Blocker: open codes; more contexts are in no. 19 ff. 41–43, which are not yet transcribed. dnh : “porque según la [dnh] no la seguirán en venir tan adelante”. Roma, suggested on 18 September, does not fit. bnq : “dificultoso el bolver y que mas el quedar y [bnq] y finalmente no podrían”. rar (twice): “es ganar en el camino a [rar] y ponella debaxo el mando de V. M.”; “si no los suyços se acogieren [rar]”. Florencia or Luca are candidates; neither is settled. car : “sera poner espanto a [car] y ocasión a estos enemigos”. cny : “en esta empresa servirá … mil [cny]”. bny : “de hazelles hazer [bny] un movimiento”. beb : “podrase ir más fácilmente a socorrella [beb] porque es mejor el camino”. bnc : “podrase tomar apuntamiento [es bnc]”. ge+ : after “como si se estuviese el exército dentro”; possibly a stop. der at 17va.2: “la principal de [der de] país”. Elsewhere der = poca , which does not fit here. Nine short stretches, 23 signs besides the codes. The signs are transcribed, but the syllable values that make sense elsewhere make none here, most likely because Lasry’s labels merge different glyphs, as they do for es/en and con/tan/ellos. Blocker: open codes; they need a glyph-level retranscription of these words. the head of f. 16v, “[y y por] [mq] creo mas presto”; “[en de las los] que más se ha de trabajar”; “el duque de Urbino [es de] otro exército está en Narni y Todi”; “servirá [que de con] mil [cny]”; “irá [que l] camino”; “la principal de [der de] país”; “si caminara en [cnt] parte” ( ninguna or otra ); “se puede esperar [es] más ventaja”; “apuntamiento [es] [bnc]”. A third letter in the same key would settle most of them. No. 19 is one. Lasry decrypted its first leaf; ff. 41r and 41v were searched on the images for the open groups, which gave bet = dello and the switch markers, but ff. 41–43 have not been transcribed in full. CSP Spain III.2 no. 233 summarises its content from a copy in the Salazar collection, not its words, so it gives no crib.
