Galeazzo Visconti, a Milanese captain in French service, wrote from the League armies in Lombardy after the collapse of Lautrec’s expedition to Naples. The letter to Angelo Bolano (fr. 3045 f. 28) has twenty cipher lines, the name Bolano in clear at the head, and a clear close: che sarà la fine de la mia, cum ricomandarme ala sua bona gra[tia]. Da Alexandria ali XV de ottobre 1528 . The letter to Francis I (fr. 3096 f. 91r, the right half of Gallica view 94) opens in clear, Syre: Sapendo , runs nineteen lines in cipher and closes in clear with a plea for his pay, dated in campo in la pieve de Loccate ali XV de Giugno M D XXIX and signed Galeazo Vesconte . fr. 3096 f. 91r, lines 1–5: the clear Syre: Sapendo , then “il timore hano Venetiani di la pace …”; the overbarred code rr stands in line 3. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 91r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 94). The cipher replaces each letter with an invented sign, with homophones for the vowels, a sign written like far , and code groups for names. Lasry’s table and its extension on the Landriano letter gave the letters. These two letters added: a bare Λ doubles the letter after it: queΛla = quella , ceΛsarò = cessarò , tuΛte = tutte , aΛsai = assai ; the dotted Λ is E; the far sign is CHE, and also NTO ( altrotanto , mancamento , quanto ); ρ = F ( fine ); θ is both D ( veda , tarditate , perduta ) and G ( ogni , coligati , Puglia ); q is H ( hano , che ), and F in the letter to the King ( facio , fece , farà ).

In English The Venetians fear the peace, above all being bound to act against the Turk, “which they will never do”. Yesterday [rr] did the office of the King’s good servant with the Duke of Urbino and the Venetian proveditor, assuring them that His Majesty will never abandon the Signoria, and said as much of the Duke of Milan, who will hardly ever feel secure, even with the departure of [48]. The two lords were satisfied all the same. [rr] will report well of the negotiations Visconti conducts, which he will not stop while he lives. He had urged in council that the army should try to force Milan. In his opinion the others will fail through their own shortcomings, raising difficulties at every hour. “And the whole thing, Sire, is heading to no good end.” In clear he begs the King to have his two quarters’ pay sent, for he can no longer live. Six days later Saint-Pol’s army was destroyed at Landriano (21 June 1529).

The Venetians fear the peace (the Cambrai talks, with the Treaty of Barcelona just concluded between the Emperor and the Pope). Above all they fear being bound to act against the Turk, "which they will never do". Yesterday [rr] did the office of the King's good servant with the Duke of Urbino and the Venetian proveditor. He assured them that His Majesty will never abandon the Signoria, and he said as much of the Duke of Milan. The Duke of Milan, Visconti adds, will hardly ever feel secure, even with the arrival or departure ("l'andata") of [48]. Visconti assures the King that the two lords were well satisfied all the same. He had urged in council that, once terms were concluded, the army should try to force Milan. German; the opening, the date and the address are in clear. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 257–259; DECODE R9414, part of catalogue entry 162 (“to unknown recipient, 3 ciphertexts”). The cipher A homophonic alphabet of 42 invented signs, several for each common letter, with a few signs for whole words; it matches no other key in the volume. How it was deciphered A clerk of the time wrote the plain text over lines 6–8 of the first page. Those values seeded a solver (simulated annealing and a search over candidate values with a sixteenth-century German letter model); four passes against the images followed. What it says The Sultan has ordered his pashas to be ready and is arming a hundred thousand men to win Hungary and then turn on Austria; Ferdinand’s party is taking towns; the writer asks the duke to intercede with his brother Wilhelm. Postscript: “der herr Camermaister hat mein ziffer”. Still open The reading stands at 89.2% of its words (measured 24 October 2026). Six bands (P1.12–32, P2.15–19, P3.01–09, P3.39–P4.01, P4.21–35 and the postscript P5.05–07) are decoded, not read: they hold most of the about ten word signs with no key, fifteen blotted words, and about fifty-five legible words whose homophones do not settle. Re-read on 23 October 2026: DECODE R9414 has six images and no attachment, its neighbouring records are other letters in other systems, and no edition is known, so nothing outside the letter can settle them. The lines that read were written out the same day ( r9414/R9414_reading.md , English R9414_en.md ). Until 15 October 2026 this letter shared a page with two others of the same catalogue entry. They are different ciphers, each with its own page: Łaski’s letter of 1531 , in Łaski’s own key, and the Latin letter of 18 April 1533 , in the key of the Sperantio file.

… dan der turkisch kaiser irn herrn befolhen hab das si in aller eil, ieder mit […] pferden gerust sein … The writer describes his journey back into Hungary (“got weis wie mich die rais mit groser sorg ist ankummen”) and the state of Hungarian affairs; envoys of the pashas of Belgrade and Bosnia; the Turkish emperor ordering them to be ready and arming a hundred thousand men to win Hungary and then turn on Austria; Ferdinand’s party taking towns and villages; a copy of the truce “von Lunden”, from the Archbishop of Lund, Charles V’s negotiator with King John. Duke Wilhelm never writes to him, so he asks Ludwig to intercede, citing his service to their father; he writes of his debts and leave, of mining and ore specimens, and of Hans Schwab of Kraków as carrier. The date is in clear: “Datum Wardein … den vierzehenden tag Marcii anno siben und dreissigisten”; the address reads “Herzogen Ludwigen in Bayrn”.

The gloss over lines 6–8 gave the first values of a new homophonic alphabet. A solver (simulated annealing) and a search over candidate values with a language model of sixteenth-century German printed texts brought it to about half; three passes over every line against the image and a search for dictionary words one letter away brought it to 91.3%. A fourth pass on full-resolution crops of every gap (5 October 2026) brought it to 92.2%. A statistical check passes: the reading scores far above random keys and above keys fitted to shuffled text. Łaski’s key, the System A′ key, Augurelio’s key of 1531 and the key of the 1533 letter were tried on it and do not fit.

A barred ∂ at five places fits no letter or short word better than leaving it out: probably a null or a mark. About fifteen words are blotted or struck. Almighty God […] has granted me by His grace that I have come here. Your Princely Grace to … (P1.33-P2.14) … Your Princely Grace, I send you herewith a copy of the truce made again from Lund, [?…] the orator of […] has left, first […] seven weeks ago been sent. In the meantime the Ferdinandists have taken towns […] and several villages, and likewise made a great plan to surprise […], but fortune has [turned] with […], also he […], as Your Princely Grace will learn herewith. Gracious lord, these […] have come here: the embassy of the Pasha of Greek Belgrade and of the Pasha of Bosnia. I have heard their errand [?…]: the lords have dispatched them […] to tell him […] that the Turkish emperor had ordered their lords that they, each with […] horses, should be armed in all haste, and as soon as his beloved brother should summon them […], then march at once and do all that he … (P2.20-P2.37) … [because] of it he will suffer great damage in his hereditary lands. Your Princely Grace will know without doubt how to keep good watch over your lands and people and to load no cost upon yourselves […] [?…] Your Princely Grace with […] bear; may be the […] is not well content that both your Princely Graces write him nothing at all; his […] […] me holds […] nothing has come; I give reasons as I can. For my gracious lord, Your Princely Grace's brother, has to this day neither ordered nor written me anything [?accordingly, since I such] so great danger myself, I beg Your Princely Grace in all most humble trust that you will speak with your brother, my gracious [?prince] and lord, that His Princely Grace will consider that I have stayed on as an old servant of His Princely Grace's lord and father, and such great dang[er] … (P3.10-P3.38) … the advance, that they may […], and serve Your Princely Graces as a faithful countryman and subject, since I know, without boasting in writing, that so much in all matters of war, […] as his in the Empire, be he who he will; then that I have no luck with Your Princely Graces [?not] [?that]. If Your Princely Graces knew as much of the doings of the Turks and the Hungarians as I do, [?it would without doubt wholly] [?…] come to the good of Christendom [?…]. Your Princely Graces, all in the Empire, [are] thus to see that he, for his own profit, will so stir up the Turks and bring Your Princely Grace's land and people such needless costs; yet without […] and all […] potentates of Christendom's help, Your Princely Graces, all in the Empire, would achieve little [?…] [?…] when the great need of the lords is [?…] Your Princely Grace not, that one here, as if all your Princely Graces brought together even a hundred thousand men or more, what you all could do with them, how many also on all waters be […] […] in boatmen's hands [?…] [?…] Your Princely Grace so […] […] […]; so I am driven to it that I must serve beside the Turkish dogs, so that I do not know what can be done at this time in haste. The Turk is arming himself all the while […] for such an expedition; so your graces will all … (P4.02-P4.20) … say with good ground: even if […] a hundred thousand men, what he means to do: his intention is to win Hungary, for Constantinople will certainly […], for he wants to be sure of it, he will […] march; that will hardly […] come, for it will be so provided on land and water that there will be little worry about it; but let all Your Princely Graces hold for certain that the Turks, wherever else the expedition goes, will next march up into Austria and other hereditary lands of his, the […]'s. Who will then defend [?them? I point this out therefore] Your Princely Grace, that you take steps towards a peace with other princes until […] comes out of his affairs and a proper expedition by water and land may then be undertaken, and such cost spared. But how one should set about it, of that I will give Your Princely Graces such a thorough account that [?…] Your Princely Grace and all other soldiers will regard it as … (P4.36-P5.04) Your Princely Grace will [to] this […], who belongs to Hans Schwab of Kraków [?…] [?give], for the letters may come to me […] through the same Schwab […] Your Princely Grace not so much cost on it. I beg Your Princely Grace in all humility […] to keep me and my children commended, as my highest trust in Your Princely Grace stands. I commend myself herewith to Your Princely Graces. Given at Wardein […] the fourteenth day of March in the year thirty-seven.
